subject: Physics
q: A particle moves along a straight line such that its displacement $x$ at any time $t$ is given by $x=\left(t^{3}-6 t^{2}+3 t+4\right)$ meters. The velocity when the acceleration is zero is:
s:
Velocity ( $v$ ) and acceleration ( $a$ ) are found by differentiating displacement ( $x$ ).
$$
v=\frac{d x}{d t}=3 t^{2}-12 t+3
$$
$$
a=\frac{d v}{d t}=6 t-12
$$
Set acceleration to zero: $6 t-12=0 \Longrightarrow t=2 s$. Substitute this time into the velocity equation:
$$
v(t=2)=3(2)^{2}-12(2)+3=12-24+3=-9 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}
$$

subject: Physics
q: The position of a particle is given by $\vec{r}=\left(3 t \hat{i}-2 t^{2} \hat{j}+4 \hat{k}\right) \mathrm{m}$ where $t$ is in seconds. The magnitude of the velocity of the particle at $t=2 \mathrm{~s}$ is:
s:
The velocity vector $\vec{v}$ is the derivative of the position vector $\vec{r}$.
$$
\vec{v}=\frac{d \vec{r}}{d t}=3 \hat{i}-4 t \hat{j}
$$
At $t=2 \mathrm{~s}$, the velocity vector is: $\vec{v}(t=2)=3 \hat{i}-4(2) \hat{j}=3 \hat{i}-8 \hat{j}$. 
The magnitude is: $|\vec{v}|=\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(-8)^{2}}=\sqrt{9+64}=\sqrt{73} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: The relation between time $t$ and distance $x$ is $t=a x^{2}+b x$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. The acceleration is:
s:
Differentiate $t=a x^{2}+b x$ with respect to $t$ :
$$
1=2 a x \frac{d x}{d t}+b \frac{d x}{d t} \Longrightarrow 1=v(2 a x+b) \Longrightarrow v=\frac{1}{2 a x+b}
$$
Differentiate $v$ with respect to $t$ to find acceleration:
$$
a_{a c c}=\frac{d v}{d t}=\frac{-1}{(2 a x+b)^{2}} \cdot\left(2 a \frac{d x}{d t}\right)=-(2 a v) \cdot v^{2}=-2 a v^{3}
$$

subject: Physics
q: A ball is thrown vertically upward. It has a speed of $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ when it has reached one-half of its maximum height. What is the maximum height reached? (Use $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s:
Let max height be $H$. At $H$, final velocity is $0.0^{2}=u^{2}-2 g H \Longrightarrow u^{2}=2 g H$. At $H / 2$, speed is $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} .10^{2}=u^{2}-2 g(H / 2) \Longrightarrow 100=u^{2}-g H$. 
Substituting $u^{2}: 100=2 g H-g H= g H \Longrightarrow H=100 / 10=10 \mathrm{~m}$.

subject: Physics
q:
Refer to the figure. What is the ratio of speed in the first two seconds to the speed in the next four seconds?
 [IMAGE: images/MB000157_1.webp]
s:
Speed is the magnitude of the slope of the displacement-time (S-t) graph.
- Speed in the first 2 seconds $\left(v_{1}\right)$ : The graph is a line from $(0,0)$ to $(2, \mathrm{~s})$.
$$
v_{1}=\frac{\Delta S}{\Delta t}=\frac{s-0}{2-0}=\frac{s}{2}
$$
- Speed in the next 4 seconds $\left(v_{2}\right)$ : The graph is a line from $(2, \mathrm{~s})$ to $(6,0)$. The time interval is from $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}$ to $\mathrm{t}=6 \mathrm{~s}$.
$$
\text { velocity }=\frac{\Delta S}{\Delta t}=\frac{0-s}{6-2}=-\frac{s}{4}
$$
Speed is the magnitude of velocity, so $v_{2}=\left|-\frac{s}{4}\right|=\frac{s}{4}$.
section*{- Ratio of speeds:}
$$
\frac{v_{1}}{v_{2}}=\frac{s / 2}{s / 4}=\frac{s}{2} \times \frac{4}{s}=\frac{4}{2}=2
$$
The ratio $v_{1}: v_{2}$ is $2: 1$.

subject: Physics
q: The displacement $x$ of a particle varies with time $t$ as $x=a e^{-\alpha t}+b e^{\beta t}$, where $a, b, \alpha, \beta$ are positive constants. The velocity of the particle will: [Given ( $b{\beta} > a{\alpha}$ ) ]
s: $v=\frac{d x}{d t}=-a \alpha e^{-\alpha t}+b \beta e^{\beta t}$. As $t$ increases, the first term ( $e^{-\alpha t}$ ) approaches zero while the second term ( $e^{\beta t}$ ) increases exponentially. Thus, the velocity will increase with time.

subject: Physics
q: A particle moves in a straight line with a constant acceleration. It changes its velocity from $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ to $20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ while passing through a distance of 135 m in $t$ seconds. The value of $t$ is:
s:
Using $s=\left(\frac{u+v}{2}\right) t$ :
$$
135=\left(\frac{10+20}{2}\right) t \Longrightarrow 135=15 t \Longrightarrow t=9 \mathrm{~s}
$$

sub_topic: Graphs of motion in a straight line
q:
A train moves from one station to another in 2 hours time. Its speed-time graph during this motion is shown in the figure. The maximum acceleration during the journey is
 [IMAGE: images/MB000162_1.webp]
s:
Acceleration is the slope of the speed-time graph. We need to find the steepest positive slope.
- Segment AB ( $\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{0}$ to $\mathbf{0 . 7 5 h}$ ): $a_{A B}=\frac{20-0}{0.75-0}=\frac{20}{3 / 4} \approx 26.67 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-2}$.
- Segment BC ( $\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{0 . 7 5}$ to $\mathbf{1 . 0 0 h}$ ): The speed is constant, so the slope is $a_{B C}=0$.
- Segment CD ( $\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{1 . 0 0}$ to 1.25h): The speed increases from 20 to $60 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$.
$$
a_{C D}=\frac{60-20}{1.25-1.00}=\frac{40}{0.25}=160 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-2}
$$
- Segment DE ( $\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{1 . 2 5}$ to $\mathbf{2 . 0 0 h}$ ): The speed decreases (deceleration). The slope is negative.
The maximum acceleration occurs during the interval CD and is $160 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-2}$.

subject: Physics
q: Two cars A and B are moving in the same direction with velocities $30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and $20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. When car A is at a distance $d$ behind car B, the driver of car A applies the brake producing a uniform retardation of $2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. There will be no collision when:
s: Relative velocity $u_{\text {rel }}=30-20=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. Relative acceleration $a_{\text {rel }}=-2-0=-2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. For no collision, the relative separation covered before relative velocity becomes zero must be less than $d . v_{\text {rel }}^{2}=u_{\text {rel }}^{2}+2 a_{\text {rel }} s_{\text {rel }} \Longrightarrow 0^{2}=10^{2}+2(-2) s_{\text {rel }} \Longrightarrow s_{\text {rel }}=25 \mathrm{~m}$. Thus, for no collision, the initial separation must be $d>25 \mathrm{~m}$.

subject: Physics
q: The velocity of a particle is $v=v_{0}+g t+f t^{2}$. If its position is $x=0$ at $t=0$, then its displacement after unit time ( $t=1$ ) is:
s: $x=\int v d t=\int\left(v_{0}+g t+f t^{2}\right) d t=v_{0} t+\frac{1}{2} g t^{2}+\frac{1}{3} f t^{3}+C$. Given $x(0)=0 \Longrightarrow C=0$. At $t=1$, $x(1)=v_{0}(1)+\frac{g}{2}(1)^{2}+\frac{f}{3}(1)^{3}=v_{0}+g / 2+f / 3$.

subject: Physics
q: A body travels for 15 seconds starting from rest with constant acceleration. If it travels distances $S_{1}, S_{2}$, and $S_{3}$ in the first five seconds, second five seconds and next five seconds respectively, the relation between $S_{1}, S_{2}$, and $S_{3}$ is:
s: The ratio of distances covered in successive equal time intervals is $1: 3: 5$. Thus, $S_{1}: S_{2}: S_{3}= 1: 3: 5$, which means $S_{1}=S_{2} / 3=S_{3} / 5$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Graphs of motion in a straight line
q:
The velocity $v$ versus $t$ graph of a body in a straight line is as shown in figure The displacement of the body in 5 sec is
 [IMAGE: images/MB000166_1.webp]
s:
Displacement is the net area under the velocity-time graph.
- Area $1(\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{0}$ to $\mathbf{3 s})$ : Triangle above the axis. Base $=3 \mathrm{~s}$, Height $=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.
$$
A_{1}=\frac{1}{2} \times \text { base } \times \text { height }=\frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 2=3 \mathrm{~m}
$$
- Area 2 ( $\mathbf{t}=\mathbf{3}$ to $\mathbf{4 s}$ ): Triangle below the axis. Base $=1 \mathrm{~s}$, Height $=-2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.
$$
A_{2}=\frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times(-2)=-1 \mathrm{~m}
$$
- Area $3(t=4$ to 5 s$)$ : Rectangle above the axis. Base $=1 \mathrm{~s}$, Height $=1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.
$$
A_{3}=1 \times 1=1 \mathrm{~m}
$$
Total displacement $\Delta x=A_{1}+A_{2}+A_{3}=3+(-1)+1=3 \mathrm{~m}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Graphs of motion in a straight line
q:
The diagram shows the displacement-time graph for a particle moving in a straight line. The average velocity for the interval $t=0$ to $t=5$ is
 [IMAGE: images/MB000167_1.webp]
s:
Average velocity is defined as total displacement divided by total time.
$$
v_{\text {avg }}=\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}=\frac{x_{\text {final }}-x_{\text {initial }}}{t_{\text {final }}-t_{\text {initial }}}
$$
From the graph:
- Initial position at $t=0$ is $x_{\text {initial }}=0 \mathrm{~m}$.
- Final position at $t=5$ is $x_{\text {final }}=-10 \mathrm{~m}$.
- The time interval is $\Delta t=5-0=5 \mathrm{~s}$.
$$
v_{a v g}=\frac{-10-0}{5-0}=\frac{-10}{5}=-2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}
$$

subject: Physics
q: The motion of a particle is described by the equation $x=a+b t^{2}$ where $a=15 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $b=3 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. Its instantaneous velocity at time $t=3 \mathrm{~s}$ will be:
s: $v=\frac{d x}{d t}=2 b t$. At $t=3 s, v=2(3)(3)=18 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: If a car at rest accelerates uniformly to a speed of $144 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$ in 20 s , it covers a distance of:
s: $v=144 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h} \times \frac{5}{18}=40 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} . u=0 . s=\left(\frac{u+v}{2}\right) t=\left(\frac{0+40}{2}\right) \times 20=400 \mathrm{~m}$.

subject: Physics
q: A particle moves along a path such that its displacement is given by $x^{2}=t^{2}+1$. Its acceleration is given by:
s: Differentiating $x^{2}=t^{2}+1$ w.r.t. time: $2 x \frac{d x}{d t}=2 t \Longrightarrow x v=t$. Differentiating again: $v \cdot v+x \cdot a=1 \Longrightarrow v^{2}+x a=1$. $a=\frac{1-v^{2}}{x}$. Substitute $v=t / x$ : $a=\frac{1-(t / x)^{2}}{x}=\frac{x^{2}-t^{2}}{x^{3}}$. From the original equation, $x^{2}-t^{2}=1$, so $a=\frac{1}{x^{3}}$.

subject: Physics
q: A person travelling on a straight line moves with a uniform velocity $v_{1}$ for some time and with a uniform velocity $v_{2}$ for the next equal time. The average velocity is $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. If $v_{1}=6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, then $v_{2}$ is_______ $$\left( {{\text{in}}\,m/s} \right)$$.
s:
For equal time intervals, $v_{a v g}=\frac{v_{1}+v_{2}}{2}$.
$$
10=\frac{6+v_{2}}{2} \Longrightarrow 20=6+v_{2} \Longrightarrow v_{2}=14 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}
$$

subject: Physics
q: The position of a particle along the x -axis is given by $x=t^{3}-6 t^{2}+5 t$. The magnitude of velocity of the particle when its acceleration becomes zero is______$\qquad$(in $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$).
s: $v=\frac{d x}{d t}=3 t^{2}-12 t+5 . \quad a=\frac{d v}{d t}=6 t-12$. Set $a=0 \Longrightarrow \quad 6 t-12=0 \Longrightarrow t=2 s$. $v(2)=3(2)^{2}-12(2)+5=12-24+5=-7 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The magnitude is $|-7|=7 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: The velocity of a particle moving on the x -axis is given by $v=3 \sqrt{x}$. The acceleration of the particle is $\alpha$ $ m / s^{2}$.Find value of 2$\alpha$. (Assume particle starts from $x>0$ )
s:
Use $ a =v \frac{d v}{d x}$. Given $v=3 x^{1 / 2}$. $\frac{d v}{d x}=3 \times \frac{1}{2} x^{-1 / 2}=\frac{1.5}{\sqrt{x}} . a=(3 \sqrt{x})\left(\frac{1.5}{\sqrt{x}}\right)=4.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. 2

$\alpha$ = 2 x 4.5 = 9$\mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$

subject: Physics
q: A car moving with a speed of $54 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$ is brought to rest in a distance of 22.5 m . The uniform retardation is________ $$({\text{in}}\quad \;\;\;m/{s^2})$$.
s: $u=54 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}=15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} . v=0, s=22.5 \mathrm{~m}$. Using $v^{2}=u^{2}+2 a s \Longrightarrow 0=15^{2}+2 a(22.5) \Longrightarrow 0=225+45$ a. $a=-5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. Retardation is $5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$.

subject: Physics
q: A stone is dropped from a tower of height 125 m . The time taken to reach the ground is__________ $$({\text{in}}\quad \;\;\;s)$$. (Use $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: Using $s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$. $125=0 \cdot t+\frac{1}{2}(10) t^{2} \Longrightarrow 125=5 t^{2} \Longrightarrow t^{2}=25 \Longrightarrow t=5 \mathrm{~s}$.

subject: Physics
q: A projectile is thrown with an initial kinetic energy $K$. If it is projected at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal, its kinetic energy at the highest point will be:
s: At the highest point, the velocity is $v^{\prime}=v \cos \theta$. The kinetic energy is $K^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2} m(v \cos \theta)^{2}= \left(\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}\right) \cos ^{2} \theta=K \cos ^{2}\left(30^{\circ}\right)=K\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{3 K}{4}$.

subject: Physics
q: A ball of mass 500 g is projected with a velocity of $30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. The change in kinetic energy from the point of projection to the highest point is: ( $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: The decrease in kinetic energy is equal to the initial vertical kinetic energy: $\Delta K= \frac{1}{2} m(u \sin \theta)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(0.5)\left(30 \sin 60^{\circ}\right)^{2}=0.25 \times(15 \sqrt{3})^{2}=168.75 \mathrm{~J}$.

subject: Physics
q: Two projectiles are fired with the same initial speed at angles $30^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. The ratio of their maximum heights, $H_{30}: H_{60}$, is:
s:
Maximum height $H=\frac{u^{2} \sin ^{2} \theta}{2 g}$, so $H \propto \sin ^{2} \theta$. 
The ratio is $\frac{H_{30}}{H_{60}}=\frac{\sin ^{2} 30^{\circ}}{\sin ^{2} 60^{\circ}}=\frac{(1 / 2)^{2}}{(\sqrt{3} / 2)^{2}}= \frac{1 / 4}{3 / 4}=\frac{1}{3}$.

subject: Physics
q: Two projectiles are fired from the ground with the same initial speed at angles $\left(45^{\circ}-\theta\right)$ and ( $45^{\circ}+\theta$ ) with the horizontal. The ratio of their times of flight is:
s: Time of flight $T \propto \sin \alpha$. The ratio is $\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}=\frac{\sin \left(45^{\circ}-\theta\right)}{\sin \left(45^{\circ}+\theta\right)}=\frac{\sin 45 \cos \theta-\cos 45 \sin \theta}{\sin 45 \cos \theta+\cos 45 \sin \theta}= \frac{\cos \theta-\sin \theta}{\cos \theta+\sin \theta}=\frac{1-\tan \theta}{1+\tan \theta}$.

subject: Physics
q: The speed of a projectile at its maximum height is half of its initial speed. The angle of projection $\theta$ is:
s: At the maximum height, speed is $v_{x}=u \cos \theta$. Given $u \cos \theta=u / 2$, so $\cos \theta=1 / 2$, which means $\theta=60^{\circ}$.

subject: Physics
q: For a projectile, the horizontal range is four times the maximum height. The angle of projection is:
s: Given $R=4 H \Longrightarrow \frac{u^{2} \sin (2 \theta)}{g}=4\left(\frac{u^{2} \sin ^{2} \theta}{2 g}\right) \Longrightarrow 2 \sin \theta \cos \theta=2 \sin ^{2} \theta \Longrightarrow \tan \theta= 1 \Longrightarrow \theta=45^{\circ}$.

subject: Physics
q: At the highest point of a projectile's trajectory, which of the following is zero?
s: At the highest point, the projectile momentarily stops moving upward before falling down, so its vertical component of velocity ( $v_{y}$ ) is zero.

subject: Physics
q: A stone is projected from the top of a tower horizontally. It strikes the ground at a distance $R$ from the foot of the tower. If the tower's height is doubled, the new horizontal range will be:
s: Range $R=u T=u \sqrt{\frac{2 H}{g}}$. Thus, $R \propto \sqrt{H}$. If height becomes $H^{\prime}=2 H$, the new range will be $R^{\prime}=R \sqrt{2}$.

subject: Physics
q: From a certain height, ball A is dropped and ball B is thrown horizontally with some velocity. Which of the following is true?
o: Ball A reaches the ground first.
Ball B reaches the ground first.
Both balls reach the ground simultaneously.
Depends on the mass of the balls.
s: The time to reach the ground depends only on the initial vertical velocity and the height. Both balls have an initial vertical velocity of zero and fall from the same height, so their time of flight is identical ( $t=\sqrt{2 h / g}$ ).

subject: Physics
q: An airplane flying horizontally at an altitude of 500 m with a speed of $720 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$ releases a food packet. What is the horizontal distance it travels before hitting the ground? (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: First, convert speed: $v=720 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}=200 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The time to fall is $t=\sqrt{2 h / g}= \sqrt{2 \times 500 / 10}=10 \mathrm{~s}$. The horizontal range is $x=v \times t=200 \times 10=2000 \mathrm{~m}=2 \mathrm{~km}$.

subject: Physics
q: For two projectiles A and B thrown with the same initial velocity, the ratio of their times of flight $T_{A} / T_{B}=3$. The ratio of their maximum heights $H_{A} / H_{B}$ will be:
s: Since $T=\frac{2 u \sin \theta}{g}$ and $H=\frac{u^{2} \sin ^{2} \theta}{2 g}$, we can see that $H \propto(u \sin \theta)^{2}$ and $T \propto u \sin \theta$. Therefore, $H \propto T^{2}$. The ratio $\frac{H_{A}}{H_{B}}=\left(\frac{T_{A}}{T_{B}}\right)^{2}=3^{2}=9$.

subject: Physics
q: The trajectory of a projectile is given by the equation $y=12 x-\frac{3}{4} x^{2}$. The horizontal range of the projectile is:
s: The equation of trajectory can be written as $y=x \tan \theta\left(1-\frac{x}{R}\right)$. Factoring out $12 x$, we get $y=12 x\left(1-\frac{x}{16}\right)$. Comparing the two forms, the range $R=16 \mathrm{~m}$.

subject: Physics
q: A stone is projected with a speed of $20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. Its speed at the highest point of its trajectory is:
s: The speed at the highest point is only the horizontal component of the initial velocity, $v_{x}=u \cos \theta=20 \cos 60^{\circ}=20 \times \frac{1}{2}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: A body of mass 2 kg has an initial velocity of $(20 \hat{i}+30 \hat{j}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$. The magnitude of change in its momentum from the point of projection until it reaches the highest point is: (x axis is horizontal and y axis is vertical)
s: The change in momentum is $\Delta \vec{p}=m\left(\vec{v}_{f}-\vec{v}_{i}\right)$. Here, $\vec{v}_{i}=(20 \hat{i}+30 \hat{j})$ and at the highest point, $\vec{v}_{f}=20 \hat{i}$. So, $\Delta \vec{p}=2((20 \hat{i})-(20 \hat{i}+30 \hat{j}))=-60 \hat{j} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The magnitude is $60 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: The time $t$ at which the velocity vector of a projectile is perpendicular to its initial velocity vector is given by:
s:
For the vectors to be perpendicular, their dot product is zero. \[\vec u \cdot \vec v(t) = 0\]
\[\left( {{u_x}\hat i + {u_y}\hat j} \right) \cdot \left( {{u_x}\hat i + \left( {{u_y} - gt} \right)\hat j} \right) = 0\]
\[u_x^2 + {u_y}\left( {{u_y} - gt} \right) = 0\]
\[u_x^2 + u_y^2 - {u_y}gt = 0\]
\[{u^2} = {u_y}gt\]
\[t = \frac{{{u^2}}}{{g{u_y}}} = \frac{{{u^2}}}{{gu\sin \theta }} = \frac{u}{{g\sin \theta }}\]

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Introduction to motion in a plane
q: A body of mass 1 kg is moving with a velocity of $5 \hat{i} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. A constant force of $10 \hat{j} \mathrm{~N}$ starts acting on it for 2 seconds. The final velocity of the body is:
s: Acceleration $\vec{a}=\vec{F} / m=10 \hat{j} / 1=10 \hat{j} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. Using $\vec{v}_{f}=\vec{v}_{i}+\vec{a} t$, we get $\vec{v}_{f}= 5 \hat{i}+(10 \hat{j})(2)=(5 \hat{i}+20 \hat{j}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: A particle is projected such that its horizontal range is 3 times its maximum height. The angle of projection is $\theta$. Then $\tan \theta$ is equal to:
s: Given $R=3 H \Longrightarrow \frac{u^{2} \sin (2 \theta)}{g}=3\left(\frac{u^{2} \sin ^{2} \theta}{2 g}\right) \Longrightarrow 2 \sin \theta \cos \theta=\frac{3}{2} \sin ^{2} \theta \Longrightarrow 4 \cos \theta= 3 \sin \theta \Longrightarrow \tan \theta=4 / 3$.

subject: Physics
q: A projectile is fired at $30^{\circ}$ to the vertical. The horizontal range is 200 m . If it is fired with the same speed at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, its range will be:
s: An angle of $30^{\circ}$ to the vertical is equivalent to $90^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. Since $30^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$ are complementary angles, their horizontal ranges are identical for the same initial speed. Thus, the range will still be 200 m .

subject: Physics
q: The horizontal range and maximum height of a projectile are $R$ and $H$ respectively. If a constant horizontal acceleration $a=g / 2$ is imparted to the projectile due to wind, then its new horizontal range will be:
s: The time of flight $T=\frac{2 u_{y}}{g}$ is unaffected by horizontal acceleration. The new range is $R^{\prime}=u_{x} T+\frac{1}{2} a T^{2}=R+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{g}{2}\right)\left(\frac{2 u_{y}}{g}\right)^{2}=R+\frac{g}{4} \frac{4 u_{y}^{2}}{g^{2}}=R+\frac{u_{y}^{2}}{g}$. Since $H=\frac{u_{y}^{2}}{2 g}$, then $\frac{u_{y}^{2}}{g}=2 H$. Therefore, $R^{\prime}=R+2 H$.

subject: Physics
q: A man can throw a stone to a maximum horizontal distance of 100 m . The maximum height to which he can throw the stone is:
s: Maximum horizontal range is $R_{\text {max }}=u^{2} / g$, which is given as 100 m . The maximum possible height is achieved when the stone is thrown vertically upwards $\left(\theta=90^{\circ}\right)$, so $H_{\text {max }}= u^{2} /(2 g)$. Thus, $H_{\text {max }}=\left(u^{2} / g\right) / 2=100 / 2=50 \mathrm{~m}$.

subject: Physics
q:
A ball rolls off the top of a stairway with a horizontal velocity $u=\sqrt{x} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The steps are 0.2 m high and 0.2 m wide. The ball just hits the edge of the 4th step. The value of $x$ is
$\qquad$ (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: To hit the edge of the 4th step, the horizontal distance traveled is $x_{\text {dist }}=4 \times 0.2=0.8$ m and the vertical distance is $y_{\text {dist }}=4 \times 0.2=0.8 \mathrm{~m}$. From vertical motion, $y_{\text {dist }}=\frac{1}{2} g t^{2} \Longrightarrow 0.8=\frac{1}{2}(10) t^{2} \Longrightarrow t^{2}=0.16 \Longrightarrow t=0.4 \mathrm{~s}$. From horizontal motion, $x_{\text {dist }}=u t \Longrightarrow 0.8= u(0.4) \Longrightarrow u=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. Since $u=\sqrt{x}$, we have $u^{2}=x \Longrightarrow 2^{2}=4$.

subject: Physics
q: The maximum height reached by a projectile is 80 m . If the initial projection velocity is doubled, the new maximum height of the projectile will be (in $\qquad$ m).
s: Maximum height $H=\frac{u^{2} \sin ^{2} \theta}{2 g}$, which means $H \propto u^{2}$. If the velocity $u$ is doubled, the height becomes $2^{2}=4$ times larger. The new height is $H^{\prime}=4 \times 80=320 \mathrm{~m}$.

subject: Physics
q: A plane is flying horizontally at an altitude of 500 m with a speed of $100 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. It drops a supply package to a team on the ground. The horizontal distance travelled by the package, as it moves from the plane to the ground, is (in $\qquad$ km) . (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: The time taken to fall 500 m is $t=\sqrt{\frac{2 h}{g}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 \times 500}{10}}=\sqrt{100}=10 \mathrm{~s}$. The horizontal distance (range) is $R=v \times t=100 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \times 10 \mathrm{~s}=1000 \mathrm{~m}$, which is equal to 1 km .

subject: Physics
q: A particle is projected such that the vertical component of its initial velocity is 30 $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$. The height traversed by the particle in the last second of its ascent is (in $\qquad$ m). (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: The time to reach maximum height is $t_{u p}=u_{y} / g=30 / 10=3 \mathrm{~s}$. The last second of ascent is the 3rd second of its motion. The distance travelled in the $n^{t h}$ second is $s_{n}=u_{y}-\frac{g}{2}(2 n-1)$. For the 3 rd second, $h_{3 r d}=30-\frac{10}{2}(2(3)-1)=30-5(5)=5 \mathrm{~m}$.

subject: Physics
q: A ball of mass 200 g is projected with a velocity of $40 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. The decrease in kinetic energy of the ball during its motion from the point of projection to the highest point is (in $\qquad$ J).
s: The decrease in kinetic energy equals the initial kinetic energy of the vertical motion component. The vertical velocity is $u_{y}=u \sin \theta=40 \sin 30^{\circ}=40 \times 0.5=20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The decrease in KE is $\Delta K=\frac{1}{2} m\left(u_{y}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(0.2 \mathrm{~kg})(20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s})^{2}=0.1 \times 400=40 \mathrm{~J}$.

subject: Physics
q:
Three blocks with masses $m, 2 m$, and $3 m$ are connected by strings and are pulled by a force $F$ on a frictionless horizontal surface. What is the tension $T_{1}$ in the string between the $2 m$ and $3 m$ blocks?
 [IMAGE: images/MB000226_1.webp]
s: The total mass of the system is $M_{\text {total }}=m+2 m+3 m=6 m$. The acceleration of the system is $a=\frac{F}{M_{\text {total }}}=\frac{F}{6 m}$. The tension $T_{1}$ pulls the first two masses ( $m$ and $2 m$ ). Therefore, $T_{1}=(m+2 m) a=3 m \times\left(\frac{F}{6 m}\right)=\frac{F}{2}$.

subject: Physics
q: A light string passing over a smooth light pulley connects two blocks of masses $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$. If the ratio of masses $\frac{m_{1}}{m_{2}}=\frac{3}{5}$, what is the acceleration of the system?
s: The formula for acceleration in an Atwood machine is $a=\frac{\left(m_{2}-m_{1}\right) g}{m_{1}+m_{2}}$. Given $\frac{m_{1}}{m_{2}}=\frac{3}{5}$, let $m_{1}=3 k$ and $m_{2}=5 k$. Then $a=\frac{(5 k-3 k) g}{3 k+5 k}=\frac{2 k g}{8 k}=\frac{g}{4}$.

subject: Physics
q: The position of a 2 kg particle is given by $x(t)=3 t^{2}-2 t+1$ meters. The force acting on the particle at $t=2 \mathrm{~s}$ is:
s: Velocity is $v(t)=\frac{d x}{d t}=6 t-2$. Acceleration is $a(t)=\frac{d v}{d t}=6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. Since acceleration is constant, the force is $F=m a=2 \mathrm{~kg} \times 6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}=12 \mathrm{~N}$.

subject: Physics
q: A body of mass 5 kg is acted upon by two perpendicular forces of 8 N and 6 N . The magnitude of the acceleration of the body is:
s: The net force is the vector sum of the perpendicular forces: $F_{\text {net }}=\sqrt{8^{2}+6^{2}}= \sqrt{64+36}=\sqrt{100}=10 \mathrm{~N}$. According to Newton's second law, $a=\frac{F_{\text {net }}}{m}=\frac{10 \mathrm{~N}}{5 \mathrm{~kg}}=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$.

subject: Physics
q: A person of mass 60 kg is inside a lift of mass 940 kg and presses the button on the control panel. The lift starts moving upwards with an acceleration of $1.0 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. If $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$, the tension in the supporting cable is:
s: The total mass to be supported is $M=60+940=1000 \mathrm{~kg}$. For upward acceleration, the tension $T$ must overcome gravity and provide the acceleration: $T-M g= M a \Longrightarrow T=M(g+a)=1000(10+1)=11000 \mathrm{~N}$.

subject: Physics
q:
Find the values of tensions $\mathrm{T}_{1}$ & $\mathrm{T}_{2}$ as shown in fig. $\mathrm{T}_{1}$ is the tension in the left inclined string and 

$\mathrm{T}_{2}$ is the tension in right inclined string.
 [IMAGE: images/MB000231_1.webp]
s:
Let $T_{1}$ be the tension in the string making a $60^{\circ}$ angle with the horizontal and $T_{2}$ be the tension in the string making a $30^{\circ}$ angle. The system is in equilibrium, so the net force is zero. We resolve forces into horizontal (x) and vertical (y) components.
- Horizontal Equilibrium $\left(\Sigma F_{x}=0\right)$ :
$$
T_{2} \cos \left(30^{\circ}\right)-T_{1} \cos \left(60^{\circ}\right)=0 \Longrightarrow T_{2} \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=T_{1} \frac{1}{2} \Longrightarrow T_{1}=T_{2} \sqrt{3}
$$
- Vertical Equilibrium $\left(\Sigma F_{y}=0\right)$ :
$$
T_{1} \sin \left(60^{\circ}\right)+T_{2} \sin \left(30^{\circ}\right)-200=0 \Longrightarrow T_{1} \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+T_{2} \frac{1}{2}=200
$$
Substitute $T_{1}$ from the first equation into the second:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(T_{2} \sqrt{3}\right) \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{T_{2}}{2}=200 \Longrightarrow \frac{3 T_{2}}{2}+\frac{T_{2}}{2}=200 \\
& \frac{4 T_{2}}{2}=200 \Longrightarrow 2 T_{2}=200 \Longrightarrow T_{2}=100 \mathrm{~N}
\end{aligned}
$$
Now find $T_{1}$ :
$$
T_{1}=100 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~N}
$$
The tensions are $100 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~N}$ and 100 N .

subject: Physics
q:
Three equal weights of mass $m$ each are hanging on a string passing over a fixed pulley as shown in Fig. What are the tensions in the string connecting weights A to B and B to C ?
 [IMAGE: images/MB000232_1.webp]
s:
First, find the acceleration of the system.
- Mass on the left side: $m_{L}=m_{A}=m$.
- Mass on the right side: $m_{R}=m_{B}+m_{C}=2 m$.
- The net force driving the motion is $F_{n e t}=\left(m_{R}-m_{L}\right) g=(2 m-m) g=m g$.
- The total mass being accelerated is $M_{\text {total }}=m_{A}+m_{B}+m_{C}=3 m$.
- The acceleration is $a=\frac{F_{n e t}}{M_{\text {total }}}=\frac{m g}{3 m}=\frac{g}{3}$. Block A accelerates up, while B and C accelerate down. Now, find the tensions by analyzing the forces on individual blocks.
- Tension $T_{1}$ : Consider block A, which accelerates upwards.
$$
T_{1}-m_{A} g=m_{A} a \Longrightarrow T_{1}=m(g+a)=m(g+g / 3)=\frac{4 m g}{3}
$$
- Tension $T_{2}$ : Consider block C , which accelerates downwards.
$$
m_{C} g-T_{2}=m_{C} a \Longrightarrow T_{2}=m(g-a)=m(g-g / 3)=\frac{2 m g}{3}
$$

subject: Physics
q:
A balloon with mass $M$ is descending down with
an acceleration $a(a<g)$. How much mass should be removed from it so that it
starts moving up with an acceleration $a$ ?
s: Let the buoyant force (upthrust) be $T$. When descending: $M g-T=M a \Longrightarrow T=M(g-a)$. Let mass $m$ be removed. The new mass is $M^{\prime}=M-m$. When ascending: $T-M^{\prime} g=M^{\prime} a \Longrightarrow T=M^{\prime}(g+a)$. Equating the two expressions for $T$ : $M(g-a)=(M-m)(g+a)$. Solving for $m$ gives $m=\frac{2 M a}{g+a}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Addition of vectors using triangles law
q: The resultant of two forces, one double the other in magnitude, is perpendicular to the smaller of the two forces. The angle between the two forces is:
s: Let the forces be $\vec{F}$ and $2 \vec{F}$, and the angle between them be $\theta$. The resultant is $\vec{R}=\vec{F}+2 \vec{F}$. We are given $\vec{R} \cdot \vec{F}=0$. So, $(\vec{F}+2 \vec{F}) \cdot \vec{F}=0 \Longrightarrow \vec{F} \cdot \vec{F}+2 \vec{F} \cdot \vec{F}=0 \Longrightarrow F^{2}+2 F^{2} \cos \theta=0$. Since $F \neq 0,1+2 \cos \theta=0 \Longrightarrow \cos \theta=-1 / 2 \Longrightarrow \theta=120^{\circ}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Addition of vectors using triangles law
q: The resultant of two vectors $\vec{A}+\vec{B}$ and $\vec{A}-\vec{B}$ is:
s: The resultant is the sum of the vectors: $(\vec{A}+\vec{B})+(\vec{A}-\vec{B})=\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{A}-\vec{B}=2 \vec{A}$.

subject: Physics
q: A man weighing 80 kg is standing on a weighing scale in a lift which is moving upwards with a uniform acceleration of $5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. What would be the reading on the scale? (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: The reading on the scale is the normal force $N$. For upward acceleration, $N-m g=m a \Longrightarrow N=m(g+a)=80(10+5)=80 \times 15=1200 \mathrm{~N}$.

subject: Physics
q: A pendulum bob of mass $m$ is pulled aside by a horizontal force $F$ such that it makes an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the vertical. The magnitude of the force $F$ is:
s: Let $T$ be the tension in the string. In equilibrium, the forces balance. Vertically: $T \cos 60^{\circ}=m g$. Horizontally: $T \sin 60^{\circ}=F$. From the vertical equation, $T=\frac{m g}{\cos 60^{\circ}}=\frac{m g}{1 / 2}=2 m g$. Substituting into the horizontal equation: $F=(2 m g) \sin 60^{\circ}= 2 m g\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=m g \sqrt{3}$.

subject: Physics
q: A vector $\vec{C}$ has the same magnitude as $\vec{A}=3 \hat{i}+4 \hat{j}$ and is parallel to $\vec{B}=6 \hat{i}+8 \hat{j}$. The vector $\vec{C}$ is:
s: The magnitude of $\vec{A}$ is $|\vec{A}|=\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}=5$. The unit vector in the direction of $\vec{B}$ is $\hat{B}=\frac{6 \hat{i}+8 \hat{j}}{\sqrt{6^{2}+8^{2}}}=\frac{6 \hat{i}+8 \hat{j}}{10}=\frac{3 \hat{i}+4 \hat{j}}{5}$. The vector $\vec{C}$ is given by its magnitude multiplied by its direction: $\vec{C}=|\vec{A}| \hat{B}=5 \times \frac{3 \hat{i}+4 \hat{j}}{5}=3 \hat{i}+4 \hat{j}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Addition of vectors using triangles law
q: If $|\vec{A}+\vec{B}|=|\vec{A}-\vec{B}|$, the angle between vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is:
s: Squaring both sides gives $|\vec{A}+\vec{B}|^{2}=|\vec{A}-\vec{B}|^{2}$. This expands to $A^{2}+B^{2}+ 2 \vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}=A^{2}+B^{2}-2 \vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}$. This simplifies to $4 \vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}=0$, which means $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}=0$. The dot product is zero when the vectors are perpendicular, so the angle is $90^{\circ}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Addition of vectors using triangles law
q: If the resultant of two vectors $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{P}$ and has a magnitude equal to half of the magnitude of $\vec{Q}$, then the angle between $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ is:
s: Let $\vec{R}=\vec{P}+\vec{Q}$. We are given $\vec{R} \cdot \vec{P}=0$ and $|\vec{R}|=Q / 2$. From the dot product: $(\vec{P}+\vec{Q}) \cdot \vec{P}=0 \Longrightarrow P^{2}+P Q \cos \theta=0$. From the magnitude: $|\vec{P}+\vec{Q}|^{2}=R^{2} \Longrightarrow P^{2}+ Q^{2}+2 P Q \cos \theta=(Q / 2)^{2}$. From the first relation, $P Q \cos \theta=-P^{2}$. Substitute this into the second: $P^{2}+Q^{2}+2\left(-P^{2}\right)=Q^{2} / 4 \Longrightarrow Q^{2}-P^{2}=Q^{2} / 4 \Longrightarrow 3 Q^{2} / 4=P^{2} \Longrightarrow P= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} Q$. Now substitute this back into $P^{2}+P Q \cos \theta=0:\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} Q\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} Q\right) Q \cos \theta=0 \Longrightarrow \frac{3}{4} Q^{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} Q^{2} \cos \theta=0$. Dividing by $Q^{2}$ gives $\frac{3}{4}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cos \theta=0 \Longrightarrow \cos \theta=-\frac{3 / 4}{\sqrt{3} / 2}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Thus, $\theta=150^{\circ}$.

subject: Physics
q:
Three masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}$ are connected by light strings and are pulled as shown in the figure, then find the incorrect statement?
 [IMAGE: images/MB000241_1.webp]
s:
First, we find the acceleration of the entire system.
- The total mass of the system is $M=m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}$.
- The net force acting on the system is F.
- The acceleration of the system is $a=\frac{F}{M}=\frac{F}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}$.
Now, we find the tensions by considering subsystems.
- Tension $T_{1}: T_{1}$ is the force that accelerates mass $m_{1}$.
$$
T_{1}=m_{1} a=\frac{m_{1} F}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}
$$
- Tension $T_{2}: T_{2}$ is the force that accelerates the combined mass of $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$.
$$
T_{2}=\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right) a=\frac{\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right) F}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}
$$

subject: Physics
q: A body of mass 5 kg undergoes a change in velocity from $(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ to $(4 \hat{i}-1 \hat{j}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ in 2 seconds. The magnitude of the average force acting on it is:
s: The change in velocity is $\Delta \vec{v}=\vec{v}_{f}-\vec{v}_{i}=(4 \hat{i}-\hat{j})-(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j})=2 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$. The average acceleration is $\vec{a}=\frac{\Delta \vec{v}}{\Delta t}=\frac{2 \hat{i}-4 \hat{j}}{2}=\hat{i}-2 \hat{j} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. The average force is $\vec{F}=m \vec{a}=5(\hat{i}-2 \hat{j})=5 \hat{i}-10 \hat{j} \mathrm{~N}$. The magnitude is $|\vec{F}|=\sqrt{5^{2}+(-10)^{2}}=\sqrt{25+100}= \sqrt{125}=5 \sqrt{5} \mathrm{~N}$.

subject: Physics
q: The angle between the vectors $\vec{A}=\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{B}=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2 \hat{k}$ is:
s: We use the dot product formula: $\cos \theta=\frac{\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}}{|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|} \cdot \vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}=(1)(-1)+(2)(1)+ (-1)(-2)=-1+2+2=3 .|\vec{A}|=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{6} .|\vec{B}|=\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+1^{2}+(-2)^{2}}= \sqrt{6} . \cos \theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt{6} \sqrt{6}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$. Thus, $\theta=60^{\circ}$.

subject: Physics
q: A bullet of mass 20 g moving with a velocity of $500 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ strikes a tree and goes out from the other side with a velocity of $400 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. If the bullet passes through the tree in 1 ms , the average resistance offered by the tree is:
s: The average force is the rate of change of momentum: $F=\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}=\frac{m\left(v_{i}-v_{f}\right)}{\Delta t}$. Note we use $v_{i}-v_{f}$ for the magnitude of resistive force. $m=20 \mathrm{~g}=0.02 \mathrm{~kg}, \Delta t= 1 \mathrm{~ms}=10^{-3} \mathrm{~s} . F=\frac{0.02 \mathrm{~kg} \times(500-400) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}}{10^{-3} \mathrm{~s}}=\frac{0.02 \times 100}{10^{-3}}=\frac{2}{10^{-3}}=2000 \mathrm{~N}$.

subject: Physics
q: Two blocks of mass 2 kg and 4 kg are connected by a string and pulled by a force of 36 N on a smooth horizontal surface (force applied to the 4 kg block). The tension in the string between the blocks is $T$. The value of $T / 3$ is:
s: The total mass is $M=2+4=6 \mathrm{~kg}$. The system acceleration is $a= \frac{F}{M}=\frac{36}{6}=6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. The tension $T$ is the force that accelerates the 2 kg block. So, $T=m_{2 k g} \times a=2 \times 6=12 \mathrm{~N}$. The value of $T / 3$ is $12 / 3=4$.

subject: Physics
q: For the vectors $\vec{A}=2 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}, \vec{B}=\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-3 \hat{k}$ and $\vec{C}=3 \hat{i}+p \hat{j}+5 \hat{k}$ to be coplanar, the value of $p$ is $-x$. Find the integer value of $x$.
s: For three vectors to be coplanar, their scalar triple product must be zero: $\vec{A} \cdot(\vec{B} \times \vec{C})=0$. This is calculated using the determinant: $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & p & 5\end{array}\right|=0.2(10- (-3 p))-(-1)(5-(-9))+1(p-6)=0.2(10+3 p)+1(14)+(p-6)=0.20+6 p+14+p-6=$ 0 . $7 p+28=0 \Longrightarrow 7 p=-28 \Longrightarrow p=-4$. Since $p=-x$, we have $-4=-x$, so $x=4$.

subject: Physics
q: Two blocks of masses 2 kg and 3 kg are connected by a light string and are pulled upwards by a force of 60 N .Force is applied on 3 kg block. Find the tension in the string connecting the two masses. (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: The total mass is $M=2+3=5 \mathrm{~kg}$. The net upward force is $F_{n e t}=60-M g= 60-5(10)=10 \mathrm{~N}$. The upward acceleration is $a=F_{\text {net }} / M=10 / 5=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. To find the tension $T$ in the string, consider the free body diagram of the lower ( 2 kg ) mass: $T-m_{\text {lower }} g=m_{\text {lower }} a \Longrightarrow T=2(10)+2(2)=20+4=24 \mathrm{~N}$.

subject: Physics
q: For two vectors, if $|\vec{a}|=n|\vec{b}|,|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|=\sqrt{2}|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|$, and the angle between them is $\theta=\cos ^{-1}(5 / 9)$, find the integer value of $n$.
s: Square the given relation: $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|^{2}=2|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^{2} . a^{2}+b^{2}+2 a b \cos \theta=2\left(a^{2}+b^{2}-\right. 2 a b \cos \theta) . a^{2}+b^{2}+2 a b \cos \theta=2 a^{2}+2 b^{2}-4 a b \cos \theta . a^{2}+b^{2}-6 a b \cos \theta=0$. Substitute $a=n b$ and $\cos \theta=5 / 9:(n b)^{2}+b^{2}-6(n b) b(5 / 9)=0 . n^{2} b^{2}+b^{2}-\frac{10}{3} n b^{2}=0$. Divide by $b^{2}$ (since $b \neq 0$ ): $n^{2}+1-\frac{10}{3} n=0$. Multiply by 3: $3 n^{2}-10 n+3=0$. Factor the quadratic: $(3 n-1)(n-3)=0$. The solutions are $n=1 / 3$ and $n=3$. The required integer value is $n=3$.

subject: Physics
q: A wooden block of mass 10 kg rests on a soft horizontal floor. When an iron cylinder of mass 20 kg is placed on top of the block, the floor yields, and the block and cylinder together go down with an acceleration of $0.2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. The action force of the system on the floor is $49 x \mathrm{~N}$. Find the integer value of $x$. (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: The total mass of the system is $M=10+20=30 \mathrm{~kg}$. The system accelerates downwards at $a=0.2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. The action force on the floor is equal to the normal force $N$ exerted by the floor on the system. The equation of motion is $M g-N=M a$. $N=M g-M a=M(g-a) . N=30(10-0.2)=30(9.8)=294 \mathrm{~N}$. We are given that this force is equal to $49 x$ N. $49 x=294 \Longrightarrow x=\frac{294}{49}=6$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Work done by a constant force
q: A force $\vec{F}=(3 \hat{i}+4 \hat{j}-c \hat{k}) \mathrm{N}$ acts on a body and displaces it by $\vec{d}=(2 \hat{i}-3 \hat{j}+2 \hat{k}) \mathrm{m}$. If the work done is -8 J , what is the value of c ?
s:
Work done is the dot product of force and displacement: $W=\vec{F} \cdot \vec{d}$.
$$
\begin{gathered}
W=(3)(2)+(4)(-3)+(-c)(2) \\
W=6-12-2 c=-6-2 c
\end{gathered}
$$
Given that $W=-8 \mathrm{~J}$ :
$$
\begin{gathered}
-8=-6-2 c \\
-2=-2 c \\
c=1
\end{gathered}
$$

subject: Physics
q: A 10 kg block is moved from point A to point B . Path 1 is a vertical lift of 5 m . Path 2 is a 10 m long frictionless ramp inclined at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, leading to the same height. The ratio of the work done by gravity in path 1 to path 2 is:
s: Gravity is a conservative force, so the work done by gravity depends only on the initial and final vertical positions, not the path taken. The vertical height for Path 2 is $h=10 \sin \left(30^{\circ}\right)=5$ m , which is the same as Path 1. Since the mass and vertical displacement are the same for both paths, the work done by gravity is identical. Thus, the ratio is $1: 1$.

subject: Physics
q: A spring elongates by $x_{0}$ when a tension of 4 N is applied. When the tension is 10 N , the elongation is $y_{0}$. The tension required for an elongation of ( $y_{0}-x_{0}$ ) is:
s: According to Hooke's Law, $F=k x$. From the given data: $4=k x_{0}$ and $10=k y_{0}$. Dividing the two equations: $\frac{y_{0}}{x_{0}}=\frac{10}{4}=2.5 \Rightarrow y_{0}=2.5 x_{0}$. The new elongation is $y_{0}-x_{0}= 2.5 x_{0}-x_{0}=1.5 x_{0}$. The tension required for this elongation is $F^{\prime}=k\left(1.5 x_{0}\right)=1.5\left(k x_{0}\right)=1.5(4)=$ 6 N.

subject: Physics
q: A spring with a spring constant of $800 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$ is stretched from its natural length by 5 cm . The additional work required to stretch it from 5 cm to 10 cm is:
s:
The work done in stretching a spring from $x_{1}$ to $x_{2}$ is $W=\frac{1}{2} k\left(x_{2}^{2}-x_{1}^{2}\right)$. Here, $k=800 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}, x_{1}=0.05 \mathrm{~m}$, and $x_{2}=0.10 \mathrm{~m}$.
$$
W=\frac{1}{2}(800)\left(0.10^{2}-0.05^{2}\right)=400(0.01-0.0025)=400(0.0075)=3 \mathrm{~J}
$$

subject: Physics
q: A body of mass 2 kg , initially at rest, is moved by a horizontal force of 10 N on a rough horizontal surface with $\mu_{k}=0.2$. The kinetic energy of the body after moving 10 m is: (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: By the Work-Energy Theorem, the net work done equals the change in kinetic energy: $W_{\text {net }}=\Delta K=K_{f}-K_{i} . \quad W_{\text {net }}=W_{\text {applied }}-W_{\text {friction }} . \quad W_{\text {applied }}=F \cdot d=10 \times 10=100 \mathrm{~J}$. $W_{\text {friction }}=\left(\mu_{k} m g\right) d=(0.2)(2)(10)(10)=40 \mathrm{~J} . K_{f}-0=100-40=60 \mathrm{~J}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Work done by a variable force
q: A force $\vec{F}=3 x y^{2} \hat{i}+x^{2} \hat{j}$ acts on a particle. The work done by this force during a straight line displacement from $(0,0)$ to $(1 \mathrm{~m}, 3 \mathrm{~m})$ is_______ Joule (round off to the nearest integer).
s:
The work done by a variable force $\vec{F}$ is calculated using the line integral:
$$
W=\int_{C} \vec{F} \cdot d \vec{r}
$$
Given the force $\vec{F}=3 x y^{2} \hat{i}+x^{2} \hat{j}$ and the differential displacement vector $d \vec{r}=d x \hat{i}+d y \hat{j}$, the work integral is:
$$
W=\int_{C}\left(3 x y^{2} d x+x^{2} d y\right)
$$
The displacement is along a straight line path from the origin $(0,0)$ to the point $(1,3)$. The equation of this path is found by determining the slope $m=\frac{3-0}{1-0}=3$. Therefore, the equation of the line is $y=3 x$. The corresponding differential relationship is $d y=3 d x$.
We substitute the path equations into the work integral. The limits of integration for the variable $x$ are from 0 to 1 .
$$
\begin{gathered}
W=\int_{0}^{1}\left(3 x(3 x)^{2} d x+x^{2}(3 d x)\right) \\
W=\int_{0}^{1}\left(3 x\left(9 x^{2}\right)+3 x^{2}\right) d x \\
W=\int_{0}^{1}\left(27 x^{3}+3 x^{2}\right) d x
\end{gathered}
$$
Now, we perform the integration:
$$
\begin{gathered}
W=\left[27 \frac{x^{4}}{4}+3 \frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} \\
W=\left[\frac{27}{4} x^{4}+x^{3}\right]_{0}^{1}
\end{gathered}
$$
Evaluating the integral at the limits:
$$
\begin{gathered}
W=\left(\frac{27}{4}(1)^{4}+(1)^{3}\right)-\left(\frac{27}{4}(0)^{4}+(0)^{3}\right) \\
W=\frac{27}{4}+1=\frac{27+4}{4}=\frac{31}{4}=7.75 \mathrm{~J}
\end{gathered}
$$
Rounding off to the nearest integer, the work done is 8 Joules.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Vertical circular motion involving strings and similar cases
q: A particle of mass $m$ is moving in a vertical circle of radius $R$. Its speed at the lowest point is $\sqrt{7 g R}$. Its speed at the highest point will be:
s:
Using conservation of mechanical energy between the lowest and highest points:
$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{1}{2} m v_{b o t}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} m v_{t o p}^{2}+m g(2 R) \\
v_{b o t}^{2}=v_{t o p}^{2}+4 g R
\end{gathered}
$$
Given $v_{\text {bot }}=\sqrt{7 g R}$, so $v_{\text {bot }}^{2}=7 g R$.
$$
7 g R=v_{t o p}^{2}+4 g R \Longrightarrow v_{t o p}^{2}=3 g R \Longrightarrow v_{t o p}=\sqrt{3 g R}
$$

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Vertical circular motion involving strings and similar cases
q: For a particle completing a vertical loop of radius R , the velocity at the bottom is $\sqrt{5 g R}$. The ratio of its kinetic energy at the bottom to that at the horizontal position (midway point) is:
s: Let A be the bottom and C be the horizontal position. $K E_{A}=\frac{1}{2} m v_{b o t}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} m(5 g R)= \frac{5}{2} m g R$. By energy conservation between A and C: $\frac{1}{2} m v_{\text {bot }}^{2}=\frac{1}{2} m v_{C}^{2}+m g R$. $K E_{A}=K E_{C}+ m g R \Longrightarrow \frac{5}{2} m g R=K E_{C}+m g R \Longrightarrow K E_{C}=\frac{3}{2} m g R$. The ratio is $\frac{K E_{A}}{K E_{C}}=\frac{5 / 2 \cdot m g R}{3 / 2 \cdot m g R}=\frac{5}{3}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Vertical circular motion involving strings and similar cases
q: For a particle completing a vertical loop, the ratio of the maximum tension to the minimum tension in the string is $3: 1$. The square of the velocity at the top point $\left(v_{\text {top }}^{2}\right)$ is:
s:
$T_{\text {max }}=\frac{m v_{\text {bot }}^{2}}{R}+m g$ and $T_{\text {min }}=\frac{m v_{\text {top }}^{2}}{R}-m g$. Also, $v_{\text {bot }}^{2}=v_{\text {top }}^{2}+4 g R$.
$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{T_{\max }}{T_{\min }}=\frac{m\left(v_{t o p}^{2}+4 g R\right) / R+m g}{m v_{t o p}^{2} / R-m g}=\frac{v_{t o p}^{2}+5 g R}{v_{t o p}^{2}-g R}=3 \\
v_{t o p}^{2}+5 g R=3\left(v_{t o p}^{2}-g R\right) \Longrightarrow v_{t o p}^{2}+5 g R=3 v_{t o p}^{2}-3 g R \\
8 g R=2 v_{t o p}^{2} \Longrightarrow v_{t o p}^{2}=4 g R
\end{gathered}
$$

subject: Physics
q: A bob of mass $m$ is suspended by a string of length $L$. It is imparted a horizontal velocity at the lowest position. The string becomes slack when it makes an angle of $120^{\circ}$ with the downward vertical. The initial velocity imparted was:
s: The string becomes slack when tension $T=0$. At an angle $\theta, T=\frac{m v^{2}}{L}+m g \cos \theta$. For $T=0$ at $\theta=120^{\circ}, 0=\frac{m v^{2}}{L}+m g(-1 / 2) \Longrightarrow v^{2}=g L / 2$. The height risen is $h= L(1-\cos \theta)=L(1-(-1 / 2))=1.5 L$. By energy conservation from the bottom (initial velocity $u): \frac{1}{2} m u^{2}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}+m g h . u^{2}=v^{2}+2 g h=g L / 2+2 g(1.5 L)=0.5 g L+3 g L=3.5 g L=\frac{7 g L}{2}$. $u=\sqrt{7 g L / 2}$.

subject: Physics

q: A particle is moving in a vertical circle of radius R . If the velocity at the top is $\sqrt{2 g R}$, the ratio of kinetic energy at the bottom to that at the top is:
s: $v_{\text {bot }}^{2}=v_{\text {top }}^{2}+4 g R$. Given $v_{\text {top }}^{2}=2 g R . v_{\text {bot }}^{2}=2 g R+4 g R=6 g R$. The ratio of kinetic energies is $\frac{K E_{b o t}}{K E_{\text {top }}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} m v_{\text {bot }}^{2}}{\frac{1}{2} m v_{\text {top }}^{2}}=\frac{v_{\text {bot }}^{2}}{v_{\text {top }}^{2}}=\frac{6 g R}{2 g R}=3$. The ratio is $3: 1$.

subject: Physics
q: The potential energy of a particle is given by $U(r)=\frac{A}{r^{2}}-\frac{B}{r}$, where A and B are positive constants. The particle is in stable equilibrium when its distance $r$ from the center of the field is:
s: For equilibrium, the net force is zero: $F=-d U / d r=0 . \quad F=-\left[-\frac{2 A}{r^{3}}-\left(-\frac{B}{r^{2}}\right)\right]= \frac{2 A}{r^{3}}-\frac{B}{r^{2}}=0 . \frac{2 A}{r^{3}}=\frac{B}{r^{2}} \Longrightarrow r=\frac{2 A}{B}$. For stable equilibrium, the second derivative of potential energy must be positive, $d^{2} U / d r^{2}>0$. $\frac{d^{2} U}{d r^{2}}=\frac{d}{d r}\left(-\frac{2 A}{r^{3}}+\frac{B}{r^{2}}\right)=\frac{6 A}{r^{4}}-\frac{2 B}{r^{3}}$. At $r=2 A / B$, this is positive, confirming stability.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Vertical circular motion involving strings and similar cases
q:
With what minimum speed $v$ must a small ball should be pushed inside a smooth vertical tube from a height $h$ so that it may reach the top of the tube ? Radius of the tube is $R$:
 [IMAGE: images/MB000268_1.webp]
s:
We use the principle of conservation of mechanical energy. For the minimum initial speed, the ball's speed at the very top of the tube will be zero.
- Initial Energy ( $E_{i}$ ): At height $h$, with speed $v$.
$$
E_{i}=K_{i}+U_{i}=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}+m g h
$$
- Final Energy $\left(E_{f}\right)$ : At the top of the tube, height $2 R$, with speed $v_{f}=0$.
$$
E_{f}=K_{f}+U_{f}=0+m g(2 R)
$$
By conservation of energy, $E_{i}=E_{f}$ :
$$
\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}+m g h=m g(2 R)
$$
Divide by $m$ :
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{2} v^{2}+g h=2 g R \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{2} v^{2}=g(2 R-h) \\
& v^{2}=2 g(2 R-h) \Longrightarrow v=\sqrt{2 g(2 R-h)}
\end{aligned}
$$

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Vertical circular motion involving strings and similar cases
q: A ball swings in a vertical plane such that its acceleration at the lowest point is twice its acceleration at the extreme position. The angle of deflection of the thread in the extreme position will be:
s: At the lowest point, acceleration is purely centripetal: $a_{\text {low }}=v_{\text {low }}^{2} / L$. At the extreme position, velocity is zero, so acceleration is purely tangential: $a_{\text {ext }}=g \sin \theta$. Given $a_{\text {low }}= 2 a_{\text {ext }} \Longrightarrow v_{\text {low }}^{2} / L=2 g \sin \theta$. From energy conservation between extreme and lowest points: $m g L(1-\cos \theta)=\frac{1}{2} m v_{\text {low }}^{2} \Longrightarrow v_{\text {low }}^{2}=2 g L(1-\cos \theta)$. Substituting: $\frac{2 g L(1-\cos \theta)}{L}=2 g \sin \theta \Longrightarrow 1-\cos \theta=\sin \theta$. Squaring both sides: $1-2 \cos \theta+\cos ^{2} \theta=\sin ^{2} \theta=1-\cos ^{2} \theta .2 \cos ^{2} \theta-2 \cos \theta= 0 \Longrightarrow 2 \cos \theta(\cos \theta-1)=0$. Since $\theta \neq 0$, we must have $\cos \theta=0$, which means $\theta=90^{\circ}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Vertical circular motion involving strings and similar cases
q: A bob of mass ' $m$ ' is suspended by a light string of length ' $L$ '. It is imparted a minimum horizontal velocity at the lowest point A such that it just completes the vertical circle. The kinetic energy at the horizontal position C is:
s: To just complete the circle, the minimum velocity at the lowest point is $v_{\text {low }}=\sqrt{5 g L}$. The kinetic energy at this point is $K E_{A}=\frac{1}{2} m(5 g L)=\frac{5}{2} m g L$. By conservation of energy between the lowest point (A) and the horizontal point (C, height L ): $K E_{A}=K E_{C}+P E_{C} \Longrightarrow \frac{5}{2} m g L= K E_{C}+m g L . K E_{C}=\frac{5}{2} m g L-m g L=\frac{3}{2} m g L$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Work done by a constant force
q: A block of mass 2 kg is pulled up a rough inclined plane of inclination $30^{\circ}$ and length 10 m . The coefficient of kinetic friction is $1 /(2 \sqrt{3})$. If the block is pulled with constant velocity, the work done against friction is________ \[\left( {{\text{in}}\,\,\,\,\,\,{\text{J}}} \right).\] (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: Work done against friction is $W_{f}=f_{k} \cdot d=\left(\mu_{k} N\right) d$. On an inclined plane, the normal force is $N=m g \cos \theta . W_{f}=\left(\mu_{k} m g \cos \theta\right) d=\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}}\right)(2)(10)\left(\cos 30^{\circ}\right)(10) . W_{f}=\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}}\right)(20)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)(10)= \frac{200}{4}=50 \mathrm{~J}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Work done by a variable force
q: A force $\vec{F}=y^{2} \hat{i}+x^{2} y \hat{j}$ acts on a particle. The work done by this force during a straight line displacement from $(1 \mathrm{~m}, 1 \mathrm{~m})$ to $(3 \mathrm{~m}, 3 \mathrm{~m})$ is________\[\left( {{\text{in}}\,\,\,\,\,\,{\text{Joule}}} \right)\] (round off to the nearest integer).
s:
The work done by the force $\vec{F}$ is given by the integral $W=\int_{C} \vec{F} \cdot d \vec{r}$.
With the force given as $\vec{F}=y^{2} \hat{i}+x^{2} y \hat{j}$, the work integral becomes:
$$
W=\int_{C}\left(y^{2} d x+x^{2} y d y\right)
$$
The particle moves along a straight line path from $(1,1)$ to $(3,3)$. The equation for this path is $y=x$. The differential relationship is $d y=d x$.
We substitute $y=x$ and $d y=d x$ into the integral. The limits for the variable $x$ will be from 1 to 3 .
$$
\begin{gathered}
W=\int_{1}^{3}\left(x^{2} d x+x^{2}(x) d x\right) \\
W=\int_{1}^{3}\left(x^{2}+x^{3}\right) d x
\end{gathered}
$$
Now, we evaluate the definite integral:
$$
\begin{gathered}
W=\left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{x^{4}}{4}\right]_{1}^{3} \\
W=\left(\frac{3^{3}}{3}+\frac{3^{4}}{4}\right)-\left(\frac{1^{3}}{3}+\frac{1^{4}}{4}\right) \\
W=\left(\frac{27}{3}+\frac{81}{4}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}\right) \\
W=\left(9+\frac{81}{4}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$
Grouping like terms:
$$
\begin{gathered}
W=\left(9-\frac{1}{3}\right)+\left(\frac{81}{4}-\frac{1}{4}\right) \\
W=\frac{27-1}{3}+\frac{80}{4}=\frac{26}{3}+20 \\
W=\frac{26+60}{3}=\frac{86}{3} \approx 28.67 \mathrm{~J}
\end{gathered}
$$
Rounding off to the nearest integer, the work done is 29 Joules.

subject: Physics
q: A bullet of mass 50 g strikes a pendulum bob of mass 950 g . The bullet gets embedded in the bob and the system rises to a vertical height of 0.2 m . The initial speed of the bullet was________$\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$. (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: First, find the velocity (V) of the combined mass just after collision using energy conservation: $\frac{1}{2}\left(M_{\text {total }}\right) V^{2}=\left(M_{\text {total }}\right) g h \Longrightarrow V=\sqrt{2 g h} . \quad V=\sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 0.2}=\sqrt{4}=2 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$. Now, use momentum conservation for the collision: $m_{\text {bullet }} u_{\text {bullet }}=\left(m_{\text {bullet }}+m_{\text {bob }}\right) V$. $(0.05 \mathrm{~kg}) \times u_{\text {bullet }}=(0.05+0.95 \mathrm{~kg}) \times 2 \Longrightarrow 0.05 u_{\text {bullet }}=1 \times 2 . u_{\text {bullet }}=2 / 0.05=40 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: The moment of inertia of a uniform circular disc of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about an axis tangent to the disc and lying in its plane is:
s:
The moment of inertia of a disc about its diameter is $I_{\text {dia }}=\frac{1}{4} M R^{2}$. 
Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a tangential axis in the plane is $I_{\text {tangent }}=I_{\text {dia }}+M R^{2} . I_{\text {tangent }}=\frac{1}{4} M R^{2}+M R^{2}=\frac{5}{4} M R^{2}$.

subject: Physics
q: Two uniform rods, each of mass ' $M$ ' and length ' $L$ ', are joined to form an ' $L$ ' shape. The moment of inertia of the system about an axis passing through the corner O and perpendicular to the plane of the ' $L$ ' is:
s: The moment of inertia of a single rod of mass M and length L about an axis passing through its end and perpendicular to it is $I_{\text {end }}=\frac{M L^{2}}{3}$. The system consists of two such rods joined at their ends. The total moment of inertia is the sum of the moments of inertia of the two rods about the corner O. $I_{\text {total }}=I_{\text {rod } 1}+I_{\text {rod } 2}=\frac{M L^{2}}{3}+\frac{M L^{2}}{3}=\frac{2 M L^{2}}{3}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Moment of inertia of truncated bodies/combined bodies
q: From a uniform circular disc of radius $R$ and mass $M$, a smaller disc of radius $R / 2$ is removed, with its center at a distance $R / 2$ from the center of the original disc. The moment of inertia of the remaining part about the axis passing through the center O and perpendicular to the plane of the disc is:
s: Let $\sigma$ be the mass per unit area. $M=\sigma \pi R^{2}$. Mass of the removed disc: $m=\sigma \pi(R / 2)^{2}=\frac{\sigma \pi R^{2}}{4}=\frac{M}{4}$. MI of the full disc about $\mathrm{O}: I_{\text {full }}=\frac{1}{2} M R^{2}$. MI of the removed disc about its own center: $I_{\text {cm,removed }}=\frac{1}{2} m(R / 2)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{M}{4}\right)\left(\frac{R^{2}}{4}\right)=\frac{M R^{2}}{32}$. Distance of the center of the removed disc from O is $d=R / 2$. Using the parallel axis theorem, MI of the removed disc about O is: $I_{\text {removed }}=I_{\text {cm,removed }}+m d^{2}=\frac{M R^{2}}{32}+\left(\frac{M}{4}\right)\left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^{2}= \frac{M R^{2}}{32}+\frac{M R^{2}}{16}=\frac{3 M R^{2}}{32}$. MI of the remaining portion: $I_{\text {rem }}=I_{\text {full }}-I_{\text {removed }}=\frac{M R^{2}}{2}-\frac{3 M R^{2}}{32}= \frac{16 M R^{2}-3 M R^{2}}{32}=\frac{13 M R^{2}}{32}$.

subject: Physics
q: The ratio of the radius of gyration of a solid sphere of mass M and radius R about its own axis to that of a thin hollow sphere of the same mass and radius about its axis is:
s: For a solid sphere, $I_{\text {solid }}=\frac{2}{5} M R^{2}=M k_{\text {solid }}^{2} \Longrightarrow k_{\text {solid }}=R \sqrt{\frac{2}{5}}$. For a hollow sphere, $I_{\text {hollow }}=\frac{2}{3} M R^{2}=M k_{\text {hollow }}^{2} \Longrightarrow k_{\text {hollow }}=R \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}$. The ratio is $\frac{k_{\text {solid }}}{k_{\text {hollow }}}= \frac{R \sqrt{2 / 5}}{R \sqrt{2 / 3}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 / 5}{2 / 3}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{5}}=\sqrt{3}: \sqrt{5}$.
