o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
s: LEDs work on the principle of electroluminescence. When forwardbiased, minority carriers are injected across the junction and recombine with majority carriers, releasing energy corresponding to the band gap in the form of light. Reason (R) correctly explains Assertion (A).

subject: Physics
q: A photodiode is preferably operated in reverse bias because:
o: it allows a large current to flow.
the reverse current is highly sensitive to light intensity.
its breakdown voltage is very high.
s: In reverse bias, the dark current (current without light) is very small. When light falls on the photodiode, the generated electron-hole pairs contribute to the reverse current. This fractional change in current is easily detectable, making the device sensitive to light.

subject: Physics
q: The band gap of silicon is 1.1 eV . The maximum wavelength of light that can be absorbed by silicon to produce an electron-hole pair is approximately: (Given $h c=1240 \mathrm{eV}-\mathrm{nm}$ )
s: The minimum energy required to create an electron-hole pair is the band gap energy, $E_{g}$. This corresponds to the maximum wavelength $\lambda_{\text {max }}$. $E_{g}= \frac{h c}{\lambda_{\text {max }}} \Longrightarrow \lambda_{\text {max }}=\frac{h c}{E_{g}}=\frac{1240 \mathrm{eV}-\mathrm{nm}}{1.1 \mathrm{eV}} \approx 1127 \mathrm{~nm}$.

subject: Physics
q: An LED is fabricated from a semiconductor material with a band gap ( $E_{g}$ ) of 1.9 eV . The color of the light emitted by this LED is likely to be: (Given $h c=1240$ eV-nm)
s: The wavelength of the emitted light is $\lambda=\frac{h c}{E_{g}}=\frac{1240 \mathrm{eV}-\mathrm{nm}}{1.9 \mathrm{eV}} \approx 653 \mathrm{~nm}$. This wavelength corresponds to red light in the visible spectrum.

The direction of conventional current in forward bias.

q: Which of the following statements about an LED is false?
o: It must be forward-biased to emit light.
It is fabricated from a heavily doped p-n junction.
The intensity of light is directly proportional to the forward current.
The reverse breakdown voltage is very high.

q: The knee voltage of a silicon diode is approximately:
s: The knee voltage (or threshold voltage) is the forward voltage at which the diode starts to conduct significantly. For silicon diodes, this value is approximately 0.7 V . For germanium diodes, it is about 0.3 V .

subject: Physics
q: The conductivity of a photodiode starts changing only if the wavelength of incident light is less than 990 nm . The band gap of the photodiode is found to be $(x / 8) \mathrm{eV}$. The value of x is________. (Given, $h c=1242 \mathrm{eV} \mathrm{nm}$ ). (x is an integer)
s: The maximum wavelength (threshold wavelength) corresponds to the band gap energy. $E_{g}=\frac{h c}{\lambda_{\max }}=\frac{1242 \mathrm{eV} \mathrm{nm}}{990 \mathrm{~nm}}=1.254 \mathrm{eV}$. Given that $E_{g}=(x / 8) \mathrm{eV}$. $\frac{x}{8}=1.254 \Longrightarrow x=8 \times 1.254 \approx 10.032$. Rounding to the nearest integer, $x=10$.

subject: Physics
q: In a single-slit diffraction experiment, if the width of the slit is doubled, the width of the central maximum will be:
s: The linear width of the central maximum is $W=\frac{2 \lambda D}{d}$. Therefore, $W \propto \frac{1}{d}$. If the slit width 'd' is doubled, the width 'W' becomes half.

subject: Physics
q: The fundamental frequency of a closed organ pipe of length 25 cm is equal to the second harmonic of an open organ pipe. The length of the open organ pipe is:
s: $f_{\text {closed }}=\frac{v}{4 L_{c}}, f_{\text {open,2nd }}=\frac{2 v}{2 L_{o}}=\frac{v}{L_{o}}$. Equating them: $\frac{v}{4 \times 25}=\frac{v}{L_{o}} \Rightarrow L_{o}=100 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: A parallel beam of light of wavelength 600 nm is incident on a single slit of width 0.3 mm . The angular position of the second dark fringe (minimum) is:
s: For the n-th minimum, $d \sin \theta=n \lambda$. For small angles, $\theta \approx \sin \theta$. For the second minimum $(\mathrm{n}=2), \theta=\frac{2 \lambda}{d}=\frac{2 \times\left(600 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}\right)}{0.3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}}=\frac{1200}{0.3} \times 10^{-6}=4000 \times 10^{-6}=4 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{rad}$.

subject: Physics
q: An open organ pipe is suddenly closed at one end. As a result, the frequency of the third harmonic of the closed pipe is found to be 100 Hz higher than the fundamental frequency of the open pipe. The fundamental frequency of the open pipe is:
s:
Let the initial fundamental frequency of the open pipe be $f_{o}=\frac{v}{2 L}$. 
The new closed pipe has length L , so its fundamental is $f_{c}=\frac{v}{4 L}=\frac{f_{o}}{2}$. 
The third harmonic of the closed pipe is $3 f_{c}=3\left(\frac{f_{o}}{2}\right)$. 
Given, $3 f_{c}-f_{o}=100 \Rightarrow \frac{3 f_{o}}{2}-f_{o}=100 \Rightarrow \frac{f_{o}}{2}=100 \Rightarrow f_{o}=200 \mathrm{~Hz}$.

subject: Physics
q: If a single-slit diffraction experiment is performed in water instead of air, the width of the central maximum:
s:
The wavelength of light in water decreases ( $\lambda^{\prime}=\lambda / \mu$ ). 
The width of the central maximum is $W=\frac{2 \lambda^{\prime} D}{d}$. 
Since $\lambda^{\prime}$ decreases, W also decreases.

subject: Physics
q: The fifth overtone of a closed organ pipe is equivalent to which harmonic?
s:
For a closed pipe, only odd harmonics exist. 
The fundamental is the 1st harmonic. 
1st overtone $=3$ rd harmonic. 2 nd overtone $=5$ th harmonic. n-th overtone $=(2 n+1)$-th harmonic. 
So, 5 th overtone $=(2(5)+1)$-th harmonic $=11$ th harmonic.

subject: Physics
q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, 10 interference maxima are observed within the central diffraction maximum. If the slit separation 'a' is 1 mm , what is the slit width 'd'?
s: 10 maxima within the central peak means 5 maxima on each side. The 5 th interference maximum should coincide with the 1 st diffraction minimum. Position of 5 th $\max : y_{5}=\frac{5 \lambda D}{a}$. Position of 1st min: $y_{1}^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$. Equating them: $\frac{5 \lambda D}{a}=\frac{\lambda D}{d} \Rightarrow a=5 d . d=a / 5=1 \mathrm{~mm} / 5=0.2 \mathrm{~mm}$.

subject: Physics
q: Two closed organ pipes, when sounded together, produce 5 beats per second. If the length of the shorter pipe is 40 cm , what is the length of the longer pipe? (Speed of sound $=330 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ )
s: Frequency of shorter pipe $f_{1}=\frac{v}{4 L_{1}}=\frac{330}{4 \times 0.40}=206.25 \mathrm{~Hz}$. The longer pipe will have a lower frequency, so $f_{2}=f_{1}-5=201.25 \mathrm{~Hz}$. $f_{2}=\frac{v}{4 L_{2}} \Rightarrow L_{2}=\frac{v}{4 f_{2}}=\frac{330}{4 \times 201.25} \approx 0.41 \mathrm{~m}$ or 41 cm .

subject: Physics
q: Light of wavelength 500 nm is incident on a slit of width 0.1 mm . The screen is placed 2 m away. The distance between the first minima on either side of the central maximum is:
s: This distance is the total width of the central maximum, $W=\frac{2 \lambda D}{d}=\frac{2 \times\left(500 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}\right) \times(2 \mathrm{~m})}{0.1 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}}= \frac{2000 \times 10^{-9}}{0.1 \times 10^{-3}}=20000 \times 10^{-6}=0.02 \mathrm{~m}=2.0 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: The ratio of the fundamental frequencies of an open pipe and a closed pipe of the same length is:
s: $f_{\text {open }}=\frac{v}{2 L}, f_{\text {closed }}=\frac{v}{4 L}$. Ratio $\frac{f_{\text {open }}}{f_{\text {closed }}}=\frac{v / 2 L}{v / 4 L}=\frac{4}{2}=\frac{2}{1}$.

subject: Physics
q: The ratio of the width of the central diffraction maximum to the width of a secondary maximum is:
s:
Width of central max is $W_{c}=\frac{2 \lambda D}{d}$. Width of secondary max is $W_{s}=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$. 
The ratio is $W_{c} / W_{s}=2$.

subject: Physics
q: An open pipe of length 33 cm resonates with a frequency of 1500 Hz . The speed of sound is $330 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. This frequency is the:
s: Fundamental frequency $f_{1}=\frac{v}{2 L}=\frac{330}{2 \times 0.33}=500 \mathrm{~Hz}$. The given frequency is $1500 \mathrm{~Hz}=3 \mathrm{x} 500 \mathrm{~Hz}=3 f_{1}$. This is the 3rd harmonic, which is the second overtone.

q: For diffraction to occur, the size of the obstacle or slit:
o: Should be much larger than the wavelength.
Should be of the order of the wavelength.
Should be much smaller than the wavelength.
s: Diffraction effects are most prominent when the size of the aperture or obstacle is comparable to the wavelength of the wave.

subject: Physics
q: Two different gases have the same density but their bulk moduli are in the ratio $4: 1$. The ratio of the fundamental frequencies of two identical open pipes filled with these gases is:
s: The velocity of sound in a gas is $v=\sqrt{B / \rho}$. $f=\frac{v}{2 L} \propto v$. And $v \propto \sqrt{B}$. So, $f \propto \sqrt{B}$. $\frac{f_{1}}{f_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{B_{1}}{B_{2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{4}{1}}=\frac{2}{1}$.

subject: Physics
q: A light of wavelength 400 nm is used in a single slit diffraction experiment with a slit of width 0.2 mm . The screen is 1 m away. The half angular width of the central maximum is:
s: The half angular width is the position of the first minimum, $\theta_{1} \cdot \sin \theta_{1} \approx \theta_{1}=\frac{\lambda}{d}=\frac{400 \times 10^{-9}}{0.2 \times 10^{-3}}= 2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{rad}$.

subject: Physics
q: A closed organ pipe has a fundamental frequency of 100 Hz . The frequencies of the next two overtones are:
s: For a closed pipe, only odd harmonics are present. The fundamental (1st harmonic) is 100 Hz . The first overtone is the 3rd harmonic ( 300 Hz ). The second overtone is the 5th harmonic ( 500 Hz ).

subject: Physics
q: The condition for the n-th secondary maximum in single slit diffraction is approximately:
s: The secondary maxima lie approximately halfway between the minima. The condition for maxima is $d \sin \theta=\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right) \lambda=(2 n+1) \frac{\lambda}{2}$ for $n=1,2,3, \ldots$

subject: Physics
q: The end correction of a resonance tube is 1 cm . If the first resonating length is 15 cm , the next resonating length will be:
s: For a closed tube (resonance tube), $L_{1}+e=\lambda / 4$ and $L_{2}+e=3 \lambda / 4.15+1=\lambda / 4 \Rightarrow \lambda=64$ cm. $L_{2}+1=3(64) / 4=48 \Rightarrow L_{2}=47 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: In a single slit diffraction pattern, the distance between the first and third minima is 4 mm . The screen is 100 cm away and the wavelength of light used is 600 nm . The width of the slit is:
s: Position of third minimum $x_{3}=\frac{3 \lambda D}{d}$. Position of first minimum $x_{1}=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$. Distance $=x_{3}-x_{1}=\frac{2 \lambda D}{d} .4 \times 10^{-3}=\frac{2 \times\left(600 \times 10^{-9}\right) \times 1}{d} . d=\frac{1200 \times 10^{-9}}{4 \times 10^{-3}}=300 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}=0.3 \mathrm{~mm}$.

subject: Physics
q: A closed organ pipe and an open organ pipe of the same length are sounded together. The ratio of the frequencies of their 3rd overtones is:
s: 3rd overtone of closed pipe $=7$ th harmonic $=\frac{7 v}{4 L} .3$ rd overtone of open pipe $=4$ th harmonic $=\frac{4 v}{2 L}$. Ratio $=\frac{7 v / 4 L}{4 v / 2 L}=\frac{7}{4} \times \frac{2}{4}=\frac{7}{8}$.

subject: Physics
q: A single slit of width 0.5 mm is illuminated by a parallel beam of light of wavelength 500 nm . The diffraction pattern is observed on a screen 1 m away. The distance of the third dark fringe from the central bright fringe is___________(in mm).
s: The position of the $n$-th dark fringe is given by $x_{n}=\frac{n \lambda D}{d}$. For the third dark fringe ( $n=3$ ): $x_{3}=\frac{3 \times\left(500 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}\right) \times(1 \mathrm{~m})}{0.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}}=\frac{1500 \times 10^{-9}}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}}=3000 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}=3 \mathrm{~mm}$.

subject: Physics
q: An open organ pipe of length 1 m and a closed organ pipe of length 0.55 m are sounded simultaneously in their fundamental modes. The speed of sound in air is $330 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The number of beats produced per second is________(in Hz).
s: $f_{\text {open }}=\frac{330}{2 \times 1}=165 \mathrm{~Hz} . f_{\text {closed }}=\frac{330}{4 \times 0.55}=\frac{330}{2.2}=150 \mathrm{~Hz}$. Beat frequency $=|165-150|=15$ Hz.

subject: Physics
q: In a single slit diffraction, the angle of diffraction for the first minimum for red light of wavelength 660 nm is $30^{\circ}$. The width of the slit is $N \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~m}$. Find the value of N .
s: For the first minimum $(n=1)$, the condition is $d \sin \theta=n \lambda . d \sin \left(30^{\circ}\right)=1 \times\left(660 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}\right)$. $d=\frac{660 \times 10^{-9}}{0.5}=1320 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}=132 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~m}$. So, $N=132$.

subject: Physics
q: The fundamental frequency of a closed organ pipe is 50 Hz . Water is poured into the pipe so that its fundamental frequency becomes 150 Hz . The fraction of the pipe's original length that is now filled with water is $k / 3$. Find the value of k .
s:
Let the original length be L. $f_{1}=\frac{v}{4 L}=50 \mathrm{~Hz}$. Let the new length of the air column be $L^{\prime}$. 
The new frequency is $f_{2}=\frac{v}{4 L^{\prime}}=150 \mathrm{~Hz}$. 
Dividing the two equations: $\frac{f_{2}}{f_{1}}=\frac{L}{L^{\prime}} \Rightarrow \frac{150}{50}=\frac{L}{L^{\prime}} \Rightarrow 3=\frac{L}{L^{\prime}}$. 
So, $L^{\prime}=L / 3$. This is the length of the air column. 
The length filled with water is $L_{\text {water }}=L-L^{\prime}= L-L / 3=2 L / 3$. The fraction is $2 / 3$. 
So $k=2$.

subject: Physics
q: The angular width of the central maximum in a diffraction pattern is $60^{\circ}$. If the wavelength of light used is \[6000\mathop {\text{A}}\limits^ \circ \], the width of the slit is_________ (in nm).
s:
The angular width of the central maximum is $2 \theta$, where $\theta$ is the position of the first minimum. 
Given $2 \theta=60^{\circ}$, so $\theta=30^{\circ}$. For the first minimum, $d \sin \theta=\lambda . d=\frac{\lambda}{\sin \theta}=\frac{6000 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{~m}}{\sin \left(30^{\circ}\right)}=\frac{600 \times 10^{-9}}{0.5}= 1200 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}=1200 \mathrm{~nm}$.

subject: Physics
q:
Assertion (A): In a Young's double-slit experiment, the interference fringes produced by violet light are narrower than those produced by green light.
Reason (R): The fringe width in a Young's double-slit experiment is inversely proportional to the wavelength of the light used.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
s:
The fringe width is given by $\beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$, which means $\beta \propto \lambda$. Since the wavelength of violet light ( $\lambda_{V}$ ) is less than the wavelength of green light ( $\lambda_{G}$ ), the fringes for violet light are narrower ( $\beta_{V}<\beta_{G}$ ). 
Thus, Assertion (A) is true. The Reason (R) states that fringe width is inversely proportional to wavelength, which is incorrect. Therefore, (R) is false.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Variations in Young's double slit experiment
q: A Young's double-slit experiment is first performed in air and then in a medium other than air. It is found that the 8th bright fringe in the medium lies where the 5th dark fringe lies in air. The refractive index of the medium is:
s:
The wavelength in the medium is $\lambda^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}$.
Position of 8th bright fringe in medium: $y_{1}=\frac{8 \lambda^{\prime} D}{d}=\frac{8 \lambda D}{\mu d}$.
Position of 5th dark fringe in air: $y_{2}=\left(5-\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{\lambda D}{d}=\frac{9}{2} \frac{\lambda D}{d}$.
Given $y_{1}=y_{2}$, so $\frac{8 \lambda D}{\mu d}=\frac{9}{2} \frac{\lambda D}{d}$.
$\mu=\frac{16}{9} \approx 1.78$.

subject: Physics
q: Two coherent sources have intensities in the ratio $25: 1$. They interfere to form fringes. The ratio of maximum intensity to minimum intensity is:
s: Given $\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}}=\frac{25}{1}$. Since $I \propto A^{2}$, the ratio of amplitudes is $\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{25}{1}}=5$. The ratio of maximum to minimum intensity is $\frac{I_{\text {max }}}{I_{\text {min }}}=\left(\frac{A_{1}+A_{2}}{A_{1}-A_{2}}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{5+1}{5-1}\right)^{2}= \left(\frac{6}{4}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{9}{4}$.

subject: Physics
q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the width of one slit is nine times the other. The ratio of the maximum to the minimum intensity in the interference pattern is:
s:
Intensity is proportional to the slit width $(I \propto w)$. So, $\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}}=\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}=\frac{9}{1}$.
The ratio of amplitudes is $\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}}}=3$.
$\frac{I_{\text {max }}}{I_{\text {min }}}=\left(\frac{A_{1}+A_{2}}{A_{1}-A_{2}}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{3+1}{3-1}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{4}{2}\right)^{2}=4$. The ratio is 4:1.

subject: Physics
q: A monochromatic light of wavelength $6000 \mathrm{~A}^{\circ}$ is used in YDSE. If one of the slit is covered by a transparent sheet ( $\mu=1.3$ ) of thickness $1.4 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m}$, then number of fringe shifted is
s:
The number of fringes shifted, $N$, is the ratio of the fringe shift to the fringe width:
$$
N=\frac{\Delta x}{\beta}=\frac{\frac{D}{d}(\mu-1) t}{\frac{D \lambda}{d}}=\frac{(\mu-1) t}{\lambda}
$$
Given values:
- Wavelength, \[\lambda = 6000\mathop {\text{A}}\limits^ \circ = 6000 \times {10^{ - 10}}\;{\text{m}}\]
- Refractive index, $\mu=1.3$
- Thickness of the sheet, $t=1.4 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~m}$
Now, substitute these values into the formula for $N$ :
$$
\begin{aligned}
& N=\frac{(1.3-1) \times\left(1.4 \times 10^{-5}\right)}{6000 \times 10^{10}} \\
& N=\frac{0.3 \times 1.4 \times 10^{-5}}{6 \times 10^3 \times 10^{-10}} \\
& N=\frac{0.42 \times 10^{-5}}{6 \times 10^{-7}} \\
& N=\frac{0.42}{6} \times 10^2 \\
& N=0.07 \times 100 \\
& N=7
\end{aligned}
$$

subject: Physics
q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the maximum intensity is $I_{0}$. The intensity at a point on the screen where the path difference is $\lambda / 3$ is:
s:
Phase difference $\phi=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \times$ (Path Difference) $=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \times \frac{\lambda}{3}=\frac{2 \pi}{3}$.
Intensity is given by $I=I_{\text {max }} \cos ^{2}\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)=I_{0} \cos ^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=I_{0}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{I_{0}}{4}$.

subject: Physics
q: If the ratio of maximum to minimum intensity in an interference pattern is $36: 1$, the ratio of the amplitudes of the two interfering waves is:
s:
We have $\frac{I_{\text {max }}}{I_{\text {min }}}=\left(\frac{A_{1}+A_{2}}{A_{1}-A_{2}}\right)^{2}=36$.
Taking the square root, $\frac{A_{1}+A_{2}}{A_{1}-A_{2}}=6$.
Using componendo and dividendo, $\frac{\left(A_{1}+A_{2}\right)+\left(A_{1}-A_{2}\right)}{\left(A_{1}+A_{2}\right)-\left(A_{1}-A_{2}\right)}=\frac{6+1}{6-1} \Longrightarrow \frac{2 A_{1}}{2 A_{2}}=\frac{7}{5}$.

subject: Physics
q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the distance between the slits ( $d$ ) is halved and the distance between the slits and the screen ( $D$ ) is doubled. The new fringe width ( $\beta^{\prime}$ ) will be:
s:
The original fringe width is $\beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$.
The new parameters are $d^{\prime}=d / 2$ and $D^{\prime}=2 D$.
The new fringe width is $\beta^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda D^{\prime}}{d^{\prime}}=\frac{\lambda(2 D)}{(d / 2)}=4 \frac{\lambda D}{d}=4 \beta$.

subject: Physics
q: Two coherent light beams of intensities $I$ and $16 I$ are superimposed. The difference between the maximum and minimum possible intensities is:
s:
Given $I_{1}=I$ and $I_{2}=16 I$. The amplitudes are proportional to $\sqrt{I}$ and $\sqrt{16 I}=4 \sqrt{I}$.
$I_{\text {max }}=\left(\sqrt{I_{1}}+\sqrt{I_{2}}\right)^{2}=(\sqrt{I}+4 \sqrt{I})^{2}=(5 \sqrt{I})^{2}=25 I$.
$I_{\text {min }}=\left(\sqrt{I_{2}}-\sqrt{I_{1}}\right)^{2}=(4 \sqrt{I}-\sqrt{I})^{2}=(3 \sqrt{I})^{2}=9 I$.
The difference is $I_{\text {max }}-I_{\text {min }}=25 I-9 I=16 I$.

subject: Physics
q: The phase difference between the two waves reaching the location of the third dark fringe from the center is:
s:
For the $n^{\text {th }}$ dark fringe, the path difference is $\Delta x=\left(n-\frac{1}{2}\right) \lambda$.
For the 3rd dark fringe $(n=3), \Delta x=\left(3-\frac{1}{2}\right) \lambda=\frac{5 \lambda}{2}$.
The phase difference is $\phi=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \Delta x=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda}\left(\frac{5 \lambda}{2}\right)=5 \pi$.

subject: Physics
q: In a Young's double-slit experiment using white light, the fringe that is formed closest to the central white fringe is:
s: The position of the $n^{t h}$ bright fringe is $y_{n}=\frac{n \lambda D}{d}$, so $y_{n} \propto \lambda$. Since violet light has the shortest wavelength among the given options, its first bright fringe $(n=1)$ will be closest to the central maximum.

subject: Physics
q:
Assertion (A): In a Young's double-slit experiment using white light, the central fringe is white.
Reason (R): At the central position of the screen, the path difference between waves from the two slits is zero for all wavelengths.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
s: At the center of the screen, the path difference is zero. A zero path difference causes constructive interference for all wavelengths present in the white light. The superposition of all colors results in a white fringe. Therefore, both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Coherent and Incoherent Addition of Waves
q: The intensities of two light waves are in the ratio $81: 1$. The ratio of their amplitudes is:
s: Since intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude ( $I \propto A^{2}$ ), the ratio of amplitudes is the square root of the ratio of intensities: $\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}}}= \sqrt{\frac{81}{1}}=\frac{9}{1}$.

subject: Physics
q: The ratio of the slit widths in a Young's double-slit experiment is $4: 1$. The ratio of the maximum to the minimum intensity in the interference pattern is:
s:
Intensity is proportional to slit width, so $\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}}=\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}=\frac{4}{1}$.
The ratio of amplitudes is $\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{4}{1}}=2$.
$\frac{I_{\text {max }}}{I_{\text {min }}}=\left(\frac{A_{1}+A_{2}}{A_{1}-A_{2}}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{2+1}{2-1}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{3}{1}\right)^{2}=9$. The ratio is 9:1.

subject: Physics
q: The locus of all points in space having a constant path difference from the two slits in a YDSE is a:
s: By mathematical definition, a hyperbola is the locus of points where the difference in distances from two fixed points (the foci) is constant. In the YDSE, the two slits act as the foci, and the fringes are formed at locations with a constant path difference.

subject: Physics
q: If the path difference between two interfering waves at a point on the screen is $5 \lambda / 2$, the point will correspond to:
s: Destructive interference (a dark fringe) occurs when the path difference is an odd integer multiple of $\lambda / 2$. The general condition is $\Delta x=\left(n-\frac{1}{2}\right) \lambda$. For $n=3$, the path difference is $\left(3-\frac{1}{2}\right) \lambda=\frac{5 \lambda}{2}$. This corresponds to the 3rd dark fringe.

subject: Physics
q: The angular separation between consecutive bright fringes in a Young's double-slit experiment is independent of the:
s: The angular fringe width is given by $\theta=\frac{\beta}{D}$. Since $\beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d}$, the angular width is $\theta=\frac{\lambda D / d}{D}=\frac{\lambda}{d}$. This expression is independent of the screen distance $D$.

subject: Physics
q: Two slits in a Young's double-slit experiment have widths in the ratio $1: 16$. The ratio of the amplitudes of the light waves from them is:
s:
Intensity is proportional to slit width ( $I \propto w$ ), and also to the square of the amplitude ( $I \propto A^{2}$ ). Therefore, amplitude is proportional to the square root of the slit width $(A \propto \sqrt{w})$.
$\frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{w_{1}}{w_{2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{16}}=\frac{1}{4}$.

subject: Physics
q: To observe a stable and clear interference pattern, which of the following conditions is NOT essential?
o: The sources must have the same frequency.
The sources must have a constant phase difference.
The sources must have the same amplitude.
s: Coherence (same frequency and constant phase difference) is essential for a stable pattern. Monochromatic light is needed for clear, distinct fringes. While having the same amplitude provides the best contrast (with minimum intensity being zero), an interference pattern will still be observed even if the amplitudes are different.

subject: Physics
q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, light of wavelength 600 nm is used. The slits are 0.5 mm apart, and the screen is 1.5 m away. The distance of the 5th bright fringe from the central maximum is (in mm).
s:
The position of the $n^{t h}$ bright fringe is given by $y_{n}=\frac{n \lambda D}{d}$.
Given: $n=5, \lambda=600 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}, D=1.5 \mathrm{~m}, d=0.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}$.
$y_{5}=\frac{5 \times\left(600 \times 10^{-9}\right) \times 1.5}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}}=\frac{4500 \times 10^{-9}}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}}=9000 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}=9 \mathrm{~mm}$.

subject: Physics
q: In a YDSE, a thin transparent sheet of thickness $t$ and refractive index $\mu=1.6$ is placed in the path of one of the interfering beams. This causes the central fringe to shift to a position previously occupied by the 6 th bright fringe. If the wavelength of light used is 500 nm , the thickness $t$ of the sheet is $\qquad$ \[\left( {{\text{in}}\,\,\,\mu {\text{m}}} \right).\]
s:
The shift of the central fringe is $S=\frac{D(\mu-1) t}{d}$.
This shift is equal to the position of the 6th bright fringe, $y_{6}=\frac{6 \lambda D}{d}$.
Equating the two: $\frac{D(\mu-1) t}{d}=\frac{6 \lambda D}{d} \Longrightarrow(\mu-1) t=6 \lambda$.
$t=\frac{6 \lambda}{\mu-1}=\frac{6 \times\left(500 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}\right)}{1.6-1}=\frac{3000 \times 10^{-9}}{0.6}=5000 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}=5 \mu \mathrm{~m}$.

subject: Physics

q: In a YDSE, light of two wavelengths, $\lambda_{1}=520 \mathrm{~nm}$ and $\lambda_{2}=780 \mathrm{~nm}$, are used simultaneously. The minimum order of a bright fringe of $\lambda_{2}$ that coincides with a bright fringe of $\lambda_{1}$ is $n$. The value of $n$ is___
s:
For the coincidence of bright fringes, the condition is $n_{1} y_{1}=n_{2} y_{2}$, which simplifies to $n_{1} \lambda_{1}=n_{2} \lambda_{2}$.
$\frac{n_{1}}{n_{2}}=\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}=\frac{780 \mathrm{~nm}}{520 \mathrm{~nm}}=\frac{78}{52}=\frac{3}{2}$.
The minimum integer values that satisfy this ratio are $n_{1}=3$ and $n_{2}=2$. The question asks for the minimum order for the second wavelength $\left(\lambda_{2}\right)$, which is $n_{2}$. So, $n=2$.

subject: Physics
q: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the intensity at a point is $\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{\text {th }}$ of the maximum intensity. If the smallest angular position of this point is given by $\theta=\frac{\lambda}{N d}$, the value of N is____
s:
The intensity is given by $I=I_{\text {max }} \cos ^{2}\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)$.
Given $I=\frac{I_{\text {max }}}{4}$, so $\frac{I_{\text {max }}}{4}=I_{\text {max }} \cos ^{2}\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right) \Longrightarrow \cos \left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2}$.
This gives $\frac{\phi}{2}=\frac{\pi}{3}$, so the phase difference is $\phi=\frac{2 \pi}{3}$.
The phase difference is also related to the path difference ( $\Delta x$ ) by $\phi=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \Delta x$.
$\frac{2 \pi}{3}=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \Delta x \Longrightarrow \Delta x=\frac{\lambda}{3}$.
For small angles, the path difference is $\Delta x=d \sin \theta \approx d \theta$.
So, $d \theta=\frac{\lambda}{3} \Longrightarrow \theta=\frac{\lambda}{3 d}$.
Comparing this with the given expression $\theta=\frac{\lambda}{N d}$, we find $N=3$.

subject: Physics
q:
Two coherent monochromatic light beams of intensities $I_{0}$ and $25 I_{0}$ are superim-
posed. The difference between the maximum and minimum possible intensities in the resulting interference pattern is $x I_{0}$. The value of $x$ is (in ).
s:
Given $I_{1}=I_{0}$ and $I_{2}=25 I_{0}$. Let the corresponding amplitudes be $A_{1}=A$ and $A_{2}=5 A$ (since $I \propto A^{2}$ ).
$I_{\text {max }} \propto\left(A_{1}+A_{2}\right)^{2}=(A+5 A)^{2}=(6 A)^{2}=36 A^{2}$. So, $I_{\text {max }}=36 I_{0}$.
$I_{\text {min }} \propto\left(A_{2}-A_{1}\right)^{2}=(5 A-A)^{2}=(4 A)^{2}=16 A^{2}$. So, $I_{\text {min }}=16 I_{0}$.
The difference is $I_{\text {max }}-I_{\text {min }}=36 I_{0}-16 I_{0}=20 I_{0}$.
Therefore, $x=20$.

subject: Physics
q: A plane electromagnetic wave of frequency 25 MHz travels in free space along the +x direction. At a particular point in space and time, the electric field is $\vec{E}=6.3 \hat{j} \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}$. The magnetic field $\vec{B}$ at this point is:
s: The magnitude of the magnetic field is $B_{0}=E_{0} / c=6.3 /\left(3 \times 10^{8}\right)=2.1 \times 10^{-8} T$. The direction of propagation is given by $\vec{E} \times \vec{B}$. Since the wave travels in the +x direction $(\hat{i})$ and $\vec{E}$ is in the +y direction $(\hat{j}), \vec{B}$ must be in the +z direction $(\hat{k})$ because $\hat{j} \times \hat{k}=\hat{i}$.

subject: Physics
q: The magnetic field of an E.M. wave is given by $\vec{B}=2 \times 10^{-7} \sin \left(0.5 \times 10^{3} x+1.5 \times 10^{11} t\right) \hat{j} T$. The corresponding electric field is:
s:
The direction of propagation $\vec{S}$ is proportional to $\vec{E} \times \vec{B}$. Given propagation is in $-\hat{i}$ and $\vec{B}$ is in $\hat{j}$. So $\vec{E}_{d i r} \times \hat{j}=-\hat{i}$. This means $\vec{E}_{d i r}$ must be $\hat{k}$,
since $\hat{k} \times \hat{j}=-\hat{i}$. So the answer should be option A . $E_{0}=c B_{0}=3 \times 10^{8} \times 2 \times 10^{-7}=60 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}$. The wave is of the form $\sin (k x+\omega t)$, which propagates in the $-x$ direction. Direction of propagation vector is $-\hat{i} . \vec{B}$ is along $\hat{j}$. The direction of propagation is given by $\vec{E} \times \vec{B}$. So, $\vec{E}_{d i r} \times \hat{j}_{d i r}=-\hat{i}_{d i r}$. This implies $\vec{E}$ must be in the $\hat{k}$ direction, because $\hat{k} \times \hat{j}=-\hat{i}$. Thus, $\vec{E}=60 \sin \left(0.5 \times 10^{3} x+1.5 \times 10^{11} t\right) \hat{k} \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}$.

subject: Physics
q: The electric field of an electromagnetic wave in free space is $\vec{E}=E_{0} \cos (\omega t-k z) \hat{j}$. The corresponding magnetic field vector will be:
s: Wave propagates along $+\mathrm{z} . \vec{E}$ is along $+\mathrm{y}(\hat{j})$. For propagation in $+\mathrm{z}(\hat{k})$, we need $\vec{E} \times \vec{B} \propto \hat{k}$. So, $\hat{j} \times \vec{B}_{\text {dir }}=\hat{k}$. This means $\vec{B}_{\text {dir }}$ must be $\hat{i}$. Wait, $\hat{j} \times \hat{i}=-\hat{k}$. So $\vec{B}$ should be in the $-\hat{i}$ direction for the cross product to be $\hat{j} \times(-\hat{i})=-(\hat{j} \times \hat{i})=-(-\hat{k})=\hat{k}$. Correct. The magnitude is $B_{0}=E_{0} / c$. So, $\vec{B}=-\frac{E_{0}}{c} \cos (\omega t-k z) \hat{i}$.

subject: Physics
q: A light wave of frequency $6 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz}$ enters a medium of refractive index 1.5. In the medium, its frequency is:
s: When light enters a different medium, its speed and wavelength change, but its frequency remains constant.

subject: Physics
q: The relative permeability of a medium is 2 and its relative permittivity is 8 . The speed of electromagnetic waves in this medium will be:
s: The refractive index is $n=\sqrt{\mu_{r} \epsilon_{r}}=\sqrt{2 \times 8}=\sqrt{16}=4$. The speed in the $\underline{\text { medium is } v=c / n=\left(3 \times 10^{8}\right) / 4=0.75 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \text {. }}$

subject: Physics
q: If an electromagnetic wave has a wavelength of 3 m in free space, its frequency is:
s: Using $c=f \lambda$, the frequency is $f=c / \lambda=\left(3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right) /(3 \mathrm{~m})=1 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~Hz} \equiv 100 \mathrm{MHz}$.

subject: Physics
q: A plane electromagnetic wave propagates along the z -direction. Which of the following pairs of vectors is a possible representation of the electric and magnetic fields?
s: Electromagnetic waves are transverse, meaning $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ are perpendicular to the direction of propagation. So, $E_{z}$ and $B_{z}$ must be zero. Also, $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ are perpendicular to each other. In option (A), $\vec{E}$ is along $\hat{i}$ and $\vec{B}$ is along $\hat{j}$. The direction of propagation $\vec{E} \times \vec{B}$ is along $\hat{i} \times \hat{j}=\hat{k}$, which is the z-direction.

subject: Physics
q: The intensity of an electromagnetic wave is given by $I=\frac{1}{2} c \epsilon_{0} E_{0}^{2}$. The unit of $E_{0}$ is equivalent to:
s: $E_{0}$ represents the amplitude of the electric field. The standard unit for electric field is Volts per meter ( $V / m$ or $V m^{-1}$ ), which is equivalent to Newtons per Coulomb $(N / C)$.

subject: Physics
q: The electric field for a plane electromagnetic wave is given by $\vec{E}=\hat{j} 50 \cos [\omega(t-x / c)] N / C$. The magnetic field is:
s: Wave propagates along $+\mathrm{x} . \vec{E}$ is along $+\mathrm{y}(\hat{j})$. We need $\vec{E} \times \vec{B} \propto \hat{i}$. So, $\underline{\hat{j} \times B_{d i r}=\hat{i}}$. This is satisfied if $\vec{B}_{d i r}=\hat{k}$. The magnitude is $B_{0}=E_{0} / c$.

subject: Physics
q: An electromagnetic wave travels in a medium of relative permittivity 2.25 and relative permeability 4 . Its speed is:
s: $n=\sqrt{\mu_{r} \epsilon_{r}}=\sqrt{4 \times 2.25}=\sqrt{9}=3$. The speed is $v=c / n=\left(3 \times 10^{8}\right) / 3= \underline{1 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \text {. }}$

subject: Physics
q: The equation for the magnetic field of an EM wave in vacuum is $B_{y}=4 \times 10^{-6} \sin (\omega t+k x)$. The amplitude of the corresponding electric field is:
s: The amplitude is $E_{0}=c B_{0}=\left(3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right) \times\left(4 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~T}\right)=12 \times 10^{2}= \underline{1200 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m} \text {. }}$

subject: Physics
q: An EM wave is propagating in a medium with velocity $\vec{v}=v \hat{i}$. The instantaneous electric field is $\vec{E}=E_{0} \hat{j}$. The direction of the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is:
s: The direction of propagation is given by $\vec{E} \times \vec{B}$. So, $\hat{j} \times \vec{B}_{d i r}=\hat{i}$. This condition is satisfied if $\vec{B}$ is along the $\hat{k}$ direction, since $\hat{j} \times \hat{k}=\hat{i}$.

subject: Physics
q: A monochromatic light of wavelength 500 nm traveling in air enters a glass slab of refractive index 1.5. The wavelength of light in the glass will be:
s: Wavelength in medium is $\lambda_{\text {medium }}=\lambda_{\text {air }} / n=500 \mathrm{~nm} / 1.5 \approx 333.3 \mathrm{~nm}$.

subject: Physics
q: The ratio of the amplitude of the magnetic field to the amplitude of the electric field for an electromagnetic wave propagating in vacuum is equal to:
o: the speed of light in vacuum, $c$.
the reciprocal of the speed of light, $1 / c$.
s: We know $E_{0}=c B_{0}$. Therefore, the ratio $B_{0} / E_{0}=1 / c$.

subject: Physics
q: The electric field part of an electromagnetic wave in a medium is represented by $E_{x}=0$; $E_{y}=2.5 \frac{\mathrm{~N}}{\mathrm{C}} \cos \left[\left(2 \pi \times 10^{6} \frac{\mathrm{rad}}{\mathrm{s}}\right) t-\left(\pi \times 10^{-2} \frac{\mathrm{rad}}{\mathrm{m}}\right) x\right] ; E_{z}=0$. The wave is:
o: moving along $-x$ direction with wavelength 200 m .
s: The term $\omega t-k x$ indicates propagation along the +x -axis. Comparing with the standard form $\cos (\omega t-k x)$, we have $\omega=2 \pi \times 10^{6} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. The frequency is $f= \underline{\omega} / 2 \pi=\left(2 \pi \times 10^{6}\right) / 2 \pi=10^{6} \mathrm{~Hz}$.

subject: Physics
q: The speed of an electromagnetic wave in a material medium is given by $v=1 / \sqrt{\mu \epsilon}$, where $\mu$ is the permeability and $\epsilon$ is the permittivity of the medium. If the relative permeability is 1 and the dielectric constant (relative permittivity) is $K$, then the speed of the EM wave is:
s: $v=1 / \sqrt{\mu \epsilon}=1 / \sqrt{\left(\mu_{r} \mu_{0}\right)\left(K \epsilon_{0}\right)}=\left(1 / \sqrt{\mu_{0} \epsilon_{0}}\right) \times\left(1 / \sqrt{\mu_{r} K}\right)$. Since $\mu_{r}=1$ and $c=1 / \sqrt{\mu_{0} \epsilon_{0}}$, we get $v=c / \sqrt{K}$.

subject: Physics
q: The magnetic field of an EM wave propagating along the $-\hat{z}$ direction is $\vec{B}=(\hat{i}- \hat{j}) B_{0} \sin (\omega t+k z)$. The electric field is:
s: Propagation is along $-\hat{k} . \vec{E}$ must be perpendicular to $\vec{B}$, so $\vec{E} \cdot \vec{B}=0$. This is satisfied by $\vec{E} \propto(\hat{i}+\hat{j})$. We need the direction of propagation $\vec{S} \propto \vec{E} \times \vec{B}$. So, we need $\vec{E} \times \vec{B} \propto-\hat{k}$. Let's check: $(\hat{i}+\hat{j}) \times(\hat{i}-\hat{j})=\hat{i} \times(-\hat{j})+\hat{j} \times \hat{i}=-\hat{k}-\hat{k}=-2 \hat{k}$. This matches the direction. The magnitude is $E_{0}=c B_{0}$. Thus, $\vec{E}=c(\hat{i}+\hat{j}) B_{0} \sin (\omega t+k z)$.

subject: Physics
q: An electromagnetic wave of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident on a photosensitive surface of negligible work function. If 'm' is mass of photoelectron emitted from the surface, the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda_{d}$ is:
s: Energy of photon $E=h c / \lambda$. Since work function is negligible, kinetic energy of photoelectron is $K E=h c / \lambda$. Also, $K E=p^{2} / 2 m$, so $p=\sqrt{2 m(K E)}=\sqrt{2 m(h c / \lambda)}$. The de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda_{d}=h / p=h / \sqrt{2 m h c / \lambda}=\sqrt{h^{2} \lambda / 2 m h c}=\sqrt{h \lambda / 2 m c}$.

subject: Physics
q: For an electromagnetic wave, the phase difference between electric and magnetic field vectors $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{B}$ is:
s: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields are always in the same phase. They reach their maximum and minimum values at the same time and place.

subject: Physics
q: The energy of an electromagnetic wave is associated with:
s: The energy in an electromagnetic wave is shared equally between the electric field and the magnetic field. The energy density is $u=u_{E}+u_{B}=\frac{1}{2} \epsilon_{0} E^{2}+\frac{1}{2 \mu_{0}} B^{2}$.

subject: Physics
q: The maximum electric field in a plane electromagnetic wave is $60 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}$. The wave is going in the +z direction and the electric field is in the +x direction. The maximum magnetic field is $P \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~T}$. The value of P is______. $\qquad$
s: The magnitude of the maximum magnetic field is given by $B_{0}=E_{0} / c$. $B_{0}=60 /\left(3 \times 10^{8}\right)=20 \times 10^{-8}=2 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~T}$. Comparing with $P \times 10^{-7} T$, we get $P=2$.

subject: Physics
q: Electromagnetic waves travel in a medium with a speed of $2 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. If the relative permeability of the medium is 1.0 , its relative permittivity is n/4. The value of n is________
s: The refractive index is $n=c / v=\left(3 \times 10^{8}\right) /\left(2 \times 10^{8}\right)=1.5$. Also, $n=\sqrt{\mu_{r} \epsilon_{r}}$. $\underline{1.5}=\sqrt{1.0 \times \epsilon_{r}} \Longrightarrow \epsilon_{r}=(1.5)^{2}=9$.

subject: Physics
q: The frequency of an electromagnetic wave is 50 MHz and it travels in free space along the z -direction. The wavelength of the wave (in m ) is_______. $\qquad$

subject: Physics
q: In a medium, the speed of light is found to be $1.2 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. If the relative magnetic permeability of the medium is 1 , the dielectric constant (relative permittivity) of the medium is n/4. The value of n is ______.
s: $n=c / v=\left(3 \times 10^{8}\right) /\left(1.2 \times 10^{8}\right)=3 / 1.2=2.5 . n=\sqrt{\mu_{r} \epsilon_{r}} \Longrightarrow 2.5= \underline{\sqrt{1 \times \epsilon_{r}}} \Longrightarrow \epsilon_{r}=(2.5)^{2}= 25$.

subject: Physics
q: An electromagnetic wave in vacuum has its electric field given by $\vec{E}=\hat{j} E_{0} \sin (k x-\omega t)$, where $k=0.5 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{m}$. The wavelength of the wave in nanometers is______ \[\left( {{\text{in}}\,\,\,\,nm} \right).\] (Take $\pi=3.14$ )

subject: Physics
q: A liquid drop of radius R is split into 64 identical smaller drops. If T is the surface tension of the liquid, the work done in this process is:
s: Let the radius of the small drops be r. By conserving volume, $\frac{4}{3} \pi R^{3}= 64 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3} \Longrightarrow R=4 r \Longrightarrow r=R / 4$. Initial surface area $A_{i}=4 \pi R^{2}$. Final surface area $A_{f}=64 \times 4 \pi r^{2}=64 \times 4 \pi(R / 4)^{2}=16 \pi R^{2}$. Work done $W=T \Delta A= T\left(A_{f}-A_{i}\right)=T\left(16 \pi R^{2}-4 \pi R^{2}\right)=12 \pi R^{2} T$.

subject: Physics
q: The work done in blowing a soap bubble of radius R is W . The additional work required to double its radius is:
s: A soap bubble has two surfaces. Work done is $W=T \times \Delta A=T \times 8 \pi R^{2}$. So $W \propto R^{2}$. To double the radius to 2 R , the final work done from start is $W^{\prime}=T \times 8 \pi(2 R)^{2}=4 \times\left(T \times 8 \pi R^{2}\right)=4 W$. The additional work required is $W_{\text {add }}=W^{\prime}-W=4 W-W=3 W$.

subject: Physics
q: The work done in blowing a soap bubble from an initial radius of 2 cm to a final radius of 3 cm is $600 \pi \mathrm{ergs}$. The surface tension of the soap solution is____________ (in dyne/cm).
s: A soap bubble has two free surfaces. The work done is equal to the change in surface energy. $W=T \times \Delta A=T \times\left[8 \pi R_{f}^{2}-8 \pi R_{i}^{2}\right]$. $600 \pi=T \times 8 \pi\left(3^{2}-\right. \left.2^{2}\right)=T \times 8 \pi(9-4)=T \times 8 \pi \times 5=40 \pi T$. $T=\frac{600 \pi}{40 \pi}=15$ dyne $/ \mathrm{cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: Two wires are made of the same material. Wire 1 has twice the diameter and twice the length of wire 2. If both wires are stretched by the same force, the ratio of the elongation of wire 1 to that of wire 2 is:
s: Elongation $\Delta L=\frac{F L}{A Y}=\frac{F L}{\left(\pi d^{2} / 4\right) Y}$. So, $\Delta L \propto \frac{L}{d^{2}}$. $\quad \frac{\Delta L_{1}}{\Delta L_{2}}=\frac{L_{1}}{d_{1}^{2}} \times \frac{d_{2}^{2}}{L_{2}}= \left(\frac{2 L_{2}}{\left(2 d_{2}\right)^{2}}\right) \times \frac{d_{2}^{2}}{L_{2}}=\frac{2}{4}=\frac{1}{2}$.

subject: Physics
q: Assertion (A): Steel is more elastic than rubber. Reason (R): For a given deformation (strain), steel requires a larger restoring force (stress) than rubber.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
s:
Elasticity is measured by Young's modulus, $Y=$ Stress/Strain. A higher Y means more elastic. Since steel has a much higher Y than rubber, it is more elastic. 
This high Y value means a large stress is needed for a small strain, which is what the Reason states.

subject: Physics
q: When a load is applied to a wire, it elongates by 1 mm . If a wire of the same material and length but twice the radius is used with the same load, the elongation will be:
s: $\Delta L \propto \frac{1}{A} \propto \frac{1}{r^{2}}$. If the radius is doubled, the elongation becomes $(1 / 2)^{2}= 1 / 4$ of the original. So, $\Delta L^{\prime}=\frac{1}{4} \times 1 \mathrm{~mm}=0.25 \mathrm{~mm}$.

subject: Physics
q: For a wire to break under its own weight, its length must be greater than a certain value. This breaking length depends on:
s:
The weight of the wire is $W=m g=(A L \rho) g$. 
The stress at the top is $W / A=L \rho g$. For breaking, $L \rho g=$ Breaking Stress. 
So, the breaking length $L=\frac{\text { Breaking Stress }}{\rho g}$. 
It depends on density $(\rho)$ and g.

subject: Physics
q: A 2 kg mass is attached to the end of a wire of length 4 m and diameter 1 mm . It is whirled in a horizontal circle at a constant angular speed of $1 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. The elongation of the wire is ( $\mathrm{Y}=2 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$ ):
s: Centripetal force $F=m \omega^{2} L=2 \times(1)^{2} \times 4=8 \mathrm{~N}$. Area $A=\pi r^{2}= \pi\left(0.5 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2}$. $\Delta L=\frac{F L}{A Y}=\frac{8 \times 4}{\pi\left(0.5 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2} \times\left(2 \times 10^{11}\right)}=\frac{32}{0.5 \pi \times 10^{5}}=\frac{64}{\pi \times 10^{5}} \approx 20.4 \times 10^{-5}= 2.04 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}$.

subject: Physics
q: Two wires of the same material have their lengths in the ratio $1: 2$ and their diameters in the ratio $2: 1$. When stretched by the same force, the ratio of work done in stretching them is:
s:
Work done $W=\frac{1}{2} F \Delta L$. Since F is the same, $W \propto \Delta L$. $\Delta L \propto \frac{L}{d^{2}}$. 
So, $\frac{W_{1}}{W_{2}}=\frac{\Delta L_{1}}{\Delta L_{2}}=\frac{L_{1}}{d_{1}^{2}} \times \frac{d_{2}^{2}}{L_{2}}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{8}$.

s:
The weight of the load is $W=m g=2.16 \times 10=21.6 \mathrm{~N}$.
The force balance and Young's modulus equations, using the small angle approximation for the sag, lead to the following formula for the vertical depression:
$$
y=\left(\frac{W L^3}{8 A Y}\right)^{1 / 3}
$$
Plugging in the given values:
- $W=21.6 \mathrm{~N}$
- $L=1 \mathrm{~m}$
- $A=4.00 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m} \$^{\wedge} 2 \$$
- $Y=2.0 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m} \$^{\wedge} 2 \$$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& y=\left(\frac{21.6 \times(1)^3}{8 \times\left(4.00 \times 10^{-6}\right) \times\left(2.0 \times 10^{11}\right)}\right)^{1 / 3} \\
& y=\left(\frac{21.6}{64 \times 10^5}\right)^{1 / 3}=\left(3.375 \times 10^{-6}\right)^{1 / 3} \\
& y=0.015 \mathrm{~m}=1.5 \mathrm{~cm}
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus, the vertical depression is 1.5 cm .

subject: Physics
q: With rise in temperature, the Young's modulus of a material generally:
s: With a rise in temperature, the interatomic forces of attraction decrease, making the material less resistant to deformation. Thus, Young's modulus decreases.

subject: Physics
q: A steel wire of length 2 m is stretched through 2 mm . The crosssectional area of the wire is $4 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$. If Y for steel is $2 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$, the elastic potential energy stored in the wire is:
s: Energy $U=\frac{1}{2} \times Y \times(\text { strain })^{2} \times$ Volume. Strain $=\Delta L / L=\left(2 \times 10^{-3}\right) / 2= 10^{-3}$. Volume $=A \times L=\left(4 \times 10^{-6}\right) \times 2=8 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{3}$. $U=\frac{1}{2} \times\left(2 \times 10^{11}\right) \times \left(10^{-3}\right)^{2} \times\left(8 \times 10^{-6}\right)=10^{11} \times 10^{-6} \times 8 \times 10^{-6}=0.8 \mathrm{~J}$.

subject: Physics
q: A wire of length 1 m and cross-sectional area $10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ is suspended from a rigid support. A load of 1 kg is attached. If $\mathrm{Y}=2 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$, the strain is $N \times 10^{-5}$. Find N. ( $\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ ).
s: Stress $=F / A=(1 \times 10) / 10^{-6}=10^{7} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. Strain = Stress $/ \mathrm{Y}= 10^{7} /\left(2 \times 10^{11}\right)=0.5 \times 10^{-4}=5 \times 10^{-5}$. Thus, $\mathrm{N}=5$.

subject: Physics
q: Two blocks of mass 1 kg and 2 kg are connected by a metal wire over a smooth pulley. The radius of the wire is $2 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}$ and its Young's modulus is $2 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. The longitudinal strain developed in the wire is $\frac{1}{N \pi}$. Find the value of N . (Use $\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ ).
s:
Acceleration of the system $a=\frac{(2-1) g}{2+1}=\frac{g}{3}=\frac{10}{3} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. 
Tension in the wire $T=m_{1}(g+a)=1(10+10 / 3)=40 / 3 \mathrm{~N}$. Area $A=\pi r^{2}=\pi\left(2 \times 10^{-4}\right)^{2}=4 \pi \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{m}^{2}$. 
Stress $=\frac{T}{A}=\frac{40 / 3}{4 \pi \times 10^{-8}}=\frac{10}{3 \pi \times 10^{-8}}=\frac{10^{9}}{3 \pi} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. 
Strain $=\frac{\text { Stress }}{Y}=\frac{10^{9} / 3 \pi}{2 \times 10^{11}}= \frac{10^{9}}{6 \pi \times 10^{11}}=\frac{1}{6 \pi \times 10^{2}}=\frac{1}{600 \pi}$. 
This gives $\mathrm{N}=600$.

subject: Physics
q: A metal wire of length 2 m and diameter 1 mm is stretched by a force of 100 N . The resulting elongation is 1 mm . The Young's modulus of the metal is $\frac{x}{\pi} \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. Find the value of x .
s: $L=2 \mathrm{~m}, d=1 \mathrm{~mm}\left(r=0.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}\right), F=100 \mathrm{~N}, \Delta L=1 \mathrm{~mm} =10^{-3} \mathrm{~m} . \quad Y=\frac{F / A}{\Delta L / L}=\frac{F L}{A \Delta L} . \quad A=\pi r^{2}=\pi\left(0.5 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2}=0.25 \pi \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$. $Y=\frac{100 \times 2}{\left(0.25 \pi \times 10^{-6}\right) \times 10^{-3}}=\frac{200}{0.25 \pi \times 10^{-9}}=\frac{800}{\pi} \times 10^{9}=\frac{8}{\pi} \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. Comparing this with $\frac{x}{\pi} \times 10^{11}$, we get $\mathrm{x}=8$.

subject: Physics
q: An enclosed gas is taken through a cycle as shown in the figure. Which of the following is true? [IMAGE: images/MB000651_1.webp]
o: along AB , the temperature increases, while along BC the temperature decreases
along AB , the temperature decreases, while along BC , temperature increases
along CA, work is done on the gas, and the internal energy of the gas decreases
along CA, work is done by the gas and the internal energy remains constant
s:
Process $\mathbf{A} \rightarrow \mathbf{B}$ : This is an isobaric (constant pressure) expansion. Since volume increases, temperature must increase ( $T \propto V$ ).
Process B $\rightarrow$ C: This is an isochoric (constant volume) process where pressure increases. Since pressure increases, temperature must increase ( $T \propto P$ ).
Process $\mathbf{C} \rightarrow \mathbf{A}$ : In this process, both pressure $P$ and volume $V$ decrease. Since volume decreases, work is done on the gas. The temperature is proportional to the product $P V(T \propto P V)$. As both P and V decrease, their product $P V$ decreases, so the temperature decreases, and thus the internal energy decreases.
Evaluating the options: (A) and (B) are incorrect because temperature increases along both AB and BC . (C) is correct. Along CA, work is done on the gas (compression) and internal energy decreases (temperature drops). (D) is incorrect.

subject: Physics
q: If the root mean square (RMS) velocity of nitrogen molecules ( $N_{2}$ ) at a certain temperature is $v$, the RMS velocity of helium atoms (He) at the same temperature will be: (Molar mass of $N_{2}=28 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}, \mathrm{He}=4 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$ )
s:
The RMS velocity is given by $v_{r m s}=\sqrt{\frac{3 R T}{M}}$. 
At the same temperature $\mathrm{T}, v_{r m s} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}$.
$$
\frac{v_{H e}}{v_{N_{2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{M_{N_{2}}}{M_{H e}}}=\sqrt{\frac{28}{4}}=\sqrt{7}
$$
$$
v_{H e}=v_{N_{2}} \sqrt{7}=v \sqrt{7}
$$

subject: Physics
q: A diatomic gas ( $\gamma=1.4$ ) does 200 J of work during an isobaric expansion. The heat supplied to the gas during this process is:
s:
In an isobaric process, work done $W=n R \Delta T$ and heat supplied $Q=n C_{P} \Delta T$. 
For a diatomic gas, $C_{P}=\frac{7}{2} R$. The ratio is $\frac{W}{Q}=\frac{n R \Delta T}{n C_{P} \Delta T}=\frac{R}{C_{P}}=\frac{R}{(7 / 2) R}=\frac{2}{7}$.
$$
Q=\frac{7}{2} W=\frac{7}{2} \times 200=700 \mathrm{~J}
$$

subject: Physics
q: In an adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas, the quantity that remains constant is:
s:
The equation for an adiabatic process is $P V^{\gamma}=$ constant. 
From the ideal gas law, $P=\frac{n R T}{V}$. Substituting this gives $\left(\frac{n R T}{V}\right) V^{\gamma}=$ constant, which simplifies to $T V^{\gamma-1}=$ constant since $n$ and $R$ are constants.

subject: Physics
q: In comparing the isothermal and adiabatic expansions of an ideal gas from the same initial state, which statement is correct?
o: The work done in the adiabatic process is greater than in the isothermal process.
The final temperature in the adiabatic process is higher than in the isothermal process.
The final pressure in the adiabatic process is lower than in the isothermal process.
The slope of the adiabatic curve on a $\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{V}$ diagram is less steep than the isothermal curve.
s:
The adiabatic curve ( $P V^{\gamma}=$ const) is steeper than the isothermal curve ( $P V=$ const) because $\gamma>1$. 
For the same expansion of volume, the pressure drops more in an adiabatic process. 
This results in a lower final pressure and less work done compared to an isothermal expansion.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Degree of freedom of mixture of gases
q: One mole of a monoatomic ideal gas is mixed with one mole of a diatomic ideal gas. The value of $\gamma$ for the mixture is:
s:
$C_{V, \text { mix }}=\frac{n_{1} C_{V 1}+n_{2} C_{V 2}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}=\frac{1 \cdot \frac{3}{2} R+1 \cdot \frac{5}{2} R}{1+1}=\frac{4 R}{2}=2 R . C_{P, \text { mix }}=\frac{n_{1} C_{P 1}+n_{2} C_{P 2}}{n_{1}+n_{2}}=\frac{1 \cdot \frac{5}{2} R+1 \cdot \frac{7}{2} R}{1+1}= \frac{6 R}{2}=3 R$.
$$
\gamma_{\operatorname{mix}}=\frac{C_{P, \operatorname{mix}}}{C_{V, \operatorname{mix}}}=\frac{3 R}{2 R}=1.5
$$

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Different types of speeds of gases
q: The temperature of an ideal gas is increased from 120 K to 480 K . If at 120 K the root mean square velocity of the gas molecules is $v$, at 480 K it becomes:
s:
RMS velocity $v_{r m s} \propto \sqrt{T}$.
$$
\frac{v_{2}}{v_{1}}=\sqrt{\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}}=\sqrt{\frac{480}{120}}=\sqrt{4}=2
$$
So, $v_{2}=2 v_{1}=2 v$.

subject: Physics
q: The internal energy of 2 moles of an ideal diatomic gas at 300 K is approximately: (Use $R=8.314 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{mol}-\mathrm{K}$ )
s:
Internal energy $U=n C_{V} T$. For a diatomic gas, $C_{V}=\frac{5}{2} R$.
$$
U=2 \times\left(\frac{5}{2} R\right) \times 300=1500 R=1500 \times 8.314 \approx 12471 \mathrm{~J}
$$

subject: Physics
q: A gas is compressed adiabatically till its pressure becomes 8 times the initial pressure. The ratio of final volume to initial volume will be: (Given $\gamma=3 / 2$ )
s:
For an adiabatic process, $P_{1} V_{1}^{\gamma}=P_{2} V_{2}^{\gamma} \Longrightarrow \frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}=\left(\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}}\right)^{1 / \gamma}$.
$$
\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}=\left(\frac{P_{1}}{8 P_{1}}\right)^{1 /(3 / 2)}=\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{2 / 3}=\left(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3}\right)^{2 / 3}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{4}
$$

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Cp and Cv of a gas/gaseous mixture
q: The ratio of two specific heats $C_{P} / C_{V}$ of a gas is 1.66 . The gas is:
s:
$\gamma \approx 1.67 \approx 5 / 3$. For a monoatomic gas, degrees of freedom $\mathrm{f}=3$.
$$
\gamma=1+\frac{2}{f}=1+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{5}{3} \approx 1.67
$$

subject: Physics
q:
Figure shows a cyclic process a b c a for one mole of an ideal gas. If ab is isothermal process, then which of the following is the P-T diagram for cyclic process?
 [IMAGE: images/MB000670_1.webp]
s:
Let's analyze the given P-V diagram for the cyclic process $a \rightarrow b \rightarrow c \rightarrow a$. From the graph, we can identify the coordinates of the vertices as: State a: $\left(V, 2 P_{1}\right)$, State b: $\left(2 V, P_{1}\right)$, State c: $\left(V, P_{1}\right)$. We use the ideal gas law, $P V=n R T$. For one mole, $n=1$.
Process $\mathbf{a} \rightarrow \mathbf{b}$ : This is an isothermal process, so temperature is constant ( $T_{a}=T_{b}$ ). On a P-T diagram, this is a vertical line downwards as pressure decreases from $2 P_{1}$ to $P_{1}$.
Process $\mathbf{b} \rightarrow \mathbf{c}$ : This is an isobaric compression (constant pressure $P_{1}$ ). For an isobaric process, $V \propto T$. Since volume decreases, the temperature must also decrease. On a P-T diagram, this is a horizontal line moving to the left.
Process $\mathbf{c} \rightarrow \mathbf{a}$ : This is an isochoric heating process (constant volume $V$ ). For an isochoric process, $P \propto T$. This corresponds to a straight line passing through the origin on a P-T diagram.
Combining these steps, the P-T diagram must be a triangle formed by a vertical line segment ( $a \rightarrow b$ ), a horizontal line segment ( $b \rightarrow c$ ), and a straight line passing through the origin ( $c \rightarrow a$ ). This shape matches option (A).

subject: Physics
q: 2 moles of an ideal gas expand from a volume of 10 litres to 20 litres at a constant pressure of $1 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$. The work done by the gas is__________ J.
s:
Work done in an isobaric process is $W=P \Delta V=P\left(V_{\text {final }}-V_{\text {initial }}\right) . P=1 \times 10^{5}$ Pa. $\Delta V=20 \mathrm{~L}-10 \mathrm{~L}=10 \mathrm{~L}=10 \times 10^{-3} m^{3}$.
$$
W=\left(1 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}\right) \times\left(10 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^{3}\right)=1000 \mathrm{~J}
$$

subject: Physics
q: Calculate the change in internal energy (in J) when 2 moles of Helium (a monoatomic gas) are heated from 100 K to 200 K . (Use $R=8.3 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{mol}-\mathrm{K}$ )
s:
$\Delta U=n C_{V} \Delta T$. For a monoatomic gas, $C_{V}=\frac{3}{2} R . n=2$ moles, $\Delta T=200 \mathrm{~K}-100 \mathrm{K}=100 \mathrm{~K}$.
$$
\Delta U=2 \times\left(\frac{3}{2} R\right) \times 100=3 \times R \times 100=3 \times 8.3 \times 100=2490 \mathrm{~J}
$$

subject: Physics
q: A nucleus at rest disintegrates into two parts with masses in the ratio $3: 5$. The ratio of their kinetic energies (lighter part : heavier part) is $5: \mathrm{N}$. The value of N is__________. $\qquad$
s: By conservation of momentum, the two parts have equal and opposite momenta, $p$. Kinetic energy is $K=p^{2} /(2 m)$. Since p is the same, K is inversely proportional to mass m . $\frac{K_{\text {lighter }}}{K_{\text {heavier }}}=\frac{m_{\text {heavier }}}{m_{\text {lighter }}}=\frac{5}{3}$. The ratio is $5: 3$, so $\mathrm{N}=3$.

subject: Physics
q: The gravitational potential at the Earth's surface is V . What is the gravitational potential at a height equal to the Earth's radius (R)?
s: Gravitational potential $V=-G M / r$. At surface, $V_{s}=-G M / R$. At height $h=R$, the distance from center is $r=2 R$. So, $V_{h}=-G M /(2 R)=(1 / 2)(-G M / R)=V_{s} / 2$.

subject: Physics
q: Two point charges $+4 q$ and $+q$ are placed at a distance $L$ apart. A third charge $Q$ is placed on the line joining them such that the entire system is in equilibrium. The distance of charge $Q$ from $+4 q$ is:
s: For the system to be in equilibrium, the net force on each charge must be zero. Let the charge $Q$ be placed at a distance $x$ from $+4 q$. Force on $Q$ is zero: $\frac{k(4 q) Q}{x^{2}}= \frac{k(q) Q}{(L-x)^{2}} \Longrightarrow \frac{4}{x^{2}}=\frac{1}{(L-x)^{2}} \Longrightarrow \frac{2}{x}=\frac{1}{L-x} \Longrightarrow 2 L-2 x=x \Longrightarrow x=\frac{2 L}{3}$.

subject: Physics
q: The force between two point charges $q_{1}$ and $q_{2}$ in a vacuum is $F$. If they are placed at the same distance in a medium with a dielectric constant $K=4$, the new electric force on any one them will be:
s: The force in a medium is given by $F_{\text {medium }}=\frac{F_{\text {vacuum }}}{K}$. Given $K=4$, the new force is $F^{\prime}=\frac{F}{4}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Electric field due to a point charge or combination of point charges
q: A point charge $+q$ is placed at the origin ( $0,0,0$ ) and another point charge $+4 q$ is placed at ( $a, 0,0$ ). The point on the x-axis where the electric field is zero is:
s: Let the point be at a distance $x$ from the origin. For the net field to be zero, the magnitudes of the fields must be equal: $\frac{k q}{x^{2}}=\frac{k(4 q)}{(a-x)^{2}} \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{x^{2}}=\frac{4}{(a-x)^{2}} \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{x}= \frac{2}{a-x} \Longrightarrow a-x=2 x \Longrightarrow 3 x=a \Longrightarrow x=a / 3$.

subject: Physics
q: The ratio of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force between a proton and an electron is of the order of:
s: The ratio is $\frac{F_{e}}{F_{g}}=\frac{k e^{2}}{G m_{p} m_{e}}=\frac{\left(9 \times 10^{9}\right)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)^{2}}{\left(6.67 \times 10^{-11}\right)\left(1.67 \times 10^{-27}\right)\left(9.1 \times 10^{-31}\right)} \approx 2.27 \times 10^{39}$. The order is $10^{39}$.

subject: Physics
q: An electric field is given by $\vec{E}=(3 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}) N / C$. The electric flux through a surface of area $10 \hat{i} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ in the YZ-plane is:
s: Electric flux $\phi=\vec{E} \cdot \vec{A}=(3 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}) \cdot(10 \hat{i})=(3)(10)+(2)(0)=30 \mathrm{Vm}$.

subject: Physics
q: A charge $Q$ is placed at the center of a cube. The electric flux through one face of the cube is:
s: By Gauss's law, the total flux through the cube is $\phi_{\text {total }}=\frac{Q}{\epsilon_{0}}$. A cube has 6 $\underline{\text { identical faces, so the flux through one face is } \phi_{\text {face }}=\frac{\phi_{\text {total }}}{6}=\frac{Q}{6 \epsilon_{0}}}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Force between charges in a dielectric medium
q: Two identical charged spheres suspended from a common point by two strings of equal length make an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with each other. When suspended in a liquid of density $0.5 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$, the angle remains the same. If the density of the material of the sphere is $1.5 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$, the dielectric constant of the liquid is:
s: Since the angle is the same, the condition is $K=\frac{\rho}{\rho-\sigma}$, where $\rho$ is the density of the sphere and $\sigma$ is the density of the liquid. $K=\frac{1.5}{1.5-0.5}=\frac{1.5}{1.0}=1.5$.

subject: Physics
q: An uncharged conducting sphere of radius $R$ is brought in contact with an identical sphere having charge $Q$. After contact, they are separated by a large distance $d$. The force of repulsion between them is proportional to:
s: When brought into contact, each sphere gets a charge of $q=Q / 2$. The electrostatic force between them is $F=k \frac{(Q / 2)(Q / 2)}{d^{2}}=k \frac{Q^{2}}{4 d^{2}}$. Thus, $F \propto \frac{Q^{2}}{d^{2}}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Calculation of electric flux due to uniform electric field
q: The electric field in a region is given by $\vec{E}=(4 \hat{i}+5 \hat{j}+6 \hat{k}) \times 10^{3} N / C$. The flux through a surface of area $20 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ parallel to the y-z plane is:
s: The area vector for a surface parallel to the y -z plane is in the $\hat{i}$ direction. Area $\underline{\vec{A}=\left(20 \times 10^{-4}\right) \hat{i} m^{2} \text {. Flux } \phi=\vec{E} \cdot \vec{A}=\left(4 \times 10^{3} \hat{i}\right) \cdot\left(20 \times 10^{-4} \hat{i}\right)=80 \times 10^{-1}=8 \mathrm{Nm}^{2} / C \text {. }}$

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Force between charges in a dielectric medium
q: Force between two point charges $q_{1}$ and $q_{2}$ placed in vacuum at distance ' $r$ ' is F . Force between them when placed in a medium having dielectric constant $K=5$ at a distance ' $r / 2$ ' apart will be:
s:
Initial force $F=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{r^{2}}$. New force $F^{\prime}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} K} \frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{(r / 2)^{2}}=\frac{4}{K}\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{r^{2}}\right)=\frac{4 F}{K}$.
Given $K=5, F^{\prime}=\frac{4 F}{5}$.

subject: Physics
q: A small conducting sphere with charge $6 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{C}$ is touched by an identical uncharged sphere and then removed. The two spheres are then placed 3 cm apart. The force between them is: (Take $\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}}=9 \times 10^{9}$ SI units)
s:
After touching, charge is shared equally: $q_{1}=q_{2}=\frac{6 \times 10^{-8}}{2}=3 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{C}$.
Distance $r=0.03 \mathrm{~m}$. Force $F=k \frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{r^{2}}=\left(9 \times 10^{9}\right) \frac{\left(3 \times 10^{-8}\right)^{2}}{(0.03)^{2}}=\left(9 \times 10^{9}\right) \frac{9 \times 10^{-16}}{9 \times 10^{-4}}=9 \times 10^{-3} N$.

subject: Physics
q: The electric flux entering and leaving a closed surface are $5 \times 10^{5}$ and $4 \times 10^{5}$ units respectively. The charge enclosed by the surface is:
s: Net flux $\phi_{\text {net }}=\phi_{\text {out }}-\phi_{\text {in }}=\left(4 \times 10^{5}\right)-\left(5 \times 10^{5}\right)=-1 \times 10^{5}$ units. By Gauss's law, $\phi_{\text {net }}=\frac{q_{\text {enc }}}{\epsilon_{0}} \Longrightarrow q_{\text {enc }}=\phi_{\text {net }} \cdot \epsilon_{0}=-1 \times 10^{5} \epsilon_{0}$.

subject: Physics
q: Two positive ions, each carrying a charge $q$, are separated by a distance $d$. If $F$ is the force of repulsion between the ions, the number of electrons missing from each ion will be: ( $e$ is the charge of an electron)
s: $F=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \frac{q^{2}}{d^{2}} \Longrightarrow q=\sqrt{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} F d^{2}}$. Number of electrons $n=\frac{q}{e}=\frac{\sqrt{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} F d^{2}}}{e}= \sqrt{\frac{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} F d^{2}}{e^{2}}}$.

subject: Physics
q: A charge $q$ is located at the centre of a cube. The electric flux through any face is $\frac{q}{6 \epsilon_{0}}$. If the charge is moved to one of the corners of the cube, the flux through the diagonally opposite face is:
s: When the charge is at a corner, the total flux through the cube is $\frac{q}{8 \epsilon_{0}}$. The three adjacent faces have zero flux. The flux is shared equally by the three diagonally $\underline{\text { opposite faces. Flux through one such face is } \frac{1}{3} \times(\text { total flux })=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{q}{8 \epsilon_{0}}=\frac{q}{24 \epsilon_{0}}}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Force due to multiple charges and vector form of Coulomb's law
q: If a charge $q$ is placed at the center of the line joining two equal charges $Q$, the system of three charges will be in equilibrium if $q$ is equal to:
s: Let the distance between charges $Q$ be $2 r$. For equilibrium of one charge $Q$ : $\frac{k Q^{2}}{(2 r)^{2}}+\frac{k Q q}{r^{2}}=0 \Longrightarrow \frac{Q}{4 r^{2}}=-\frac{q}{r^{2}} \Longrightarrow q=-\frac{Q}{4}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Force due to multiple charges and vector form of Coulomb's law
q:
Four charges are arranged at the corners of a square $A B C D$ as shown in the figure. 
 [IMAGE: images/MB000893_1.webp] 
The force on the charge kept at the centre $O$ is
s:
- The charge at $\mathrm{A}(+\mathrm{q})$ and the charge at $\mathrm{C}(+\mathrm{q})$ are at equal distances from the center O . They are both positive charges, so they will exert repulsive forces on a test charge (let's assume it's positive) at O . The force from A will be along the diagonal AC , pointing away from A , and the force from $C$ will be along the diagonal $A C$, pointing away from $C$. Since the charges and distances are equal, these two forces will be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Therefore, they cancel each other out.
- Similarly, the charge at $\mathrm{B}(+2 \mathrm{q})$ and the charge at $\mathrm{D}(-2 \mathrm{q})$ are at equal distances from the center O . The charge at B is positive and will exert a repulsive force on a positive test charge at O , pointing along the diagonal BD away from B . The charge at D is negative and will exert an attractive force on the positive test charge at O , pointing along the diagonal BD toward D . Both of these forces are in the same direction, along the diagonal $B D$, pointing from $B$ towards D . Since the magnitudes of the charges are equal $(|+2 q|=|-2 q|)$ and the distances are equal, the magnitudes of the forces are equal and they add up.
- The net force is the vector sum of all these forces. The forces from A and C cancel out. The forces from $B$ and $D$ add up and are directed along the diagonal $B D$.
Therefore, the net force on the charge at the center O is along the diagonal BD .

q: The ratio of the magnitudes of electrostatic force to gravitational force for two protons separated by a distance is $P \times 10^{35}$. Find the value of $P$. (Mass of proton $m_{p}=1.67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg , Charge of proton $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$ ). [Quote nearest integer value]
s: Ratio $=\frac{F_{e}}{F_{g}}=\frac{k e^{2}}{G m_{p}^{2}}=\frac{\left(9 \times 10^{9}\right)\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)^{2}}{\left(6.67 \times 10^{-11}\right)\left(1.67 \times 10^{-27}\right)^{2}} \approx 1.24 \times 10^{36}$. We need the answer in the form $P \times 10^{35}$. So, $1.24 \times 10^{36}=12.4 \times 10^{35}$. Thus, $P=12$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Calculation of electric flux due to uniform electric field
q: An electric field $\vec{E}=(5 x \hat{i}) N / C$ exists in space. A cube of side $2 m$ is placed with one corner at the origin, with edges along the $\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y}$, and z axes. The electric flux through the cube is _______$N m^{2} / C$.
s: Flux enters the face at $x=0$ and leaves the face at $x=2$. At the left face $(x=0): \vec{E}=0$, so $\phi_{\text {in }}=0$. At the right face $(x=2): \vec{E}=5(2) \hat{i}=10 \hat{i} N / C$. Area vector $\vec{A}=4 \hat{i} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$. Flux out $\phi_{\text {out }}=\vec{E} \cdot \vec{A}=(10 \hat{i}) \cdot(4 \hat{i})=40 \mathrm{Nm}^{2} / \mathrm{C}$. Net flux $\phi_{\text {net }}=\phi_{\text {out }}-\phi_{\text {in }}=40-0=40 \mathrm{Nm}^{2} / \mathrm{C}$.

subject: Physics
q: A thin ring of radius 10 cm has a charge of $10 \mu C$ distributed uniformly over it. A charge of $5 \mu C$ is placed at its center. The tension developed in the ring is approximately________N. [Quote nearest integer value]
s: The tension $T$ in the ring is given by the formula $T=\frac{k Q_{\text {center }} Q_{\text {ring }}}{2 \pi R^{2}} . T= \frac{\left(9 \times 10^{9}\right)\left(5 \times 10^{-6}\right)\left(10 \times 10^{-6}\right)}{2 \pi(0.1)^{2}}=\frac{0.45}{2 \pi \times 0.01}=\frac{0.45}{0.0628} \approx 7 \mathrm{~N}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Calculation of electric flux due to uniform electric field
q: An electric field is given by $\vec{E}=(6 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k}) \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{C}$. The electric flux through a surface of area $20 \hat{i} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ lying in the YZ-plane is ______Vm.
s: The electric flux is given by $\phi=\vec{E} \cdot \vec{A}$. Given $\vec{E}=(6 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k}) \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{C}$ and $\vec{A}=20 \hat{i} m^{2} . \phi=(6 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k}) \cdot(20 \hat{i})=(6)(20)+(2)(0)+(4)(0)=120 \mathrm{Vm}$.

subject: Physics
q: Two identical charged spheres are suspended by strings of equal length $L$. The strings make an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the vertical. When suspended in a liquid of density $0.8 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$, the angle remains the same. If the density of the material of the sphere is $1.6 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$, the dielectric constant of the liquid is __________.$\qquad$
s: For the angle to remain the same, the dielectric constant $K$ must satisfy $K=\frac{\rho}{\rho-\sigma}$, where $\rho$ is the density of the sphere's material and $\sigma$ is the density of the liquid. $K=\frac{1.6}{1.6-0.8}=\frac{1.6}{0.8}=2$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Calculation of equivalent resistance of a circuit
q: A wire of resistance $12 \Omega$ is bent to form a circle. The equivalent resistance between two diametrically opposite points is:
s: The wire is bent into a circle. Between two diametrically opposite points, there are two semicircular paths. The resistance of each path is $12 / 2=6 \Omega$. These two paths are in parallel. $R_{e q}=\frac{6 \times 6}{6+6}=\frac{36}{12}=3 \Omega$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Calculation of equivalent resistance of a circuit
q: A wire of resistance R is cut into 'n' equal parts. These parts are then connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance of the combination will be:
s: The resistance of each part is $R^{\prime}=R / n$. When 'n' such resistors are connected in parallel, the equivalent resistance is $R_{e q}=\frac{R^{\prime}}{n}=\frac{R / n}{n}=\frac{R}{n^{2}}$.

subject: Physics
q: Two electric bulbs are rated $25 \mathrm{~W}-220 \mathrm{~V}$ and $100 \mathrm{~W}-220 \mathrm{~V}$. If they are connected in series to a 220 V supply, which bulb will glow brighter?
o: Both will glow with the same brightness
s: Resistance $R=V^{2} / P$. The 25 W bulb has higher resistance. In a series connection, the current (I) is the same through both. Power consumed is $P=I^{2} R$. The bulb with higher resistance ( 25 W bulb) will dissipate more power and glow brighter.

q: In a balanced meter bridge, the resistance in the left gap is $2 \Omega$ and the resistance in the right gap is 3 $\Omega$. The balancing point from the left end is at:
s: For a balanced meter bridge, $\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}=\frac{l}{100-l} \cdot \frac{2}{3}=\frac{l}{100-l} \Rightarrow 2(100-l)=3 l \Rightarrow 200-2 l=3 l \Rightarrow 5 l=200 \Rightarrow l=40 \mathrm{~cm}$.

q: A galvanometer of resistance $100 \Omega$ gives full-scale deflection for a current of 1 mA . To convert it into a voltmeter of range 50 V , the required series resistance is:
s: The required series resistance is $R=\frac{V}{I_{g}}-G=\frac{50 \mathrm{~V}}{1 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~A}}-100 \Omega=50000 \Omega-100 \Omega=49900 \Omega$.

subject: Physics
q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, if the positions of the cell and the galvanometer are interchanged, the bridge will:
o: show a very high current in the galvanometer.
s: The condition for a balanced Wheatstone bridge, $\frac{P}{Q}=\frac{R}{S}$, remains the same even if the battery and galvanometer are interchanged. The bridge remains balanced.

subject: Physics
q: In an ammeter, $2 \%$ of the main current passes through the galvanometer. If the resistance of the galvanometer is G , the resistance of the shunt is:
s: Current through galvanometer $I_{g}=0.02 I$. Current through shunt $I_{s}=I-I_{g}=0.98 I$. Since the shunt and galvanometer are in parallel, the voltage across them is the same: $I_{g} G=I_{s} S \Rightarrow (0.02 I) G=(0.98 I) S \Rightarrow S=\frac{0.02}{0.98} G=\frac{1}{49} G$.

subject: Physics
q: The balancing length of a meter bridge is sensitive when the resistances in the two gaps are:
o: Of the same order of magnitude.
s: The sensitivity of a meter bridge is highest when the balancing point is near the center of the wire (around 50 cm ). This occurs when the resistances in the two gaps are nearly equal.

subject: Physics
q: An ideal voltmeter has:
s: An ideal voltmeter is connected in parallel and should not draw any current from the circuit to give an accurate reading of the potential difference. This requires its resistance to be infinite.

subject: Physics
q: In a meter bridge experiment, a null point is obtained at 60 cm from the left end. If a $3 \Omega$ resistance is connected in series with the smaller of the two resistances, the null point shifts to 50 cm . The values of the two resistances are:
s: Initially, $\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}=\frac{60}{40}=\frac{3}{2}$. So $R_{1}=\frac{3}{2} R_{2}$. The smaller resistance is $R_{2}$. After adding $3 \Omega$ to $R_{2}$, the new resistance is $R_{2}+3$. The new null point is $50 \mathrm{~cm} \cdot \frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}+3}=\frac{50}{50}=1 \Rightarrow R_{1}=R_{2}+3$. Substituting the first equation into the second: $\frac{3}{2} R_{2}=R_{2}+3 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} R_{2}=3 \Rightarrow R_{2}=6 \Omega$. Then $R_{1}=\frac{3}{2}(6)=9 \Omega$.

subject: Physics
q: The deflection in a moving coil galvanometer is reduced from 50 divisions to 10 divisions when a shunt of $12 \Omega$ is connected. The resistance of the galvanometer is:
s: Let the current for 50 divisions be I. Then the current for 10 divisions is $I_{g}=I / 5$. The current through the shunt is $I_{s}=I-I_{g}=I-I / 5=4 I / 5 . I_{g} G=I_{s} S \Rightarrow(I / 5) G=(4 I / 5)(12) \Rightarrow G=4 \times 12=48 \Omega$.

subject: Physics
q: The resistance of the wire of a meter bridge does not affect the balancing condition because:
o: The wire has a very low resistance.
The wire is uniform and the condition is based on ratios.
The current through the wire is negligible.
The material of the wire is Manganin.
s: The balancing condition is $\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}=\frac{\rho l_{1} / A}{\rho l_{2} / A}=\frac{l_{1}}{l_{2}}$. As long as the wire has a uniform cross-section and resistivity, these terms cancel out, and the condition depends only on the ratio of lengths.

subject: Physics
q: A voltmeter of resistance $1000 \Omega$ reads 2 V . To make it read 20 V , the extra resistance to be connected in series is:
s: The full-scale deflection current of the original voltmeter is $I_{g}=V / R_{V}=2 / 1000=0.002 \mathrm{~A}$. To increase the range to 20 V , the new total resistance should be $R_{\text {total }}=V_{\text {new }} / I_{g}=20 / 0.002=10000 \Omega$. The extra series resistance needed is $R_{\text {extra }}=R_{\text {total }}-R_{V}=10000-1000=9000 \Omega$.

subject: Physics
q: For a Wheatstone bridge to be most sensitive, the resistances in all four arms should be:
s: The sensitivity of a Wheatstone bridge is maximum when the bridge is nearly balanced and the resistances of all four arms are of a comparable magnitude.

subject: Physics
q: The range of an ammeter can be increased by:
s: From the formula $S=\frac{I_{g} G}{I-I_{g}}$, to increase the range I, the denominator ( $I-I_{g}$ ) must increase. For the equation to hold, the shunt resistance S must decrease. A smaller shunt bypasses more current.

q: A voltmeter of resistance $2000 \Omega$ is used to measure the potential difference across a $200 \Omega$ resistor. The percentage error in the reading is approximately (Assume the current in circuit stays same):
s: The equivalent resistance of the parallel combination is $R_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{200 \times 2000}{200+2000}=\frac{400000}{2200} \approx 181.8 \Omega$. The ratio of measured resistance to true resistance is $\frac{181.8}{200} \approx 0.909$. Since voltage is proportional to resistance (assuming constant current supply), the measured voltage is about $90.9 \%$ of the true voltage. The error is $100-90.9=9.1 \%$, which is approximately $9 \%$.
