q: In the half-deflection method for finding galvanometer resistance G , a high resistance R is connected in series with the galvanometer. Then, a shunt S is connected in parallel to the galvanometer to reduce the deflection to half. The galvanometer resistance is given by:
s: In the half-deflection method, for the approximation to be valid (assuming R is very large), the resistance of the galvanometer G is approximately equal to the shunt resistance S that causes the deflection to become half.

subject: Physics
q: A galvanometer coil has a resistance of $15 \Omega$ and gives full-scale deflection for a current of 4 mA . To convert it to an ammeter of range 0 to 6 A , the shunt resistance required is approximately:
s: $S=\frac{I_{g} G}{I-I_{g}}=\frac{\left(4 \times 10^{-3}\right) \times 15}{6-\left(4 \times 10^{-3}\right)} \approx \frac{0.06}{6}=0.01 \Omega$.

subject: Physics
q: In a Wheatstone bridge, the four arms have resistances $5 \Omega, 10 \Omega, 10 \Omega$, and $20 \Omega$ respectively, and a $15 \Omega$ resistor is connected across the galvanometer terminals. What is the equivalent resistance of the combination?
s: The bridge is arranged such that $P=5, Q=10, R=10, S=20$. The condition $\frac{P}{Q}=\frac{5}{10}=\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{R}{S}=\frac{10}{20}=\frac{1}{2}$ is satisfied. The bridge is balanced. The central $15 \Omega$ resistor can be ignored. The equivalent resistance is the parallel combination of the top arm ( $5+10=15 \Omega$ ) and the bottom arm $(10+20=30 \Omega) . R_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{15 \times 30}{15+30}=\frac{450}{45}=10 \Omega$.

subject: Physics

o: The galvanometer and shunt resistance in series.
The galvanometer and shunt resistance in parallel.
s: An ammeter is constructed by connecting a shunt resistor in parallel with the galvanometer. Its total resistance is the equivalent resistance of this parallel combination.

subject: Physics
q: In a meter bridge, the balancing length is found to be 25 cm from the left end. If the resistor in the right gap is shunted by an equal resistor, the new balancing point will be:
s: Initially, $\frac{R_{L}}{R_{R}}=\frac{25}{75}=\frac{1}{3}$. So, $R_{R}=3 R_{L}$. When $R_{R}$ is shunted by an equal resistor, the new resistance in the right gap is $R_{R}^{\prime}=\frac{R_{R} \times R_{R}}{R_{R}+R_{R}}=\frac{R_{R}}{2}$. The new balance condition is $\frac{R_{L}}{R_{R}^{\prime}}=\frac{l^{\prime}}{100-l^{\prime}}$. $\frac{R_{L}}{R_{R} / 2}=\frac{2 R_{L}}{3 R_{L}}=\frac{2}{3}=\frac{l^{\prime}}{100-l^{\prime}} \Rightarrow 200-2 l^{\prime}=3 l^{\prime} \Rightarrow 5 l^{\prime}=200 \Rightarrow l^{\prime}=40 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: A galvanometer with a coil resistance of $50 \Omega$ shows full-scale deflection for a current of 1 mA . To use it as an ammeter with a range of 1 A , a shunt of resistance S is required. The value of S is________milli-ohms. (rounded to the nearest integer)
s: Using the shunt formula, $S=\frac{I_{g} G}{I-I_{g}}=\frac{\left(1 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~A}\right) \times 50 \Omega}{1 \mathrm{~A}-0.001 \mathrm{~A}}=\frac{0.05}{0.999} \approx 0.05005 \Omega$. In milli-ohms, $S=0.05005 \times 1000=50.05 \mathrm{~m} \Omega$. Rounded to the nearest integer, the value is 50 .

subject: Physics
q: A galvanometer of resistance $100 \Omega$ requires 2 mA for full-scale deflection. The value of series resistance required to convert it into a voltmeter of range $0-10 \mathrm{~V}$ is_____ \[\left( {{\text{in}}\,\,\,\Omega } \right).\]
s: The required series resistance is $R=\frac{V}{I_{g}}-G=\frac{10 \mathrm{~V}}{2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~A}}-100 \Omega=5000 \Omega-100 \Omega=4900 \Omega$.

subject: Physics
q: In a meter bridge, the left gap has a resistor of $5 \Omega$ and the right gap has a resistor of $15 \Omega$. The balancing length from the left end is_____ \[\left( {{\text{in}}\,\,\,cm} \right).\]
s: For a balanced bridge, $\frac{R_{L}}{R_{R}}=\frac{l}{100-l} \Rightarrow \frac{5}{15}=\frac{l}{100-l} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{3}=\frac{l}{100-l} \Rightarrow 100-l=3 l \Rightarrow 4 l=100 \Rightarrow l=25 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: In an ammeter, $10 \%$ of the main current passes through a galvanometer of resistance $99 \Omega$. The resistance of the shunt is______ \[\left( {{\text{in}}\,\,\,\Omega } \right).\]
s: Current through galvanometer $I_{g}=0.10 I$. Current through shunt $I_{s}=I-I_{g}=I-0.10 I= 0.90 I$. The potential difference is the same across both: $I_{g} G=I_{s} S . \quad(0.10 I) \times 99=(0.90 I) \times S$. $S=\frac{0.10 \times 99}{0.90}=\frac{9.9}{0.9}=11 \Omega$.

subject: Physics
q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, the four arms have resistances $P=10 \Omega, Q=30 \Omega, R=5 \Omega$, and S . The value of S is_____ \[\left( {{\text{in}}\,\,\,\Omega } \right).\]
s: For the bridge to be balanced, the ratio of resistances must be equal: $\frac{P}{Q}=\frac{R}{S} \Rightarrow \frac{10}{30}=\frac{5}{S} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{3}=\frac{5}{S} \Rightarrow S=15 \Omega$.

q:
The energy stored in the capacitor in the steady state is
 [IMAGE: images/MB001377_1.webp]
s:
1. In the steady state, the capacitor acts as an open circuit, meaning no current flows through the branch containing the $2 \Omega$ resistor and the capacitor.
2. The circuit simplifies to the two remaining branches connected at node $P$. The voltage at node $\mathrm{P}, V_P$, is the voltage across the capacitor since there is no voltage drop across the $2 \Omega$ resistor.
3. We can use the Node Voltage Method (or Kirchhoff's Current Law) at node P to find the potential $V_P$.
$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{\text {in }} & =I_{\text {out }} \\
\frac{8 \mathrm{~V}-V_P}{4 \Omega} & =\frac{V_P-3 \mathrm{~V}}{1 \Omega}
\end{aligned}
$$
4. Solving for $V_P$ :
$$
\begin{gathered}
8-V_P=4\left(V_P-3\right) \\
8-V_P=4 V_P-12 \\
20=5 V_P \\
V_P=4 \mathrm{~V}
\end{gathered}
$$
5. The voltage across the capacitor is $V_C=V_P=4 \mathrm{~V}$.
6. The energy stored in the capacitor is calculated using the formula $E=\frac{1}{2} C V^2$ :
$$
E=\frac{1}{2}\left(3 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~F}\right)(4 \mathrm{~V})^2
$$
$E=\frac{1}{2}\left(3 \times 10^{-6}\right)(16)=24 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~J}=24 \mu \mathrm{~J}$

subject: Physics
q:
A semicircular conducting rod of radius $r$ is rotated about one of its free end in a uniform magnetic field $B$ at constant angular velocity $\omega$. Emf induced across its ends is equal to
 [IMAGE: images/MB001378_1.webp]
s:
Formula for a rotating straight rod: The EMF induced in a straight rod of length $L$ rotating about one of its ends in a uniform magnetic field $B$ with constant angular velocity $\omega$ is given by:
$$
\epsilon=\frac{1}{2} B \omega L^2
$$
Substitute the effective length: We substitute $L=L_{\text {eff }}=2 r$ into the formula.
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \epsilon=\frac{1}{2} B \omega(2 r)^2 \\
& \epsilon=\frac{1}{2} B \omega\left(4 r^2\right) \\
& \epsilon=2 B \omega r^2
\end{aligned}
$$

subject: Physics
q: The magnetic flux linked with a coil of resistance $10 \Omega$ is given by $\phi=4 t^{2}-10 t+5$ (in SI units). The magnitude of the induced current in the coil at $t=2 \mathrm{~s}$ is:
s: Induced emf $\mathcal{E}=-\frac{d \phi}{d t}=-(8 t-10)$. At $t=2 \mathrm{~s}, \mathcal{E}=-(8(2)-10)=-(16-10)=-6$ V . The magnitude is $|\mathcal{E}|=6 \mathrm{~V}$. The induced current is $I=\frac{|\mathcal{E}|}{R}=\frac{6 \mathrm{~V}}{10 \Omega}=0.6 \mathrm{~A}$.

subject: Physics
q: A circular coil of 50 turns and radius 10 cm is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T , with its plane perpendicular to the field. If the magnetic field is reduced to zero in 0.1 s , the average induced emf in the coil is:
s: Initial flux $\Phi_{i}=N B A=50 \times 0.1 \times \pi(0.1)^{2}=0.05 \pi \mathrm{~Wb}$. Final flux $\Phi_{f}=0$. Change in flux $\Delta \Phi=0.05 \pi \mathrm{~Wb}$. Time interval $\Delta t=0.1 \mathrm{~s}$. Average $\mathrm{emf}|\mathcal{E}|=\frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t}=\frac{0.05 \pi}{0.1}=0.5 \pi \mathrm{~V}$.

q:
A loop of area A enters a region of magnetic field at position -1 and it is leaving the field at position -2. The direction of induced current in the two cases will be
 [IMAGE: images/MB001382_1.webp]
s:
As loop moves in, the outward flux increases. According to Lenz law, the induced current needs to counter this increasing flux and hence a clockwise current will be generated to produce inward flux.
As loop moves out, the outward flux decreases. According to Lenz law, the induced current needs to counter this decreasing flux and hence an anticlockwise current will be generated to produce outward flux.

subject: Physics
q: A generator produces a maximum voltage of 240 V at a frequency of 60 Hz . The number of turns in the coil is 200 and its area is $0.05 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$. The magnitude of the magnetic field in which the coil rotates is approximately:
s: The maximum voltage (peak EMF) is given by $\mathcal{E}_{\text {max }}=N A B \omega$. The angular frequency is $\omega=2 \pi f=2 \pi(60)=120 \pi \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} . B=\frac{\mathcal{E}_{\max }}{N A \omega}=\frac{240}{200 \times 0.05 \times 120 \pi}=\frac{240}{10 \times 120 \pi}=\frac{240}{1200 \pi}=\frac{0.2}{\pi} \approx \frac{0.2}{3.14} \approx$ 0.0637 T .

subject: Physics
q: In an AC circuit, a parallel plate capacitor is connected to the source. The displacement current between the plates is:
o: Equal to the conduction current in the wires
s: For a capacitor in an AC circuit, the rate of change of charge on the plates (which determines the conduction current, $I_{c}=d Q / d t$ ) is directly related to the changing electric flux between them. Maxwell's equations show that the displacement current $I_{d}=\epsilon_{0} d \Phi_{E} / d t$ is exactly equal to the conduction current $I_{c}$.

subject: Physics
q: Which of the following laws is a consequence of the fact that magnetic monopoles do not exist?
s: Gauss's law for magnetism, $\oint \vec{B} \cdot d \vec{A}=0$, states that the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero. This implies that there are no isolated magnetic "charges" (monopoles) to act as sources or sinks of magnetic field lines.

subject: Physics
q: A conducting rod of length $L$ moves with a constant velocity $v$ parallel to its length in a uniform magnetic field $B$ that is perpendicular to the rod. The induced emf between the ends of the rod is:
s: The motional emf is given by $\mathcal{E}=(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{L}$. Here, $\vec{v}$ is parallel to $\vec{L}$. Therefore, the scalar triple product is zero. Alternatively, the magnetic force on charges is $\vec{F}=q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$, which is perpendicular to the rod's length. Thus, no charge separation occurs along the length of the rod.

subject: Physics
q: A vertical square loop of side 'a' and resistance ' $R$ ' is placed in the east-west plane. A uniform magnetic field is set up in the north-east direction. The magnitude of the induced current when the field is decreased at a steady rate is proportional to:
s: The induced emf is $\mathcal{E}=-\frac{d \Phi_{B}}{d t}=-A \cos \theta \frac{d B}{d t}$. The induced current is $I=\frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}= -\frac{A \cos \theta}{R} \frac{d B}{d t}$. Since the area $A=a^{2}$, the induced current $I$ is directly proportional to $a^{2}$.

subject: Physics
q: In an RC circuit, the time constant is the time taken for the charge on the capacitor to reach approximately:
s: The charge during charging is given by $Q(t)=Q_{\max }\left(1-e^{-t / \tau}\right)$. At $t=\tau$ (one time constant), the charge is $Q(\tau)=Q_{\max }\left(1-e^{-1}\right) \approx 0.632 Q_{\max }$. This is about $63 \%$ of the final maximum charge.

subject: Physics
q: A solenoid has 2000 turns wound over a length of 0.30 m . The area of its cross section is $1.2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^2$. Around its central section a coil of 300 turns is wound. If an initial current of 2 A in the solenoid is reversed in 0.25 s , the emf induced in the coil is equal to
s:
1. Calculate the change in magnetic field ( $B$ )
The magnetic field in a solenoid is $B=\mu_0 n I$, where $n=\frac{2000}{0.30}=6666.7 \mathrm{turns} / \mathrm{m}$.
The initial field is $B_{\text {initial }}=\left(4 \pi \times 10^{-7}\right) \times(6666.7) \times(2 \mathrm{~A})=0.01676 \mathrm{~T}$.
When the current is reversed, the field becomes $B_{\text {final }}=-0.01676 \mathrm{~T}$.
The change in magnetic field is $\Delta B=B_{\text {final }}-B_{\text {initial }}=-0.03352 \mathrm{~T}$.
2. Calculate the change in magnetic flux ( $\Phi$ )
The magnetic flux through the secondary coil is $\Phi=N_2 B A$.
The change in flux is $\Delta \Phi=N_2 \Delta B A$.
$$
\Delta \Phi=300 \times(-0.03352 \mathrm{~T}) \times\left(1.2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^2\right)=-0.01207 \mathrm{~Wb} .
$$
3. Calculate the induced emf ( $\varepsilon$ )
Using Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-\frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t}$.
$$
\varepsilon=-\frac{-0.01207 \mathrm{~Wb}}{0.25 \mathrm{~s}}=0.04828 \mathrm{~V} .
$$
This can be written as $4.828 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~V}$.
The closest answer is $4.8 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~V}$.
$4.8 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~V}$

subject: Physics
q: In a series RLC circuit connected to a DC source, after the switch has been closed for a long time:
o: Energy stored in the inductor is maximum.
Energy stored in the capacitor is zero.
Energy stored in the inductor is zero and in the capacitor is maximum.
Energy is equally stored in both the inductor and capacitor.
s: In a DC circuit at steady state (after a long time), the inductor acts as a short circuit (wire) and the capacitor acts as an open circuit. Since the capacitor is an open circuit, the current $I$ becomes zero. Therefore, the energy in the inductor ( $U_{L}=\frac{1}{2} L I^{2}$ ) is zero. The capacitor charges to the full battery voltage V , so its stored energy ( $U_{C}=\frac{1}{2} C V^{2}$ ) is maximum.

subject: Physics
q: A 200 pF capacitor is connected to a 120 V AC supply with an angular frequency of $500 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. The rms value of the conduction current is:
s: The capacitive reactance is $X_{C}=\frac{1}{\omega C}=\frac{1}{500 \times 200 \times 10^{-12}}=\frac{1}{10^{-7}}=10^{7} \Omega$. The rms current is $I_{r m s}=\frac{V_{r m s}}{X_{C}}=\frac{120}{10^{7}}=12 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~A}=12 \mu \mathrm{~A}$.

subject: Physics
q: A conducting bar slides on two parallel rails with a constant velocity $v$. A uniform magnetic field $B$ is directed into the page. If the resistance of the bar is R and the rails have negligible resistance, the power dissipated as heat is:
s: The induced emf is $\mathcal{E}=B L v$. The induced current is $I=\frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}=\frac{B L v}{R}$. The power dissipated is $P=I^{2} R=\left(\frac{B L v}{R}\right)^{2} R=\frac{B^{2} L^{2} v^{2}}{R}$.

subject: Physics
q: A 12 V battery is connected to a capacitor. The energy stored is $72 \mu \mathrm{~J}$. The capacitance of the capacitor is:
s: The energy stored is $U=\frac{1}{2} C V^{2} . C=\frac{2 U}{V^{2}}=\frac{2 \times 72 \times 10^{-6}}{(12)^{2}}=\frac{144 \times 10^{-6}}{144}=1 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~F}=1 \mu \mathrm{~F}$.

subject: Physics
q: At steady state, the charge on the capacitor is $x \mu \mathrm{C}$. Find the value of x. The circuit contains a 12 V battery, a $2 \Omega$ resistor, and a $4 \Omega$ resistor in series. A $6 \mu F$ capacitor is connected in parallel with the $4 \Omega$ resistor.
s: At steady state, the capacitor acts as an open circuit. The current in the main circuit is $I=\frac{V}{R_{\text {total }}}=\frac{12 \mathrm{~V}}{2 \Omega+4 \Omega}=2 \mathrm{~A}$. The voltage across the $4 \Omega$ resistor is $V_{4}=I \times R_{4}=2 \mathrm{~A} \times 4 \Omega=8 \mathrm{~V}$. This is the voltage across the capacitor. The charge is $Q=C V=(6 \mu \mathrm{~F})(8 \mathrm{~V})=48 \mu \mathrm{C}$. So, $x=48$.

subject: Physics
q: A square loop of wire has a total resistance of $4 R$. A battery of emf $\mathcal{E}$ and negligible internal resistance is connected across one side AB . A capacitor $C$ is connected across the diagonal AC. The potential difference across the capacitor is $\mathcal{E} / x$. Find x.
s: Let each side of the square have resistance $R$. Let the vertices be $A, B, C, D$ in order. The battery is across AB . Let the potential at A be 0 and at B be $\mathcal{E}$. The circuit consists of two parallel paths from $A$ to $B$ : the direct side $A B$ (resistance $R$ ), and the path $A D C B$ (resistance $R+R+R =3 \mathrm{R}$ ). This is incorrect. The battery is connected *across* one side. Let's assume the vertices are $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D}$. Battery across AB . Due to symmetry, the paths ADB and ACB are equivalent if the battery were at the center. With the battery across AB , let's set $V_{A}=0$ and $V_{B}=\mathcal{E}$. The resistance of path ADB is $R+R=2 R$. The resistance of path ACB is $R+R=2 R$. So the current through path ADB is $I_{A D B}=\mathcal{E} /(2 R)$, and the current through ACB is $I_{A C B}=\mathcal{E} /(2 R)$. The potential at D is $V_{D}=V_{A}+I_{A D B} \times R_{A D}=0+\left(\frac{\mathcal{E}}{2 R}\right) \times R=\frac{\mathcal{E}}{2}$. The potential at C is $V_{C}=V_{A}+I_{A C B} \times R_{A C}=0+\left(\frac{\mathcal{E}}{2 R}\right) \times R=\frac{\mathcal{E}}{2}$. This is not correct as C is not adjacent to A in this path. $V_{C}=V_{B}-I_{A C B} \times R_{C B}=\mathcal{E}-\left(\frac{\mathcal{E}}{2 R}\right) \times R=\mathcal{E}-\frac{\mathcal{E}}{2}=\frac{\mathcal{E}}{2}$. The potential difference across the capacitor connected to AC is $\left|V_{C}-V_{A}\right|=\left|\frac{\mathcal{E}}{2}-0\right|=\frac{\mathcal{E}}{2}$. So, the potential difference is $\mathcal{E} / 2$, which means $x=2$.

subject: Physics
q: The magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of a circular coil of 100 turns and area $0.02 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ is changing at a rate of $0.5 \mathrm{~T} / \mathrm{s}$. The induced emf in the coil is (in V).
s: From Faraday's Law, $|\mathcal{E}|=N \frac{d \Phi_{B}}{d t}=N \frac{d(B A)}{d t}=N A \frac{d B}{d t} .|\mathcal{E}|=(100) \times\left(0.02 \mathrm{~m}^{2}\right) \times (0.5 \mathrm{~T} / \mathrm{s})=100 \times 0.01=1 \mathrm{~V}$.

subject: Physics
q: A conducting rod of length 50 cm rotates with an angular frequency of $10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ about one of its ends in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T . The induced emf between the ends of the rod is x (in V).Find the value of 2x.
s: The induced emf in a rotating rod is given by $\mathcal{E}=\frac{1}{2} B \omega L^{2}$. $\mathcal{E}=\frac{1}{2}(0.4 \mathrm{~T})(10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s})(0.5 \mathrm{~m})^{2}= (0.2)(10)(0.25)=2 \times 0.25=0.5 \mathrm{~V}$. So, x =0.5 V , 2x = 1 V

subject: Physics
q: A long solenoid having 200 turns per cm carries a current of 1.5 amp . At the centre of it is placed a coil of 100 turns of cross-sectional area $3.14 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2$ having its axis parallel to the field produced by the solenoid. When the direction of current in the solenoid is reversed within 0.05s, the induced emf in the coil is (in milivolts)
s:
The magnetic field inside the solenoid is given by $B=\mu_0 n I$. The initial magnetic flux through the coil is $\Phi_1=N B A$. When the current is reversed, the magnetic field and thus the flux also reverse, becoming $\Phi_2=-N B A$. The change in flux is $\Delta \Phi=\Phi_2-\Phi_1=-2 N B A$. By Faraday's Law, the induced EMF is $\epsilon=\left|\frac{\Delta \Phi}{\Delta t}\right|$.
Using the given values, the induced EMF is calculated to be 0.048 V .

q:
A non-uniform but spherically symmetric ball of mass M and radius R, rolls from rest down a ramp and onto a circular loop of radius r. The ball is initially at height h above the bottom of the loop. At the bottom of the loop, the normal force on the ball is twice its weight. The moment of inertia of the ball is given by $I = \beta M{R^2}.$ Find ꞵ
 [IMAGE: images/MB002886_1.webp]
s:
"THIS IS A HIGH WEIGHTAGE TOPIC"

Given :
A non uniform ball of mass $M$ and radius $R$, rolls from rest down a ramp and onto a circular loop of radius $r$. The ball is initially at height $h$ above the bottom of loop. At the bottom of loop the normal force on ball is twice its weight.
Moment of inertia of ball is given by $I=\beta M R^{2}$.
 [IMAGE NOT CAPTURED] 
Due the absence of dissipative forces, the energy of the system is conserved.
The centripetal force(F) provided by the surface at the bottom would be:Normal - weight of the body

$F = 2M g - Mg = Mg$
$2Mg-Mg=\frac{MV^{2}}{r-R}$
$V^2 = g (r-R)$
From conserving energy we get:
$Mgh = \frac{1}{2}MV^{2}+\frac{1}{2}I \omega^{2}$
As the object is rolling down the plane : $V=R \omega$
We also known: ${V}^{{2}}=({r-R}) {g}$$Mgh = \frac{1}{2}MV^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \beta MR^{2} \frac {V^{2}}{R^{2}}$
$\Rightarrow Mgh = \frac{1}{2} MV^{2}(\beta+1) = \frac{1}{2} Mg(r-R)(\beta + 1)$
Hence : $\frac{2 h}{r-R}-1=\beta$

s:
Let us consider a semi-circular disc. [IMAGE NOT CAPTURED] 

The centre of mass of this semi-circular disc is at \[\left[ {0,\frac{{4a}}{{3\pi }}} \right]\].
Now, let us consider it a combination of two quarter discs.
By symmetry we can say that the C.O.M. of 1st quarter disc will lie on the line y = x & the C.O.M of 2nd quarter disc will lie on \[y = - x\].
\[ \Rightarrow \] Let, the C.O.M of 1st quarter, disc is at (x, x) and the 2nd quarter disc is at \[\left( { - x,x} \right)\].

\[ \Rightarrow \] The C.O.M. of the combination of quarter discs \[ = \left[ {0,\frac{{4a}}{{3\pi }}} \right]\]

\[ \Rightarrow \] We know that, Y coordinate of C.O.M \[{Y_{cm}} = \frac{{{m_1}{y_1} + {m_2}{y_2}}}{{{m_1} + {m_2}}}\]

Let, mass of each quarter circle = m.
\[ \Rightarrow \frac{{4a}}{{3\pi }} = \frac{{m.x + m.x}}{{2m}}\]

\[ \Rightarrow x = \frac{{4a}}{{3\pi }}\]

\[ \Rightarrow \] C.O.M. of the 1st quarter disc is at \[\left( {x,x} \right) = \left[ {\frac{{4a}}{{3\pi }},\frac{{4a}}{{3\pi }}} \right]\]

q: A large open-top water tank has a small hole 5 m below the water surface. The velocity of water flowing out of the hole is: (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: According to Torricelli's law, the velocity of efflux from a hole at a depth $h$ below the free surface is given by $v=\sqrt{2 g h} . v=\sqrt{2 \times 10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2} \times 5 \mathrm{~m}}=\sqrt{100}= 10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Torricelli's equation and velocity of efflux
q: A large open tank has a layer of oil (density $800 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ ) of height 2 m on top of a layer of water (density $1000 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ ) of height 3 m . A small hole is made at the bottom of the tank. The initial velocity of efflux of water is: (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s:
Using Bernoulli's equation between the top surface and the hole. The pressure at the bottom due to the liquids is $P_{g}=h_{\text {oil }} \rho_{\text {oil }} g+h_{\text {water }} \rho_{\text {water }} g$. This gauge pressure is converted to kinetic energy of the effluxing water: $P_{g}=\frac{1}{2} \rho_{\text {water }} v^{2}$.
$g\left(h_{\text {oil }} \rho_{\text {oil }}+h_{\text {water }} \rho_{\text {water }}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \rho_{\text {water }} v^{2} . v=\sqrt{\frac{2 g\left(h_{\text {oil }} \rho_{\text {oil }}+h_{\text {water }} \rho_{\text {water }}\right)}{\rho_{\text {water }}}}=\sqrt{2 g\left(h_{\text {water }}+\frac{\rho_{\text {oil }}}{\rho_{\text {water }}} h_{\text {oil }}\right)}$.
$v=\sqrt{2 \times 10 \times\left(3+\frac{800}{1000} \times 2\right)}=\sqrt{20 \times(3+1.6)}=\sqrt{20 \times 4.6}=\sqrt{92} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: If 1000 identical small water droplets coalesce to form a single large drop, the ratio of the final total surface energy to the initial total surface energy is:
s: Let R be the radius of the big drop and r be the radius of small droplets. Volume conservation: $1000 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3}=\frac{4}{3} \pi R^{3} \Longrightarrow R=10 r$. Initial surface energy $E_{i}=1000 \times\left(4 \pi r^{2} T\right)$. Final surface energy $E_{f}=4 \pi R^{2} T=4 \pi(10 r)^{2} T=100 \times \left(4 \pi r^{2} T\right)$. The ratio $E_{f} / E_{i}=\frac{100 \times\left(4 \pi r^{2} T\right)}{1000 \times\left(4 \pi r^{2} T\right)}=\frac{100}{1000}=\frac{1}{10}$.

q: A sealed tank containing water up to a height of 3 m also contains air at a gauge pressure of $2.0 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{~Pa}$. A small hole is made at the bottom. The velocity of efflux is: $\left(\right.$ Density of water $\left.=1000 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}, g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}\right)$
s: Apply Bernoulli's equation between the top water surface (1) and the hole (2). $P_{1}+\rho g h_{1}=P_{2}+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_{2}^{2}$. Here $P_{1}=P_{a t m}+P_{g a u g e}$ and $P_{2}=P_{a t m}$. $P_{\text {gauge }}+\rho g h=\frac{1}{2} \rho v^{2} .2 .0 \times 10^{4}+(1000)(10)(3)=\frac{1}{2}(1000) v^{2} .20000+30000= 500 v^{2} \Longrightarrow 50000=500 v^{2} \Longrightarrow v^{2}=100 \Longrightarrow v=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: Assertion (A): Small liquid drops assume a spherical shape. Reason (R): Due to surface tension, liquids tend to minimize their surface area for a given volume, and a sphere has the minimum surface area.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
s: Surface tension is the property of a liquid that makes its surface behave like a stretched membrane, tending to contract to the smallest possible surface area. For a given volume, a sphere is the geometric shape with the minimum surface area. This explains why small drops, where gravity is negligible, are spherical.

subject: Physics
q: Water flows through a horizontal pipe. A pressure gauge attached to the pipe reads $3.0 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$ when the water is stationary. When the water starts flowing, the gauge reading drops to $2.2 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~Pa}$. The speed of the water is: (Density of water $=1000 \mathrm{kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ )
s: Using Bernoulli's equation: $P_{1}=P_{2}+\frac{1}{2} \rho v^{2} . v=\sqrt{\frac{2\left(P_{1}-P_{2}\right)}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\left(3.0 \times 10^{5}-2.2 \times 10^{5}\right)}{1000}}= \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 0.8 \times 10^{5}}{1000}}=\sqrt{160} \approx 12.6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: A stream of water flowing horizontally with a speed of $15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ gushes out of a tube of cross-sectional area $10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ and hits a vertical wall nearby. What is the force exerted on the wall by the impact of water, assuming it does not rebound?
s: Force is the rate of change of momentum. $F=\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}=\frac{m\left(v_{f}-v_{i}\right)}{\Delta t}$. Since the water does not rebound, $v_{f}=0 . \quad F=\frac{m v_{i}}{\Delta t}$. The mass hitting the wall per second is $\frac{m}{\Delta t}=$ (Volume per second) $\times \rho=\left(A v_{i}\right) \rho . \quad F=\left(A v_{i} \rho\right) v_{i}=A \rho v_{i}^{2}= \left(10^{-2}\right)(1000)(15)^{2}=10 \times 225=2250 \mathrm{~N}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Torricelli's equation and velocity of efflux
q: An open cylindrical tank of water is placed in an elevator that is accelerating upwards at $2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. If a small hole is made in the side of the tank at a depth of 2.5 m below the water surface, the velocity of efflux relative to the tank is: (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
s: In an upwardly accelerating frame, the effective acceleration due to gravity is $g_{\text {eff }}=g+a$. $g_{\text {eff }}=10+2=12 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. The velocity of efflux is given by Torricelli's law with the effective gravity: $v=\sqrt{2 g_{\text {eff }} h} . v=\sqrt{2 \times 12 \times 2.5}=\sqrt{60} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: The surface energy of a liquid drop of radius r is U . If this drop is split into 1000 identical smaller droplets, the new total surface energy will be:
s: $U=4 \pi r^{2} T$. Let the new radius be $r^{\prime}$. Volume is conserved: $\frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3}= 1000 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^{\prime 3} \Longrightarrow r=10 r^{\prime}$. New total surface energy $U^{\prime}=1000 \times\left(4 \pi r^{\prime 2} T\right)= 1000 \times 4 \pi(r / 10)^{2} T=1000 \times \frac{4 \pi r^{2} T}{100}=10 \times\left(4 \pi r^{2} T\right)=10 U$.

sub_topic: Torricelli's equation and velocity of efflux
q: The velocity of efflux of a liquid from an orifice at a depth $h$ below the free surface of the liquid in a tank is given by:
s: This is Torricelli's law, derived from Bernoulli's principle. Applying Bernoulli's equation between the free surface (1) and the orifice (2): $P_{1}+\rho g h_{1}+ \frac{1}{2} \rho v_{1}^{2}=P_{2}+\rho g h_{2}+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_{2}^{2}$. Assuming $P_{1}=P_{2}=P_{a t m}$ and $v_{1} \approx 0$, and taking $h=h_{1}-h_{2}$, we get $\rho g h=\frac{1}{2} \rho v_{2}^{2}$, which simplifies to $v_{2}=\sqrt{2 g h}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Torricelli's equation and velocity of efflux
q: A hole is made at the bottom of a tank filled with water. If the total pressure at the bottom of the tank is 3 atm ( $1 \mathrm{~atm}=10^{5} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$ ), the velocity of efflux is:
s: The total pressure at the bottom is $P=P_{\text {atm }}+\rho g h=3 \mathrm{~atm}$. The gauge pressure is $P_{g}=P-P_{\text {atm }}=2 \mathrm{~atm}=2 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. This gauge pressure is due to the water column, so $\rho g h=2 \times 10^{5}$. The velocity of efflux is $v=\sqrt{2 g h}$. Squaring gives $v^{2}=2 g h$. So, $\rho \frac{v^{2}}{2}=2 \times 10^{5} \Longrightarrow v^{2}=\frac{2 \times 2 \times 10^{5}}{1000}=400 . v=\sqrt{400}=20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: Assertion (A): To get a spray from a bottle, one has to press the bulb. Reason (R): Pressing the bulb increases the air speed inside, which decreases the pressure, allowing the liquid to rise and be sprayed out.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
s: This is a direct application of Bernoulli's principle. Pressing the bulb forces air to move at high speed over the top of the tube immersed in the liquid. This high-speed air creates a region of low pressure. The higher atmospheric pressure on the liquid surface in the bottle then pushes the liquid up the tube and into the airstream, creating a spray.

subject: Physics
q: A large liquid drop is formed by coalescing 27 small identical drops. The ratio of the surface energy of the large drop to the total surface energy of all the small drops is $1: \mathrm{N}$. The value of N is_________.
s: Let R be the radius of the large drop and r be the radius of a small drop. By volume conservation: $\frac{4}{3} \pi R^{3}=27 \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3} \Longrightarrow R=3 r$. Surface energy is proportional to the surface area. Total initial energy $E_{i} \propto 27 \times\left(4 \pi r^{2}\right)$. Final energy $E_{f} \propto 4 \pi R^{2}=4 \pi(3 r)^{2}=9 \times\left(4 \pi r^{2}\right)$. The ratio is $\frac{E_{f}}{E_{i}}=\frac{9 \times\left(4 \pi r^{2}\right)}{27 \times\left(4 \pi r^{2}\right)}=\frac{9}{27}=\frac{1}{3}$. So, $E_{f}: E_{i}=1: 3$. Thus, $\mathrm{N}=3$.

subject: Physics
q:
The reading of a pressure meter attached to a closed horizontal pipe is $5.0 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. On opening a valve, water starts flowing and the meter reading falls to $3.0 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. The velocity of water is found to be $\sqrt{V} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The value of V is________.
(Density of water $=1000 \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ )
s: Using Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe: $P_{1}+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_{1}^{2}=P_{2}+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_{2}^{2}$. Initially, water is closed, so $v_{1}=0 . P_{1}=5.0 \times 10^{4}$. Finally, water flows with velocity $v_{2} . P_{2}=3.0 \times 10^{4} . P_{1}=P_{2}+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_{2}^{2} . v_{2}^{2}=\frac{2\left(P_{1}-P_{2}\right)}{\rho}=\frac{2\left(5.0 \times 10^{4}-3.0 \times 10^{4}\right)}{1000}= \frac{2 \times 2.0 \times 10^{4}}{1000}=40$. The velocity is $\sqrt{40} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. Therefore, $\mathrm{V}=40$.

sub_topic: Different types of speeds of gases
q: For a particular ideal gas, the correct graph representing the variation of mean squared velocity $\left(\overline{v^{2}}\right)$ with absolute temperature ( T ) is:
o: A parabola opening upwards starting from the origin.
A straight line passing through the origin.
A straight line parallel to the temperature axis.
s:
The mean kinetic energy of a gas molecule is $\frac{1}{2} m \overline{v^{2}}=\frac{3}{2} k T$. The mean squared velocity is $\overline{v^{2}}=\frac{3 k T}{m}$. 
Since $3 k / m$ is a constant, $\overline{v^{2}} \propto T$. 
This is the equation of a straight line passing through the origin.

subject: Physics
q: Two containers hold helium and argon gas at the same temperature of 400 K . The ratio of the average translational kinetic energy per molecule of helium to argon is:
s:
The average translational kinetic energy per molecule for any ideal gas is given by $K E_{\text {avg }}=\frac{3}{2} k T$. It depends only on the absolute temperature (T). 
Since both gases are at the same temperature, the ratio of their average kinetic energies is $1: 1$.

subject: Physics
q: A container with a fixed volume holds an ideal gas at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and pressure P . To triple the pressure, the temperature of the gas must be raised to:
s:
For a fixed volume, $\frac{P_{1}}{T_{1}}=\frac{P_{2}}{T_{2}}$. 
Initial temperature $T_{1}=27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=300 \mathrm{~K}$. 
Given $P_{2}=3 P_{1}$.
$$
T_{2}=T_{1} \times \frac{P_{2}}{P_{1}}=300 K \times \frac{3 P_{1}}{P_{1}}=900 \mathrm{~K}
$$
In Celsius, $T_{2}=900-273=627^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Molar heat capacity of a gas
q: The molar heat capacity of an ideal gas in a process is given by $C=C_{V}-R$. This process is:
s: For a polytropic process $P V^{x}=$ constant, the molar heat capacity is $C=C_{V}+\frac{R}{1-x}$. Given $C=C_{V}-R$, we have $\frac{R}{1-x}=-R \Longrightarrow 1=-(1-x) \Longrightarrow 1=-1+x \Longrightarrow x=2$. The process is $P V^{2}=$ constant.

subject: Physics
q: The ratio of the speed of sound in helium gas to that in hydrogen gas at the same temperature is: $\left(M_{H e}=4 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}, M_{H_{2}}=2 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}, \gamma_{H e}=5 / 3, \gamma_{H_{2}}=7 / 5\right)$
s:
The speed of sound is $v_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma R T}{M}}$.
$$
\frac{v_{H e}}{v_{H_{2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_{H e} M_{H_{2}}}{\gamma_{H_{2}} M_{H e}}}=\sqrt{\frac{(5 / 3)(2)}{(7 / 5)(4)}}=\sqrt{\frac{10 / 3}{28 / 5}}=\sqrt{\frac{10}{3} \times \frac{5}{28}}=\sqrt{\frac{50}{84}}=\sqrt{\frac{25}{42}}
$$

Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer.
List IList II(A) Gas Constant (R)(I) $\left[L^{2} T^{-2} K^{-1}\right]$(B) Wien's Constant (b)(II) $\left[M T^{-3}\right]$(C) Wave Intensity(III) $[L K]$(D) Specific Heat Capacity(IV) $\left[M L^{2} T^{-2} K^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right]$
s:
- (A) Gas Constant (R): From PV $=n R T,[R]=\frac{[P][V]}{[n][T]}=\frac{\left[M L^{-1} T^{-2}\right]\left[L^{3}\right]}{[\operatorname{mol}][K]}= \left[M L^{2} T^{-2} K^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\right]$. So, A matches with IV.

- (C) Wave Intensity (I): Power per unit area. $[I]=\frac{[\text { Power }]}{[\text { Area }]}=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-3}\right]}{\left[L^{2}\right]}= \left[M T^{-3}\right]$. So, C matches with II.

The electric field $\vec{E}$ is directed away from the sheet. 
Since the dipole axis is perpendicular to the sheet with +q farther away, the dipole moment $\vec{p}$ is parallel to the electric field ( $\theta=0^{\circ}$ ). 
Torque $\tau=p E \sin \left(0^{\circ}\right)=0$. Potential energy $U=-p E \cos \left(0^{\circ}\right)=-p E$, which is the minium potential energy.

subject: Physics
q: A hollow charged sphere of radius R has a constant surface charge density $\sigma$. Which graphs shows the variation of electric field strength $E$ with distance $x$ from the centre of the sphere?
s:
A hollow charged sphere with a constant surface charge
density $\sigma$ has two distinct regions for the electric field, $\mathbf{E}$.
- Inside the sphere ( $\mathrm{x}<\mathrm{R}$ ):
According to Gauss's Law, the electric field inside a hollow charged sphere is
zero. This is because any Gaussian surface drawn within the sphere encloses no
charge. Therefore, for all distances $x$ from the center where $x<R$, the
electric field $E=0$. This eliminates options (A), (B), and (C).
- Outside the sphere ( $\mathrm{x} \geq \mathbf{R}$ ):
The electric field outside the sphere is the same as the field of a point
charge with the total charge of the sphere, $Q$, located at its center. The
total charge $Q$ is the surface charge density $\sigma$ multiplied by the
surface area of the sphere, $4 \pi R^2$. The electric field is given by
$E=\frac{k Q}{x^2}$, where $k$ is Coulomb's constant. Since $Q$ and $R$ are
constants, the electric field is inversely proportional to the square of the
distance from the center $\left(E \propto \frac{1}{x^2}\right)$. This means the
field decreases as the distance $x$ increases.
Graph (D) correctly
shows the electric field $\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{0}$ for $x<R$ and then a sharp
transition to a field that decreases as $\frac{1}{x^2}$ for \[\left( {x
\geqslant R} \right)\].

q: In the absence of an external electric field, the net dipole moment of a sample of a polar dielectric substance is:
s: In a polar dielectric, individual molecules have permanent dipole moments. However, due to thermal agitation, these dipoles are randomly oriented, so their vector sum (the net dipole moment) is zero.

subject: Physics
q: Consider two infinitely large parallel plates with surface charge densities $+\sigma$ and $+3 \sigma$. The electric field in the region between the plates is:
s: Between the plates, the field from $+\sigma$ is $\frac{\sigma}{2 \epsilon_{0}}$ (away) and from $+3 \sigma$ is $\frac{3 \sigma}{2 \epsilon_{0}}$ (away). The net field is the difference: $E_{n e t}=\frac{3 \sigma}{2 \epsilon_{0}}-\frac{\sigma}{2 \epsilon_{0}}=\frac{2 \sigma}{2 \epsilon_{0}}=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_{0}}$. The direction is from higher potential (the $+3 \sigma$ plate) to lower potential (the $+\sigma$ plate), which is towards the $+\sigma$ plate.

subject: Physics
q: The dimensions of ( $\epsilon_{0} \frac{d \phi_{E}}{d t}$ ) are the same as that of:
s: The term $\epsilon_{0} \frac{d \phi_{E}}{d t}$ is the displacement current, $I_{d}$, which has the dimensions of electric current $[\mathrm{A}]$.

subject: Physics
q: A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ is tied to a string of length $L$. It is released from rest in a uniform horizontal electric field $E$ from the position where the string is vertical. Find the kinetic energy of the particle when the string becomes horizontal.
s: By the work-energy theorem, $\Delta K=W_{\text {field }}$. The displacement in the direction of the electric field is $L . K_{f}-K_{i}=q E \times L$. Since $K_{i}=0$, the final kinetic energy is $K_{f}=q E L$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Electric field due to standard bodies
q: The kinetic energy of an electron revolving in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around an infinitely long positively charged wire with linear charge density $\lambda$ is:
s: The electric force provides the centripetal force: $e E=\frac{m v^{2}}{r} \Longrightarrow e\left(\frac{\lambda}{2 \pi \epsilon_{0} r}\right)=\frac{m v^{2}}{r}$. This gives $m v^{2}=\frac{e \lambda}{2 \pi \epsilon_{0}}$. Kinetic Energy $K E=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}=\frac{e \lambda}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}}$, which is independent of $r$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Electric field due to standard bodies
q: An electric field due to a uniformly charged arc AB of a ring at the center O is E . The ring has mutually perpendicular diameters AC and BD . The magnitude of the electric field at O due to the arc BCD is:
s:
By symmetry, the magnitude of the electric field from each quadrant arc ( $\mathrm{AB}, \mathrm{BC}$, $\mathrm{CD}, \mathrm{DA}$ ) at the center is the same, E . The field from arc BC and arc CD are perpendicular to each other. 
The resultant field from arc BCD is the vector sum $\vec{E}_{B C}+\vec{E}_{C D}$. 
The magnitude is $\sqrt{E^{2}+E^{2}}=\sqrt{2} E$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Electric field due to standard bodies
q: The electric field at a distance $r$ from the surface of a thin spherical shell of radius R with surface charge density $\sigma(r>R)$ is:
s: For a point outside, the shell acts as a point charge $Q=\sigma\left(4 \pi R^{2}\right)$ at the center. The distance from the center is $R+r$. So, $E=\frac{k Q}{(R+r)^{2}}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \frac{\sigma\left(4 \pi R^{2}\right)}{(R+r)^{2}}=\frac{\sigma R^{2}}{\epsilon_{0}(R+r)^{2}}$. Correction Note: If 'r' is the distance from the center, the answer is $\frac{\sigma R^{2}}{\epsilon_{0} r^{2}}$. The question states ' $r$ ' is the distance from the surface, making the distance from the center $R+r$. So option (b) is correct as written.

subject: Physics
q: Faraday's law of induction is represented by:

subject: Physics
q: An electron is released from rest at a distance of 1 m from a large, uniformly charged non-conducting sheet with surface charge density $+\sigma$. The time it takes for the electron to strike the sheet depends on:
s: The acceleration is constant: $a=\frac{e E}{m}=\frac{e \sigma}{2 m \epsilon_{0}}$. From kinematics, $d=\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$, so $t= \sqrt{\frac{2 d}{a}}=\sqrt{\frac{4 d m \epsilon_{0}}{e \sigma}}$. Time $t$ depends on both distance $d$ and charge density $\sigma$.

q: Three infinite plane sheets are placed at $z=-a, z=0, z=a$. The charge densities are $-\sigma,+2 \sigma,-\sigma$ respectively. The electric field is zero in the region(s):
s: For $z>a$, the fields from the three sheets are (positive direction is $+z$ ): $E=\frac{-\sigma}{2 \epsilon_{0}}(+\hat{k})+ \frac{2 \sigma}{2 \epsilon_{0}}(+\hat{k})+\frac{-\sigma}{2 \epsilon_{0}}(+\hat{k})=0$. By symmetry, the field is also zero for $za$, the field is zero.

subject: Physics
q: An electric dipole consists of charges $+2 \mu \mathrm{C}$ and $-2 \mu \mathrm{C}$ separated by 10 cm . It is placed in a uniform electric field of $10^{5} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{C}$. The work done in rotating it from its position of stable equilibrium to unstable equilibrium is_________(in mJ).
s:
Dipole moment $p=q(2 l)=\left(2 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{C}\right)(0.10 \mathrm{~m})=2 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{m}$.
Stable equilibrium is $\theta_{1}=0^{\circ}$; unstable is $\theta_{2}=180^{\circ}$.
$W=p E\left(\cos \theta_{1}-\cos \theta_{2}\right)=\left(2 \times 10^{-7}\right)\left(10^{5}\right)\left(\cos 0^{\circ}-\cos 180^{\circ}\right)=\left(2 \times 10^{-2}\right)(1-(-1))=4 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~J}=$ 40 mJ .

subject: Physics
q: A small insulating bob of mass 50 mg and charge $+5 \mu \mathrm{C}$ is suspended by a string of length 50 cm . It is in equilibrium in a region with a uniform horizontal electric field, with the string making an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with the vertical. The magnitude of the electric field is_________(in N/C). (Take $g=10 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$ ).
s: In equilibrium, $T \cos \left(45^{\circ}\right)=m g$ and $T \sin \left(45^{\circ}\right)=q E$. Dividing gives $\tan \left(45^{\circ}\right)=\frac{q E}{m g}$. Since $\tan \left(45^{\circ}\right)=1$, we have $q E=m g . E=\frac{m g}{q}=\frac{\left(50 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~kg}\right)\left(10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}\right)}{5 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{C}}=100 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{C}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Electric field due to standard bodies
q: A uniformly charged ring of radius $R$ has a total charge $Q$. The maximum electric field on its axis is $E_{\text {max }}=\frac{k Q}{R^{2}} \times \frac{2}{3 \sqrt{x}}$. The value of $x$ is___________.
s: The field is maximum at $z=R / \sqrt{2} . E_{\text {max }}=\frac{k Q z}{\left(R^{2}+z^{2}\right)^{3 / 2}}=\frac{k Q(R / \sqrt{2})}{\left(R^{2}+R^{2} / 2\right)^{3 / 2}}=\frac{k Q R / \sqrt{2}}{\left(3 R^{2} / 2\right)^{3 / 2}}= \frac{k Q R / \sqrt{2}}{3 \sqrt{3} R^{3} /(2 \sqrt{2})}=\frac{2 k Q}{3 \sqrt{3} R^{2}}$. Comparing this with the given expression $\frac{k Q}{R^{2}} \times \frac{2}{3 \sqrt{x}}$, we get $x=3$.

subject: Physics
q: An electron moves in a stable circular orbit around an infinite line charge of linear density $\lambda=5.05 \mathrm{nC} / \mathrm{m}$. The speed of the electron is $x \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The value of $x$ is_______. (Use $e / m_{e}=1.76 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{kg}, k=9 \times 10^{9}$ SI units).
s: The centripetal force is provided by the electric force: $m_{e} v^{2} / r=e E=e(2 k \lambda / r)$. The speed is independent of the radius: $v^{2}=\frac{2 k e \lambda}{m_{e}}=2 k \lambda\left(\frac{e}{m_{e}}\right) . v^{2}=2 \times\left(9 \times 10^{9}\right) \times\left(5.05 \times 10^{-9}\right) \times \left(1.76 \times 10^{11}\right) \approx 16 \times 10^{12}(\mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s})^{2} . v=\sqrt{16 \times 10^{12}}=4 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. Thus, $x=4$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Electric field due to a point charge or combination of point charges
q: Two point charges, $q_{1}$ and $q_{2}$, are placed at ( $-a, 0$ ) and ( $+a, 0$ ) respectively. The x - component of net electric field at point $\mathrm{P}(0, a \sqrt{3})$ is zero. The ratio $\left|q_{1} / q_{2}\right|$ must be________.
s: For the net field at P to be zero, the fields from $q_{1}$ and $q_{2}$ must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. This requires them to lie on the same line, which is not possible. For the vector sum to be zero, the vertical components must cancel and horizontal components must cancel. The distance from each charge to P is $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+(a \sqrt{3})^{2}}=\sqrt{a^{2}+3 a^{2}}=2 a$. For the vertical components to cancel, $E_{1} \sin \theta=E_{2} \sin \theta$, which means $E_{1}=E_{2}$. For the horizontal components to cancel, the charges must have the same sign. Since the distances are equal, for the field magnitudes to be equal ( $k\left|q_{1}\right| / r^{2}=k\left|q_{2}\right| / r^{2}$ ), the magnitudes of the charges must also be equal: $\left|q_{1}\right|=\left|q_{2}\right|$. The ratio is 1.

subject: Physics
q: A charge $q$ is placed at one corner of a cube. The electric flux linked with the cube is:
s: Imagine 8 identical cubes sharing that corner, enclosing the charge $q$. The total flux through these 8 cubes is $\frac{q}{\epsilon_{0}}$. By symmetry, the flux through any one cube is $\frac{1}{8}$ of the total flux, which is $\frac{q}{8 \epsilon_{0}}$.

s:
Given that radius of inner sphere = a and of the outer sphere = 2aThe inner shell has net charge Q on its surface. The outer shell is neutral.Initially, the charge distribution will be as shown in the following figure. Before closing the switch [IMAGE NOT CAPTURED] The total energy stored in the system \[U = {S_1} + {S_2} + {S_3} + {U_{12}} + {U_{23}} + {U_{13}}\],where \[{S_1}\] refers to self energy of innermost charge distribution. Numbering is increasing radially outwards. \[ \Rightarrow U = \frac{{k{Q^2}}}{{2a}} + \frac{{k{Q^2}}}{{2\left( {2a} \right)}} + \frac{{k{Q^2}}}{{2\left( {2a} \right)}} + 0 + \frac{{kQ}}{{2a}}\left( { - Q} \right),\] as \[{U_{12}} + {U_{13}} = 0\]
\[ \Rightarrow U = \frac{{k{Q^2}}}{{2a}}\]If the outer shell is connected to the earth then the charge distribution will be as shown in the following figure. Charges are transferred from outer shell to earth till the potential of the outer shell becomes zero.After closing the switch [IMAGE NOT CAPTURED] Finally, total energy stored in the system is, \[{U_f} = {S_1} + {S_2} + {U_{12}}\]\[ \Rightarrow {U_f} = \frac{{k{Q^2}}}{{2a}} + \frac{{k{Q^2}}}{{2\left( {2a} \right)}} + \frac{{kQ}}{{2a}}\left( { - Q} \right) = \frac{{k{Q^2}}}{{4a}}\]\[ \Rightarrow {U_f} = \frac{1}{2}U\]Heat generated \[ = U - {U_f} = \frac{1}{2}U\]So, \[n = 2\].

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
q: A body starting from rest moves with uniform acceleration. The ratio of the distance covered in the 4 th second to the distance covered in the 3rd second is:
s:
Distance covered in the $n^{\text {th }}$ second ( $u=0$ ) is $S_{n}=\frac{a}{2}(2 n-1)$.
$$
\frac{S_{4}}{S_{3}}=\frac{\frac{a}{2}(2(4)-1)}{\frac{a}{2}(2(3)-1)}=\frac{7}{5}
$$

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
q: A train moving at $30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ reduces its speed to $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ while covering a distance of 100 m . If the retardation is constant, how much further will it travel before coming to rest?
s:
First, find acceleration $a: 10^{2}=30^{2}+2 a(100) \Longrightarrow 100=900+200 a \Longrightarrow a=-4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. Now, find the further distance $s^{\prime}$ from $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ to rest ( $v=0$ ):
$$
0^{2}=10^{2}+2(-4) s^{\prime} \Longrightarrow 8 s^{\prime}=100 \Longrightarrow s^{\prime}=12.5 \mathrm{~m}
$$

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Simple harmonic motion/ various parameters in SHM
q: A particle starts SHM from the mean position. Its amplitude is A and time period is T . What is the time taken to cover a distance of $\mathrm{A} / 2$ from the mean position?
s: Starting from mean position, $x=A \sin (\omega t)$. We need $x=A / 2$. So, $A / 2=A \sin (\omega t) \Longrightarrow \sin (\omega t)=1 / 2 . \omega t=\pi / 6 . \frac{2 \pi}{T} t=\frac{\pi}{6} \Longrightarrow t=\frac{T}{12}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Simple harmonic motion/ various parameters in SHM
q: A particle starts its SHM from its extreme position. The time taken by the particle to travel a distance equal to half its amplitude is $\mathrm{T} / \mathrm{N}$, where T is the time period. Find the value of N.
s:
Starting from extreme position, the equation is $x=A \cos (\omega t)$. 
The particle travels a distance of $\mathrm{A} / 2$. 
So its new position is $x=A-A / 2=A / 2$. $A / 2=A \cos (\omega t) \Longrightarrow \cos (\omega t)=1 / 2 . \omega t=\pi / 3 . \frac{2 \pi}{T} t=\frac{\pi}{3} \Longrightarrow t=\frac{T}{6}$. Thus, $\mathrm{N}=6$.

subject: Physics
q: A student performs an experiment to find the focal length of a convex lens. The object distance $(u)$ and image distance $(v)$ are measured from the center of the lens. The $\frac{1}{v}$ versus $\frac{1}{u}$ plot is a straight line. If the $y$-intercept of the plot is $0.2 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$, what is the focal length of the lens?
s: The lens formula is $\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f}$. Rearranging, $\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{f}$. This is in the form $y=m x+c$. The $y$-intercept is $\frac{1}{f}$. Given the intercept is $0.2 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$, we have $\frac{1}{f}=0.2$, which gives $f=\frac{1}{0.2}=5 \mathrm{~cm}$.

q: Three towns P, Q and R are such that the distance between Q and R is double that between P and Q. A car covers the distance between P and Q with a speed 36 km/h and the distance between Q and R with a speed 48 km/h. The average speed for the entire journey is:
s:
"THIS IS A HIGH WEIGHTAGE TOPIC"

If t_1 is time taken during 1st part of the journey, t_2 is time taken for 2nd part of the journey and t is total time (t_1 + t_2) of the journey then assuming d to be the distance between P and Q, $${t_1} = \frac{d}{{{v_1}}},{t_2} = \frac{2d}{{{v_2}}},t = \frac{{\left( {{2v_1} + {v_2}} \right)d}}{{{v_1}{v_2}}}$$Since average speed = Total distance/total time taken,
Average speed $$=\frac{{3d}}{t} = \frac{{3{v_1}{v_2}}}{{{2v_1} + {v_2}}}$$
Average speed of a body \[ = \frac{{3{v_1}{v_2}}}{{{2v_1} + {v_2}}} = \frac{{3 \times 36 \times 48}}{{120}}\] = 43.2 km/h

From $v = u - a\,t$⇒ $0 = 6 - 2 \times {t_1}$ ⇒ ${t_1} = 3\,\sec $
But retardation works on it for 4 sec. It means after reaching point A direction of motion get reversed and acceleration works on the particle for next one second.
 ${S_{OA}} = u\,{t_1} - \frac{1}{2}a\,t_1^2$$ = 6 \times 3 - \frac{1}{2}(2)\;{(3)^2} = 18 - 9 = 9m$
 ${S_{AB}} = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times {(1)^2} = 1m$
 $\therefore $ ${S_{BC}} = {S_{OA}} - {S_{AB}}$ $ = 9 - 1$$ = 8m$
 Now velocity of the particle at point B in return journey
 $v = 0 + 2 \times 1$$ = 2m/s$ (using v = u + at)
 In return journey from B to C, particle moves with constant velocity 2 m/s to cover the distance 8m.
 Time taken $ = \frac{{{\text{Distance }}}}{{{\text{Velocity}}}} = \frac{8}{2} = 4\sec $
 Total time taken by particle to return at point O is ⇒$T = {t_{OA}} + {t_{AB}} + {t_{BC}}$$ = 3 + 1 + 4 = 8\sec $

subject: Physics
q: Two bodies begin a free fall from the same height at a time interval of $${\text{N}}\,{\text{s}}$$. If vertical separation between the two bodies is $${\text{1 m}}$$ after $$n$$ second from the start of the first body, then $$n$$ is equal to $(n > N)$
s:
Let $${y_1}$$ be the height through which body 1 falls in n seconds and $${y_2}$$ be the height through which body 2 falls in (n - N) seconds (because body 2 starts after N seconds) then since there starting velocity $$u = 0$$, we can write
$${y_1} = \frac{1}{2}g{n^2},{y_2} = \frac{1}{2}g{\left( {n - N} \right)^2}$$$$\therefore {y_1} - {y_2} = \frac{1}{2}g\left[ {{n^2} - {{\left( {n - N} \right)}^2}} \right]$$

$$ \Rightarrow 1 = \frac{g}{2}\left( {2n - N} \right)N$$ $$\left[ {\because {y_1} - {y_2} = 1} \right]$$

$$ \Rightarrow n = \frac{1}{{gN}} + \frac{N}{2}$$

s: First, apply conservation of linear momentum for the collision: $m_{1} u_{1}=\left(m_{1}+m_{2}\right) V$. $(0.02 \mathrm{~kg})(300 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s})=(0.02+0.98 \mathrm{~kg}) V \Longrightarrow 6=(1) V \Longrightarrow V=6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. q: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble is twice the excess pressure inside another soap bubble. The ratio of the volume of the first bubble to the second bubble is:
s: Excess pressure inside a soap bubble is $\Delta P=\frac{4 T}{r}$. Given $\Delta P_{1}= 2 \Delta P_{2} \Longrightarrow \frac{4 T}{r_{1}}=2 \frac{4 T}{r_{2}} \Longrightarrow r_{2}=2 r_{1}$. The ratio of volumes is $\frac{V_{1}}{V_{2}}=\frac{\frac{4}{3} \pi r_{1}^{3}}{\frac{4}{3} \pi r_{2}^{3}}= \left(\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}\right)^{3}=\left(\frac{r_{1}}{2 r_{1}}\right)^{3}=\frac{1}{8}$.

q: The speed of air is $50 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ below a wing and $60 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ above it. The dynamic lift on the wing is proportional to:
s: The pressure difference is $\Delta P=\frac{1}{2} \rho\left(v_{\text {above }}^{2}-v_{\text {below }}^{2}\right)$. The lift force is $F=\Delta P \times A$. Therefore, the lift is proportional to $\left(v_{\text {above }}^{2}-v_{\text {below }}^{2}\right)$, which is $60^{2}-50^{2}$.

the smaller bubble to the larger one.
one bubble to another until their sizes are equal.
one bubble to another until the interface is flat.
s: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble is inversely proportional to its radius ( $\Delta P=4 T / r$ ). The smaller bubble ( $r_{1}$ ) has a higher internal pressure than the larger bubble ( $r_{2}$ ). Therefore, air will flow from the region of higher pressure (smaller bubble) to the region of lower pressure (larger bubble).

s: Using Bernoulli's principle, the pressure difference is $\Delta P=\frac{1}{2} \rho\left(v_{\text {upper }}^{2}-\right. \left.v_{\text {lower }}^{2}\right) . \Delta P=\frac{1}{2} \times 1.2 \times\left(120^{2}-100^{2}\right)=0.6 \times(14400-10000)=0.6 \times 4400=2640 \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$. Lift Force $F=\Delta P \times A=2640 \times 10=26400 \mathrm{~N}=26.4 \mathrm{kN}$. Rounding to the nearest integer gives 26 kN .

q: A stone is thrown horizontally with a velocity of 10 m/s from top of a very tall tower. If the radius of curvature of its trajectory at the end of 3s after the motion began is $n\sqrt {10} m$, then find n . (Take, g = 10 m/s^2)
s:
Given that a stone is thrown horizontal with a velocity of 10m/s. If the radius of curvature of its trajectory at the end of 3s after the motion began is \[n\sqrt {10} m\], then we have to find n. (Taking \[g = 10m/{s^2}\]) [IMAGE NOT CAPTURED] 

To find the radius of curvature of a particle at a particular point when it moves on a curved path (not necessary circular), we draw the tangent to the curve at that point. 
The direction perpendicular to it is radial direction. we resolve all the forces in the radial direction and equate the resultant to \[\frac{{m{v^2}}}{r}\]. where v = the speed of the particle at that moment and r = the radius of curvature. 
Let us choose the co-ordinate axes as shown in the above figure. Please note that we have the downward direction as the positive y-axis.
Here, \[{u_x} = 10m/s,{u_r} = 0,{a_x} = 0\,{\text{and}}\,{a_r} = + 10m/{s^2}\], where the terms have their usual meaning.
Now, the horizontal component of the velocity in projectile motion remains constant as \[{a_x} = 0\].
So, \[{v_x} = 10m/s\]
Using \[{v_y} = {u_y} + {a_r}t\] we get, \[{v_y} = \left( {10} \right)\left( 3 \right) = 30m/s\]
The speed of the particle at that instant is \[v = \sqrt {v_x^2 + v_y^2} \]
\[ \Rightarrow v = \sqrt {{{10}^2} + {{30}^2}} = \sqrt {1000} m/s\]

Also, as shown in the above figure, \[\tan \theta = \frac{{{v_y}}}{{{v_x}}}\]
\[ \Rightarrow \tan \theta = \frac{{30}}{{10}} = 3\]

There is only one force acting on the stone, its weight (which acts vertically downwards). The component of the weight in the radial direction is \[mg\cos \theta \].
So, we get \[mg\cos \theta = \frac{{m{v^2}}}{r}\].
\[ \Rightarrow g\cos \theta = \frac{{{v^2}}}{r}\]

From \[\tan \theta = 3,\cos \theta = \frac{1}{{\sqrt {10} }}\]. (This can be easily obtained by making a right - angled triangle of perpendicular length 3 and and base length \[l\])
\[ \Rightarrow g\left( {\frac{1}{{\sqrt {10} }}} \right) = \frac{{1000}}{r}\]

\[ \Rightarrow \left( {10} \right)\left( {\frac{1}{{\sqrt {10} }}} \right) = \frac{{1000}}{r}\]

\[ \Rightarrow r = 100\sqrt {10} m\]

Three logic gates are connected as shown in the figure. If the inputs are $A=1, B=0$ and $C=1$, then the values of $y_{1}, y_{2}$ and $y_{3}$ respectively are:
 [IMAGE: images/MB002003_1.webp]
s:
The outputs are calculated step-by-step:
- The first gate $\left(y_{1}\right)$ is a NAND gate with inputs $\mathrm{A}=1$ and $\mathrm{B}=0$. So, $y_{1}=\overline{1 \cdot 0}=\overline{0}=1$.
- The second gate $\left(y_{2}\right)$ is a NOR gate with inputs $\mathrm{B}=0$ and $\mathrm{C}=1$. So, $y_{2}=\overline{0+1}=\overline{1}=0$.
- The final gate $\left(y_{3}\right)$ is an AND gate with inputs $y_{1}=1$ and $y_{2}=0$. So, $y_{3}=1 \cdot 0=0$.
The values are 1,0 , and 0 .

bank_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
q: In the breakdown region of a Zener diode, a small increase in reverse voltage will cause:
o: a large increase in reverse current.
a large decrease in reverse current.
a large increase in forward current.
s: The I-V characteristic of a Zener diode is very steep in the breakdown region. This means the voltage across it remains almost constant (Zener voltage), while the reverse current can increase by a large amount with only a very tiny increase in the reverse voltage.

subject: Physics
bank_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
q: In an intrinsic semiconductor at a finite temperature:
o: the number of electrons is greater than the number of holes.
the number of holes is greater than the number of electrons.
the number of electrons and holes are equal.
there are no free charge carriers.
s: In an intrinsic (pure) semiconductor, charge carriers are created by thermal excitation, which generates electron-hole pairs. Therefore, the number of free electrons ( $n_{e}$ ) is always equal to the number of holes ( $n_{h}$ ).

subject: Physics
bank_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
q: In a half-wave rectifier circuit, the output frequency is $f_{\text {out }}$ and the input frequency is $f_{i n}$. The relationship between them is:
s: A half-wave rectifier allows only one half-cycle of the input AC waveform to pass through. The resulting output waveform has the same period, and therefore the same frequency, as the input AC signal.

subject: Physics
bank_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
sub_topic: Semiconductor Diode - I-V Characteristics in Forward and Reverse Bias
q: A Zener diode with a breakdown voltage of 6 V is connected in reverse bias to a variable voltage source. When the source voltage is 4 V , the voltage across the Zener diode is:
s: The Zener diode only maintains a constant voltage of 6 V across it when the applied reverse voltage is equal to or greater than its breakdown voltage. Since the applied voltage ( 4 V ) is less than the breakdown voltage ( 6 V ), the diode does not break down and acts like a normal reverse-biased diode with very high resistance. Almost the entire source voltage appears across it.

subject: Physics
bank_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
q: Doping a pure semiconductor with pentavalent impurities results in:
o: an increase in the number of holes.
a change in its chemical properties.
s: Pentavalent impurities (like Phosphorus or Arsenic) have five valence electrons. When added to a semiconductor like silicon (four valence electrons), four electrons form covalent bonds, and the fifth becomes a free electron, increasing the electron concentration and creating an n-type semiconductor.

subject: Physics
bank_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
q:
In a half-wave rectifier circuit, the input signal is $V_{i n}=20 \sin (100 \pi t)$. Assuming the diode is ideal, the average of the output voltage is approximately _____(in V). (Use $\pi=3.14$ ). 

(Mention nearest integer value)
s: The input voltage has a peak value of $V_{m}=20 \mathrm{~V}$. For a half-wave rectifier, the DC component (or average value) of the output voltage is given by $V_{d c}=\frac{V_{m}}{\pi} . \quad V_{d c}=\frac{20}{\pi}=\frac{20}{3.14} \approx 6.37 \mathrm{~V}$. Rounding to the nearest integer, the DC voltage is 6 V .

subject: Physics
bank_chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
q: In a potential divider circuit, a DC source of 30 V is used. The total length of the resistive wire PR is 15 cm . The circuit includes an LED with a glow voltage of 2.5 V and a Zener diode with a breakdown voltage of 5.5 V , connected in series between the tap point Q and the positive terminal P . The minimum length of PQ required to just make the devices conduct is_________(in cm). [IMAGE: images/MB002050_1.webp]
s:
For the devices to just start conducting, the voltage across the segment
PQ must be equal to the sum of the LED's forward voltage and the Zener's reverse breakdown voltage. $V_{P Q}=V_{L E D}+V_{\text {Zener }}=2.5 \mathrm{~V}+5.5 \mathrm{~V}=8.0 \mathrm{~V}$. The potential divider wire PR has a total voltage of 30 V across its length of 15 cm . The voltage gradient along the wire is $\frac{30 \mathrm{~V}}{15 \mathrm{~cm}}=2 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{cm}$. The length corresponding to a voltage of 8.0 V is Length $\mathrm{PQ}=\frac{\text { Voltage } V_{P Q}}{\text { Voltage Gradient }}=\frac{8.0 \mathrm{~V}}{2 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{cm}}=4 \mathrm{~cm}$.
