subject: Physics
q: An alternating voltage is given by $V=140 \sin (100 \pi t)$. The RMS value of the voltage and the frequency of the supply are respectively:
s: The peak voltage is $V_{0}=140 \mathrm{~V}$, so $V_{\text {rms }}=V_{0} / \sqrt{2}=140 / \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~V}$. The angular frequency is $\omega=100 \pi$. Since $\omega=2 \pi f$, the frequency is $f=\omega / 2 \pi= 100 \pi / 2 \pi=50 \mathrm{~Hz}$.

subject: Physics
q: In a purely inductive AC circuit, the current:
o: Is in phase with the voltage.
s: In a purely inductive circuit, the voltage across the inductor leads the current flowing through it by a phase angle of $90^{\circ}$ or $\pi / 2$ radians. Therefore, the current lags behind the voltage.

subject: Physics
q: An LCR series circuit has $V_{L}=40 \mathrm{~V}, V_{C}=40 \mathrm{~V}$, and $V_{R}=60 \mathrm{~V}$. The EMF of the source is:
s: The total source voltage is $V=\sqrt{V_{R}^{2}+\left(V_{L}-V_{C}\right)^{2}}$. Since $V_{L}=V_{C}=40$ V , the circuit is in resonance. $V=\sqrt{60^{2}+(40-40)^{2}}=\sqrt{60^{2}}=60 \mathrm{~V}$.

subject: Physics
q: The RMS value of the current given by $I=(3 \sin \omega t+4 \cos \omega t) \mathrm{A}$ is:
s: The given current can be written as $I=I_{0} \sin (\omega t+\phi)$, where the peak value $I_{0}=\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}=\sqrt{9+16}=\sqrt{25}=5$ A. The RMS value is $I_{r m s}=I_{0} / \sqrt{2}= 5 / \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~A}$.

subject: Physics
q: At resonance in a series LCR circuit, the power factor is:
s: At resonance, $X_{L}=X_{C}$, so the impedance $Z=R$. The phase angle $\phi=0$. The power factor, $\cos \phi=\cos (0)=1$. The circuit behaves as a purely resistive circuit.

subject: Physics
q: An electric bulb is rated $220 \mathrm{~V}-100 \mathrm{~W}$. The peak voltage of the source it can withstand and the peak current through the bulb are respectively:
s: The rated voltage is the RMS value, $V_{\text {rms }}=220 \mathrm{~V}$. The peak voltage is $V_{0}=V_{r m s} \sqrt{2}=220 \sqrt{2} \approx 311 \mathrm{~V}$. The RMS current is $I_{r m s}=P / V_{r m s}=100 / 220 \approx$ 0.45 A . The peak current is $I_{0}=I_{r m s} \sqrt{2} \approx 0.45 \sqrt{2} \approx 0.64 \mathrm{~A}$.

subject: Physics
q: In a series LCR circuit, the frequency of the AC source is increased from below resonance to above resonance. The impedance of the circuit will:
s: Impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^{2}+\left(X_{L}-X_{C}\right)^{2}}$. At resonance frequency, $X_{L}=X_{C}$ and Z is minimum ( $Z=R$ ). As frequency moves away from resonance in either direction, the term $\left(X_{L}-X_{C}\right)^{2}$ increases, causing Z to increase. So, it first decreases to a minimum at resonance and then increases.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Average and RMS value of a function
q: The time taken for an AC of 50 Hz to change from zero to its RMS value is:
s: Let $I=I_{0} \sin (\omega t)$. The RMS value is $I_{\text {rms }}=I_{0} / \sqrt{2} . \quad I_{0} / \sqrt{2}= I_{0} \sin (\omega t) \Longrightarrow \sin (\omega t)=1 / \sqrt{2} . \quad \omega t=\pi / 4$. Since $\omega=2 \pi f=2 \pi(50)=100 \pi$. $100 \pi t=\pi / 4 \Longrightarrow t=1 / 400 \mathrm{~s}=0.0025 \mathrm{~s}=2.5 \mathrm{~ms}$.

subject: Physics
q: A capacitor of capacitance C has a reactance X . If both the capacitance and frequency are doubled, the new reactance will be:
s: Capacitive reactance is $X_{C}=\frac{1}{2 \pi f C}$. So, $X_{C} \propto 1 /(f C)$. The new reactance $X_{C}^{\prime} \propto \frac{1}{(2 f)(2 C)}=\frac{1}{4 f C}$. So, $X_{C}^{\prime}=X_{C} / 4$.

subject: Physics
q: Assertion (A): A capacitor is a conductor for AC but a blocker for DC . Reason (R): The capacitive reactance is inversely proportional to frequency.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
s: Reason (R) is true as $X_{C}=1 /(2 \pi f C)$. For $\mathrm{AC}, \mathrm{f}$ is finite, so $X_{C}$ is finite, allowing current to flow. For $\mathrm{DC}, \mathrm{f}=0$, so $X_{C}$ is infinite, blocking the current. Thus, (R) correctly explains (A).

subject: Physics
q: An inductor ( $\mathrm{L}=100 \mathrm{mH}$ ), a capacitor ( $\mathrm{C}=100 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ ) and a resistor $(\mathrm{R}=100 \Omega)$ are connected in series to an AC source $V=100 \sin (100 t)$. The impedance of the circuit is:

subject: Physics
q: In an AC circuit containing only a resistor, the phase difference between voltage and current is:
s: In a purely resistive circuit, the voltage and current are always in the same phase.

subject: Physics
q: The average power dissipated in a purely inductive or purely capacitive circuit is:
s: In purely inductive or capacitive circuits, the phase difference between voltage and current is $\pi / 2$. The power factor $\cos (\pi / 2)=0$. Therefore, the average power dissipated ( $P_{\text {avg }}=V_{\text {rms }} I_{\text {rms }} \cos \phi$ ) is zero.

subject: Physics
q: A series LCR circuit with $\mathrm{L}=0.12 \mathrm{H}, \mathrm{C}=480 \mathrm{nF}, \mathrm{R}=23 \Omega$ is connected to a 230 V variable frequency supply. The resonant angular frequency is:
s: $\omega_{0}=1 / \sqrt{L C}=1 / \sqrt{0.12 \times 480 \times 10^{-9}}=1 / \sqrt{57.6 \times 10^{-9}}=1 / \sqrt{5.76 \times 10^{-8}}= 1 /\left(2.4 \times 10^{-4}\right)=\frac{10000}{2.4} \approx 4167 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Average and RMS value of a function
q: An AC current is described by $I=10 \sin (200 \pi t)+20 \cos (200 \pi t)$. The RMS value of the current is:
s: The peak value of the current is $I_{0}=\sqrt{10^{2}+20^{2}}=\sqrt{100+400}=\sqrt{500}$ A. The RMS value is $I_{r m s}=I_{0} / \sqrt{2}=\sqrt{500} / \sqrt{2}=\sqrt{250} \mathrm{~A}$.

subject: Physics
q: The quality factor (Q-factor) of a series LCR circuit is given by:
s: The Q -factor is defined as $Q=\frac{\omega_{0} L}{R}$. Substituting $\omega_{0}=1 / \sqrt{L C}$, we get $Q=\frac{L}{R \sqrt{L C}}=\frac{1}{R} \sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Working of transformers and losses in transformers
q: In a step-up transformer, the quantity that decreases is:
s:
In an ideal step-up transformer, the voltage is
increased ( $V_{s}>V_{p}$ ). To conserve power ( $P=V I$ ), the current must
decrease in the secondary coil ( $I_{s}<I_{p}$ ). Frequency remains
unchanged.

subject: Physics
q: A hot-wire ammeter measures:
s: A hot-wire ammeter works on the principle of the heating effect of current ( $H \propto I^{2}$ ). Since the heating effect is proportional to the square of the current, the deflection is proportional to the mean square current, thus it measures the RMS value.

subject: Physics
q: A 50 mH inductor is connected to a $220 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~Hz} \mathrm{AC}$ source. The inductive reactance is approximately:
s: $X_{L}=\omega L=2 \pi f L=2 \times 3.14 \times 50 \times\left(50 \times 10^{-3}\right)=314 \times 0.05=15.7 \Omega$.

subject: Physics
q: In a series LCR circuit, if the applied frequency is less than the resonant frequency, then:
s:
If $f<f_{0}$, then $\omega<\omega_{0}$.
This means $X_{L}(=\omega L)$ is small and $X_{C}(=1 / \omega C)$ is large. So,
$X_{C}>X_{L}$. The circuit is predominantly capacitive, and the current
leads the voltage.

subject: Physics
q: The expression for an alternating current is given by $i=(1+4 \sin (\omega t))$ A. The RMS value of the current is____________(in A).
s: The current is a superposition of a DC component ( $I_{D C}=1 \mathrm{~A}$ ) and an AC component with peak value $I_{0}=4 \mathrm{~A}$. The RMS value of the AC component is $I_{A C, r m s}=I_{0} / \sqrt{2}=4 / \sqrt{2}$. The total RMS value is $I_{r m s}=\sqrt{I_{D C}^{2}+\left(I_{A C, r m s}\right)^{2}}= \sqrt{1^{2}+(4 / \sqrt{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{1+16 / 2}=\sqrt{1+8}=\sqrt{9}=3 \mathrm{~A}$.

subject: Physics
q: A series LCR circuit has $\mathrm{R}=40 \Omega, X_{L}=50 \Omega$, and $X_{C}=20 \Omega$. It is connected to a 150 V (RMS) AC source. The average power dissipated by the circuit is____________(in W).
s: Impedance $Z=\sqrt{R^{2}+\left(X_{L}-X_{C}\right)^{2}}=\sqrt{40^{2}+(50-20)^{2}}=\sqrt{1600+900}= \sqrt{2500}=50 \Omega$. RMS current $I_{r m s}=V_{r m s} / Z=150 / 50=3$ A. Average power $P_{\text {avg }}=I_{\text {rms }}^{2} R=(3)^{2} \times 40=9 \times 40=360 \mathrm{~W}$.

subject: Physics
q: In a series LCR circuit, the RMS voltages across the resistor, inductor, and capacitor are $80 \mathrm{~V}, 100 \mathrm{~V}$, and 40 V respectively. The RMS voltage of the AC source is____________ (in V).
s: The total source voltage is given by the phasor sum: $V=\sqrt{V_{R}^{2}+\left(V_{L}-V_{C}\right)^{2}}$. $V=\sqrt{80^{2}+(100-40)^{2}}=\sqrt{80^{2}+60^{2}}=\sqrt{6400+3600}=\sqrt{10000}=100 \mathrm{~V}$.

subject: Physics
q: The peak value of an AC voltage is $100 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~V}$. Its RMS value is_________V.
s: The RMS value is related to the peak value by $V_{r m s}=V_{0} / \sqrt{2} . \quad V_{r m s}= (100 \sqrt{2}) / \sqrt{2}=100 \mathrm{~V}$.

subject: Physics
q: An AC circuit has a resonant frequency of 50 Hz . If the inductance is 2 H , the capacitance required for resonance is $1 /\left(N \pi^{2}\right) \mathrm{F}$. The value of N is__________ $\qquad$ .
s: The resonant frequency is $f_{0}=\frac{1}{2 \pi \sqrt{L C}}$. Squaring both sides: $f_{0}^{2}=\frac{1}{4 \pi^{2} L C}$. $C=\frac{1}{4 \pi^{2} \int_{0}^{2} L}=\frac{1}{4 \pi^{2}(50)^{2}(2)}=\frac{1}{4 \pi^{2}(2500)(2)}=\frac{1}{20000 \pi^{2}}$ F. Comparing this with $1 /\left(N \pi^{2}\right)$, we get $\mathrm{N}=20000$.

subject: Physics
q: A point object is placed in air at a distance of 3 R from the pole of a convex spherical refracting surface of refractive index 1.5 and radius of curvature $R$. The image is formed at a distance:
s:
Using the formula for refraction at a spherical surface: $\frac{n_{2}}{v}-\frac{n_{1}}{u}=\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{R}$. Here, $n_{1}=1$, $n_{2}=1.5, u=-3 R$, and the surface is convex so $R=+R$.
$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{1.5}{v}-\frac{1}{-3 R}=\frac{1.5-1}{R} \Rightarrow \frac{1.5}{v}=\frac{0.5}{R}-\frac{1}{3 R}=\frac{1.5-1}{3 R}=\frac{0.5}{3 R} \\
v=\frac{1.5 \times 3 R}{0.5}=9 R
\end{gathered}
$$
The image is real and formed in the glass.

subject: Physics
q: The critical angle for light travelling from medium $X$ to medium $Y$ is $\theta$. If the speed of light in medium X is v , then the speed of light in medium Y is:
s: By Snell's law at the critical angle, $n_{X} \sin \theta=n_{Y} \sin \left(90^{\circ}\right)=n_{Y}$. The refractive index is inversely proportional to the speed of light, $n=c / v_{\text {light. }}$. So, $\frac{c}{v_{X}} \sin \theta=\frac{c}{v_{Y}}$. Given $v_{X}=v$, we have $\frac{c}{v} \sin \theta=\frac{c}{v_{Y}}$, which gives $v_{Y}=\frac{v}{\sin \theta}$.

subject: Physics
q: For a prism of refracting angle $A=60^{\circ}$, the angle of minimum deviation is $\delta_{m}=30^{\circ}$. The refractive index of the prism material is:
s:
Using the prism formula, $\mu=\frac{\sin \left(\frac{A+\delta_{m}}{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$.
$$
\mu=\frac{\sin \left(\frac{60^{\circ}+30^{\circ}}{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\frac{60^{\circ}}{2}\right)}=\frac{\sin \left(45^{\circ}\right)}{\sin \left(30^{\circ}\right)}=\frac{1 / \sqrt{2}}{1 / 2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{2}
$$

subject: Physics
q: For the combination of two thin prisms to produce dispersion without deviation, which of the following conditions must be met? (A is prism angle, $\mu$ is refractive index)
s: The condition for zero net deviation for the mean color is that the sum of individual deviations is zero. For thin prisms, the deviation is $\delta=(\mu-1) A$. Therefore, $\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}=0 \Rightarrow \left(\mu_{1}-1\right) A_{1}+\left(\mu_{2}-1\right) A_{2}=0$. This requires the prisms to be placed in opposition.

subject: Physics
q: When a ray of light passes through a prism at the angle of minimum deviation:
o: the angle of incidence is greater than the angle of emergence.
the angle of refraction is equal to the angle of the prism.
the refracted ray inside the prism is parallel to its base.
the angle of deviation is twice the angle of the prism.
s: At minimum deviation, the path of the light ray is symmetric. This means the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence ( $i=e$ ), and the two angles of refraction inside the prism are equal ( $r_{1}=r_{2}$ ). This symmetry makes the refracted ray parallel to the base of the prism.

subject: Physics
q: An air bubble inside a glass sphere of radius 15 cm and refractive index 1.5 appears to be at 6 cm from the surface when viewed along a diameter from the closest side. Its actual distance from the surface is:

subject: Physics
q: A thin prism of $4^{\circ}$ angle made from glass of refractive index 1.5 gives a deviation of:
s:
For a thin prism, the deviation is given by $\delta=(\mu-1) A$.
$$
\delta=(1.5-1) \times 4^{\circ}=0.5 \times 4^{\circ}=2^{\circ}
$$

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Dispersion due to a thin prism
q:
Assertion (A): White light is dispersed when it passes through a prism.
Reason (R): The refractive index of the material of a prism depends on the wavelength of light.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
s: According to Cauchy's relation, the refractive index $\mu$ is a function of wavelength $\lambda$. Since different colors in white light have different wavelengths, they travel at different speeds inside the prism and bend by different amounts, causing dispersion. Thus, (A) is true and (R) is the correct explanation for it.

subject: Physics
q: For a prism, the angle of minimum deviation is equal to its refracting angle A . The refractive index of the material of the prism is:
s:
Given $\delta_{m}=A$. The prism formula is $\mu=\frac{\sin \left(\left(A+\delta_{m}\right) / 2\right)}{\sin (A / 2)}$. Substituting $\delta_{m}=A$, we get:
$$
\mu=\frac{\sin ((A+A) / 2)}{\sin (A / 2)}=\frac{\sin (A)}{\sin (A / 2)}
$$
Using the identity $\sin (A)=2 \sin (A / 2) \cos (A / 2)$, we get $\mu=\frac{2 \sin (A / 2) \cos (A / 2)}{\sin (A / 2)}=2 \cos (A / 2)$.

subject: Physics
q: When light travels from air into glass, which of the following physical quantities remains unchanged?
s: When light passes from one medium to another, its frequency remains constant because it is a characteristic of the source. Both the speed and wavelength change.

subject: Physics
q: The refractive index of the material of a prism is $\cot (A / 2)$ where A is the angle of the prism. The angle of minimum deviation is:
s:
We have $\mu=\frac{\sin \left(\left(A+\delta_{m}\right) / 2\right)}{\sin (A / 2)}$. Given $\mu=\cot (A / 2)=\frac{\cos (A / 2)}{\sin (A / 2)}$. Equating the two expressions for $\mu$ :
$$
\frac{\cos (A / 2)}{\sin (A / 2)}=\frac{\sin \left(\left(A+\delta_{m}\right) / 2\right)}{\sin (A / 2)} \Rightarrow \cos (A / 2)=\sin \left(\left(A+\delta_{m}\right) / 2\right)
$$
Using $\cos (x)=\sin \left(90^{\circ}-x\right)$, we get $\sin \left(90^{\circ}-A / 2\right)=\sin \left(\left(A+\delta_{m}\right) / 2\right)$.
$$
90^{\circ}-A / 2=\left(A+\delta_{m}\right) / 2 \Rightarrow 180^{\circ}-A=A+\delta_{m} \Rightarrow \delta_{m}=180^{\circ}-2 A
$$

subject: Physics
q: An object is placed at the center of curvature of a concave spherical refracting surface separating a rarer medium (refractive index $n_{1}$ ) from a denser medium (refractive index $n_{2}$ ). The image is formed at:
s:
Rays from the center of curvature strike the surface normally and pass undeviated. Thus, the image is also formed at the center of curvature. Using the formula with $u=-R$ (for a concave surface, $R$ is negative):
$$
\frac{n_{2}}{v}-\frac{n_{1}}{-R}=\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{-R} \Rightarrow \frac{n_{2}}{v}=\frac{-\left(n_{2}-n_{1}\right)}{R}-\frac{n_{1}}{R}=\frac{-n_{2}}{R} \Rightarrow v=-R
$$

subject: Physics
q:
A ray of light passes through four transparent media with refractive indices $\mu_{1}, \mu_{2}, \mu_{3}$, and $\mu_{4}$ as shown in the figure. The surfaces of all media are parallel. If the emergent ray $C D$ is parallel to the incident ray AB , we must have:
 [IMAGE: images/MB001713_1.webp]
s: For a series of parallel media, the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray if the refractive index of the first medium is equal to the refractive index of the final medium. Thus, $\mu_{1}=\mu_{4}$.

subject: Physics
q: A ray of light passes through an equilateral glass prism $(\mu=\sqrt{3})$ such that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of emergence. If the angle of emergence is $60^{\circ}$, the angle of deviation suffered by the ray is:
s: For an equilateral prism, $A=60^{\circ}$. Given $i=e=60^{\circ}$. The angle of deviation is $\delta=i+e-A=60^{\circ}+60^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$.

subject: Physics
q: A biconvex lens has radii of curvature 20 cm and 30 cm . If the refractive index of the material of the lens is 1.5, its focal length is:
s:
Using the Lens Maker's formula: $\frac{1}{f}=(\mu-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_{1}}-\frac{1}{R_{2}}\right)$. Here, $R_{1}=+20 \mathrm{~cm}, R_{2}=-30$ cm, $\mu=1.5$.
$$
\frac{1}{f}=(1.5-1)\left(\frac{1}{20}-\frac{1}{-30}\right)=0.5\left(\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{30}\right)=0.5\left(\frac{3+2}{60}\right)=0.5 \times \frac{5}{60}=\frac{2.5}{60}=\frac{1}{24}
$$
$f=24 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: The graph of angle of deviation ( $\delta$ ) versus angle of incidence (i) for a triangular prism is best represented by:
o: A straight line passing through the origin.
A curve that first decreases and then increases.
s: The $\delta$ vs i curve for a prism is not symmetric. As the angle of incidence increases, the angle of deviation first decreases, reaches a minimum value ( $\delta_{m}$ ), and then increases.

subject: Physics
q: A small coin is at the bottom of a beaker filled with a liquid of refractive index $4 / 3$ to a depth of 6 cm . What is the apparent depth of the coin when viewed from above?
s: Apparent depth $d^{\prime}=\frac{\text { Real Depth }}{\mu}=\frac{6 \mathrm{~cm}}{4 / 3}=\frac{18}{4}=4.5 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q:
A ray incident at a point at an angle of incidence of $60^{\circ}$ enters a glass sphere of refractive index $\mu=\sqrt{3}$ and is reflected and refracted at the farther surface of the sphere. The angle between the reflected and refracted rays at this surface is:
 [IMAGE: images/MB001718_1.webp]
s: First, find the angle of refraction $\theta_{2}$ inside the sphere using Snell's Law: $1 \cdot \sin \left(60^{\circ}\right)= \sqrt{3} \cdot \sin \theta_{2}$, which gives $\sin \theta_{2}=1 / 2$, so $\theta_{2}=30^{\circ}$. This is the angle of incidence at the second surface. The angle of reflection is also $30^{\circ}$. The angle of refraction $\theta_{3}$ for the exiting ray is found by $\sqrt{3} \cdot \sin \left(30^{\circ}\right)=1 \cdot \sin \theta_{3}$, which gives $\theta_{3}=60^{\circ}$. The angle between the reflected and refracted rays is $30^{\circ}+60^{\circ}=90^{\circ}$.

subject: Physics
q:
A beam of light consisting of red, green, and blue is incident on a right-angled prism. The refractive indices of the material for the red, green, and blue wavelengths are $1.39,1.44$, and 1.47 respectively. The prism will:
 [IMAGE: images/MB001719_1.webp]
o: separate the red color from the green and blue colors.
separate the blue color from the red and green colors.
separate all three colors from one another.

q: Wire of an original length of 10 m is fixed at one end and is being stretched with force of 200 N which elongates it by 4 mm. Find the difference in the diameter as a multiple of ${10^{ - 7}}$ during the stretching of the wire. Where, Young’s modulus ${\text{Y}} = 2 \times {10^{11}}{\text{N}} - {{\text{m}}^2}$ and Poisson’s ratio = 0.32 (Report nearest integral value as answer)
s:
"THIS IS A HIGH WEIGHTAGE TOPIC"

Length of the given wire is, \[l = 10m\] force applied on the wire is, F = 200 N.
Elongation produced in the wire is, \[\Delta l = 4mm\].
Young's modulus of the wire is, \[Y = 2 \times {10^{11}}N - {m^2}\]
Poisson's ratio of the wire is, \[\sigma = 0.32\]
 [IMAGE NOT CAPTURED] 

According to Hooke's law, Stress = (Young's modulus) Strain
\[ = \frac{{4F}}{{\pi {d^2}}} = Y \times \frac{{\Delta l}}{l}\]

\[ \Rightarrow d = 2\sqrt {\frac{{Fl}}{{Y\pi \left( {\Delta l} \right)}}} \]

\[ \Rightarrow d = 2\sqrt {\frac{{200\left( {10} \right)}}{{2\pi \times {{10}^{11}} \times 4 \times {{10}^{ - 3}}}}} \]

\[d = 1.78 \times {10^{ - 3}}m\].

We also know that poisson's ratio \[\sigma = - \frac{{\frac{{\Delta d}}{d}}}{{\frac{{\Delta l}}{l}}}\]
\[ = 0.32 = - \frac{{\frac{{\Delta d}}{{1.78 \times {{10}^{ - 3}}}}}}{{\frac{{4 \times {{10}^{ - 3}}}}{{10}}}}\]

\[ \Rightarrow \Delta d = 2.30 \times {10^{ - 7}}m\].

q: A cyclist rides along the circumference of a circular horizontal track of radius r. The coefficient of friction \[\mu = {\mu _{\,0}}\left[ {1 - \frac{r}{R}} \right]\] where μ _o is a constant, and r is the distance from the centre of the circle. The maximum velocity of the cyclist is
s:
When a cyclist moves through a circular path, the cyclist does not slide on the rod because of the centripetal force given by the frictional force.
So, we can equate the frictional force to the centripetal force to find the maximum velocity of the cyclist.
Now, the centripetal force is given by, $${f_c} = \frac{{m{v^2}}}{r}$$
The frictional force is given as, $${f_f} = \mu N = \mu mg$$
Where, m is the mass of the system, v is the velocity of the cyclist, r is the distance from the centre of the plane, $$\mu $$ is the frictional coefficient and g is the acceleration due to gravity. 
The frictional coefficient is given as, $$\mu = {\mu _0}\left( {1 - \frac{r}{R}} \right)$$
Equating the two forces we get,
$$\frac{{m{v^2}}}{r} = \mu mg$$

Putting the value of the coefficient of friction,
$$\frac{{{v^2}}}{r} = {\mu _0}\left( {1 - \frac{r}{R}} \right)g\frac{{{v^2}}}{r} = {\mu _0}\left( {1 - \frac{r}{R}} \right)g$$
Now the velocity of the cyclist will be maximum if the space derivative of the velocity is zero.
Putting the value of the coefficient of friction,
$$\frac{{{v^2}}}{r} = {\mu _0}\left( {1 - \frac{r}{R}} \right)g$$
$${v^2} = {\mu _0}\left( {r - \frac{{{r^2}}}{R}} \right)g$$
Now, the velocity of the cyclist will be maximum if the space derivative of the velocity is zero.
$$\frac{{dv}}{{dr}} = \frac{{d{v^2}}}{{dr}} = 0$$
$${\mu _0}g\left( {1 - \frac{{2r}}{R}} \right) = 0$$
$$r = \frac{R}{2}$$
Now, 
$$v = \sqrt {{\mu _0}\left( {r - \frac{{{r^2}}}{R}} \right)g} $$
So, the maximum velocity will be,
$${v_{\max }} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt {{\mu _0}gR} $$
Note: Whenever we move in a circular path, we feel a force towards the centre of the circular path. This force is called the centripetal force. In this case the centripetal force is given by the frictional force between the wheel of the cycle of and the road.

q: A thin circular disc of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rotating in a horizontal plane about its central axis with angular velocity $\omega$. If another disc of the same radius but of mass $\frac{M}{4}$ is placed gently on the first disc co-axially, then the new angular velocity of the system is:
s: By conservation of angular momentum, $L_{i}=L_{f} \Longrightarrow I_{1} \omega=\left(I_{1}+I_{2}\right) \omega_{f}$. Here $I_{1}=\frac{1}{2} M R^{2}$ and $I_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{M}{4}\right) R^{2}=\frac{I_{1}}{4} . I_{1} \omega=\left(I_{1}+\frac{I_{1}}{4}\right) \omega_{f} \Longrightarrow I_{1} \omega=\frac{5}{4} I_{1} \omega_{f} \Longrightarrow \omega_{f}=\frac{4}{5} \omega$.

They are brought into contact. The loss in kinetic energy of the system is:
s: The final common angular velocity is $\omega_{f}=\frac{I_{1} \omega_{1}+I_{2} \omega_{2}}{I_{1}+I_{2}}=\frac{3(2)+1(6)}{3+1}=\frac{12}{4}=3 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. Initial KE: $K_{i}=\frac{1}{2} I_{1} \omega_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} I_{2} \omega_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(3)\left(2^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2}(1)\left(6^{2}\right)=6+18=24 J$. Final KE: $K_{f}=\frac{1}{2}\left(I_{1}+I_{2}\right) \omega_{f}^{2}= \frac{1}{2}(4)\left(3^{2}\right)=18 \mathrm{~J}$. Loss $=K_{i}-K_{f}=24-18=6 \mathrm{~J}$.

From conservation of angular momentum

$$

We are given $T=k S^{a} \rho^{b} r^{c}$. Writing dimensions on both sides: $\left[T^{1}\right]=\left[M T^{-2}\right]^{a}\left[M L^{-3}\right]^{b}[L]^{c} \left[M^{0} L^{0} T^{1}\right]=\left[M^{a+b} L^{-3 b+c} T^{-2 a}\right]$ Equating the exponents:
- T: $-2 a=1 \Longrightarrow a=-1 / 2$.
- M: $a+b=0 \Longrightarrow-1 / 2+b=0 \Longrightarrow b=1 / 2$.
- $\mathrm{L}:-3 b+c=0 \Longrightarrow-3(1 / 2)+c=0 \Longrightarrow c=3 / 2$.
So, the values are $a=-1 / 2, b=1 / 2, c=3 / 2$.

subject: Physics
q: The maximum number of spectral lines emitted when electrons in a hydrogen sample de-excites from the 5th excited state is_______. $\qquad$
s: The 5th excited state corresponds to $n=6$. The number of lines is $N=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. For $n=6, N=\frac{6(6-1)}{2}=\frac{6 \times 5}{2}=15$.

subject: Physics
q: The ratio of the shortest wavelength of the Paschen series to the shortest wavelength of the Balmer series for a hydrogen atom is:
s: The shortest wavelength (series limit) corresponds to a transition from $n_{2}=\infty$ to $n_{1}$. $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{\infty^{2}}\right)=\frac{R}{n_{1}^{2}}$. So, $\lambda=\frac{n_{1}^{2}}{R}$. For Paschen series, $n_{1}=3, \lambda_{P}=9 / R$. For Balmer series, $n_{1}=2, \lambda_{B}=4 / R$. The ratio $\lambda_{P}: \lambda_{B}=(9 / R):(4 / R)=9: 4$.

subject: Physics
q: An electron in a hydrogen atom transitions from $\mathrm{n}=5$ to $\mathrm{n}=2$. The emitted photon belongs to which spectral series?
s: The Balmer series is defined by electronic transitions that end in the $\mathrm{n}=2$ energy level. Since the final state is $n_{1}=2$, the line belongs to the Balmer series.

subject: Physics
q: If the wavelength of the first line of the Balmer series of hydrogen is $\lambda$, the wavelength of the first line of the Lyman series is:
s: For the first line of Balmer series $(\mathrm{n}=3$ to $\mathrm{n}=2): \frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{3^{2}}\right)=R\left(\frac{5}{36}\right)$. For the first line of Lyman series ( $\mathrm{n}=2$ to $\mathrm{n}=1$ ): $\frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}=R\left(\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{2^{2}}\right)=R\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)$. Dividing the two equations: $\frac{\lambda^{\prime}}{\lambda}=\frac{5 R / 36}{3 R / 4}=\frac{5}{36} \times \frac{4}{3}=\frac{5}{27}$. So, $\lambda^{\prime}=\frac{5}{27} \lambda$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
q: The inization energy for a hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV . What is the ionization energy for a doubly ionized Lithium atom $\left(\mathrm{Li}^{++}\right)$?
s: The energy levels for a hydrogen-like atom are given by $E_{n}=-13.6 \frac{Z^{2}}{n^{2}} \mathrm{eV}$. The ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from the ground state ( $\mathrm{n}=1$ ) to infinity, which is $\left|E_{1}\right|$. For $\mathrm{Li}^{++}$, the atomic number $Z=3$. Ionization Energy $=13.6 \times Z^{2}=13.6 \times 3^{2}= 13.6 \times 9=122.4 \mathrm{eV}$.

subject: Physics
q: A gas containing hydrogen atoms is excited from its ground state to the $\mathrm{n}=4$ state. The maximum number of distinct spectral lines that can be emitted during de-excitation is:
s: The number of possible spectral lines emitted when an electron de-excites from the nth level is given by the formula $N=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. For $\mathrm{n}=4, N=\frac{4(4-1)}{2}=\frac{4 \times 3}{2}=6$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
q: The minimum energy required to excite a hydrogen atom from its ground state is:
s: The minimum excitation corresponds to the transition from the ground state $(\mathrm{n}=1)$ to the first excited state $(\mathrm{n}=2) . E_{1}=-13.6 \mathrm{eV}, E_{2}=-13.6 / 2^{2}=-3.4 \mathrm{eV}$. The required energy is $\Delta E=E_{2}-E_{1}=-3.4-(-13.6)=10.2 \mathrm{eV}$.

subject: Physics
q: The Paschen series of the hydrogen spectrum is formed by electron transitions from higher energy levels to the level with quantum number $n$ equal to:
s: The spectral series in hydrogen are named after the final energy level ( $n_{1}$ ) of the transition. Lyman series has $n_{1}=1$, Balmer series has $n_{1}=2$, and Paschen series has $n_{1}=3$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Energy, radius and speed of electron in hydrogen like elements
q: The energy of an electron in the ground state of a hydrogen atom is -13.6 eV . The kinetic energy of this electron is:
s: For an electron in a Bohr orbit, the total energy $E_{T}$ is the sum of kinetic energy (KE) and potential energy (PE). The relationship is $K E=-E_{T}$ and $P E=2 E_{T}$. Given $E_{T}=-13.6$ eV , the kinetic energy is $K E=-(-13.6 \mathrm{eV})=13.6 \mathrm{eV}$.

subject: Physics
q: If the wavelength of the first member of Lyman series of hydrogen is $\lambda$, the wavelength of the second member will be:
s: First member of Lyman $(\mathrm{n}=2$ to 1$): \frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{2^{2}}\right)=\frac{3 R}{4}$. Second member of Lyman $(\mathrm{n}=3$ to 1$): \frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}=R\left(\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{3^{2}}\right)=\frac{8 R}{9}$. Dividing the equations: $\frac{\lambda^{\prime}}{\lambda}=\frac{3 R / 4}{8 R / 9}=\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{9}{8}=\frac{27}{32}$. So, $\lambda^{\prime}=\frac{27}{32} \lambda$.

subject: Physics
q: According to Bohr's model, the radius of the nth orbit is proportional to:
s: The radius of the nth Bohr orbit for a hydrogen atom is given by the formula $r_{n}=a_{0} n^{2}$, where $a_{0}$ is the Bohr radius. Thus, the radius is directly proportional to the square of the principal quantum number, $n$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Energy, radius and speed of electron in hydrogen like elements
q: The potential energy of an electron in the $\mathrm{n}=2$ state of a hydrogen atom is:
s:
The total energy in the $\mathrm{n}=2$ state is $E_{2}=-13.6 / 2^{2}=-3.4 \mathrm{eV}$. The potential energy (PE) is twice the total energy, $P E=2 E_{T}$. 
Therefore, $P E=2 \times(-3.4 \mathrm{eV})=-6.8 \mathrm{eV}$.

subject: Physics
q: The Franck-Hertz experiment for a certain gas shows a first excitation potential of 4.9 V . The wavelength of the first line of the emission spectrum will be: (Use hc $=1240 \mathrm{eV}$-nm)
s:
The first excitation potential corresponds to the energy required to lift an electron from the ground state to the first excited state. 
This energy is $\Delta E=4.9 \mathrm{eV}$. 
The emitted photon will have this energy. 
$\lambda=\frac{h c}{E}=\frac{1240 \mathrm{eV}-\mathrm{nm}}{4.9 \mathrm{eV}} \approx 253 \mathrm{~nm}$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Energy, radius and speed of electron in hydrogen like elements
q: The minimum energy required by a hydrogen atom in the ground state to emit radiation in the Paschen series is:
s:
To emit radiation in the Paschen series, the electron must transition to the $\mathrm{n}=3$ level. 
The minimum energy transition in the Paschen series is from $\mathrm{n}=4$ to $\mathrm{n}=3$. 
For this to be possible, the atom must first be excited from the ground state ( $\mathrm{n}=1$ ) to at least the $\mathrm{n}=4$ level. 
The energy required for this excitation is $\Delta E=E_{4}-E_{1}=\left(-\frac{13.6}{4^{2}}\right)-\left(-\frac{13.6}{1^{2}}\right)=-0.85-(-13.6)=12.75 \mathrm{eV}$.

subject: Physics
q: The ratio of the speeds of an electron in the ground state of a hydrogen atom to the speed of light in vacuum is approximately:
s: The speed of an electron in the nth orbit is $v_{n}=\frac{c}{137} \frac{Z}{n}$. For the ground state $(\mathrm{n}=1)$ of hydrogen $(\mathrm{Z}=1), v_{1}=\frac{c}{137}$. The ratio $v_{1} / c$ is $1 / 137$. This is known as the fine-structure constant.

subject: Physics
q: What is the wavelength of the series limit of the Brackett series for hydrogen? ( $R=1.097 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{m}^{-1}$ )
s: The Brackett series has $n_{1}=4$. The series limit corresponds to the transition from $n_{2}=\infty . \frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{4^{2}}-\frac{1}{\infty^{2}}\right)=\frac{R}{16} . \lambda=\frac{16}{R}=\frac{16}{1.097 \times 10^{7}} \approx 14.58 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$, or $1.458 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}$.

subject: Physics
q: If an electron in a hydrogen atom jumps from the $\mathrm{n}=3$ orbit to the $\mathrm{n}=2$ orbit, it emits a photon of wavelength $\lambda_{0}$. If the electron jumps from $\mathrm{n}=4$ to $\mathrm{n}=2$, the wavelength of the emitted photon will be:
s: For $\mathrm{n}=3$ to $2: \frac{1}{\lambda_{0}}=R\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right)=\frac{5 R}{36}$. For $\mathrm{n}=4$ to $2: \frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}=R\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}\right)=\frac{3 R}{16}$. Dividing the equations: $\frac{\lambda^{\prime}}{\lambda_{0}}=\frac{5 R / 36}{3 R / 16}=\frac{5}{36} \times \frac{16}{3}=\frac{5 \times 4}{9 \times 3}=\frac{20}{27}$. So, $\lambda^{\prime}=\frac{20}{27} \lambda_{0}$.

subject: Physics
q: The angular momentum of an electron in the $\mathrm{n}=3$ orbit of a hydrogen atom is: $\left(h=6.63 \times 10^{-34}\right.$ J-s)
s: According to Bohr's second postulate, the angular momentum is quantized: $L=\frac{n h}{2 \pi}$. For $\mathrm{n}=3, L=\frac{3 \times\left(6.63 \times 10^{-34}\right)}{2 \times 3.14159} \approx \frac{19.89 \times 10^{-34}}{6.283} \approx 3.165 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~J}-\mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics
q: If Rydberg's constant is R , the longest wavelength of radiation in the Paschen series will be $\frac{\alpha}{7 R}$. The value of $\alpha$ is___________. $\qquad$
s: The Paschen series corresponds to transitions ending at $n_{1}=3$. The longest wavelength is for the transition from $n_{2}=4 . \quad \frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{3^{2}}-\frac{1}{4^{2}}\right)=R\left(\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{16}\right)=R\left(\frac{16-9}{144}\right)=\frac{7 R}{144} . \quad \lambda=\frac{144}{7 R}$. Comparing this with $\frac{\alpha}{7 R}$, we get $\alpha=144$.

subject: Physics
q: A hydrogen atom in the ground state absorbs a 12.09 eV photon. The quantum number of the final state is__________. $\qquad$
s: The energy of the ground state is $E_{1}=-13.6 \mathrm{eV}$. After absorbing a 12.09 eV photon, the energy of the final state becomes $E_{n}=-13.6+12.09=-1.51 \mathrm{eV}$. We know that $E_{n}=-13.6 / n^{2}$. $-1.51=-13.6 / n^{2} \Longrightarrow n^{2}=\frac{-13.6}{-1.51} \approx 9$. So, $n=3$.

q: The shortest wavelength in the Lyman series of the hydrogen spectrum is \[912\mathop {\text{A}}\limits^ \circ \]. The longest wavelength (rounded to nearest integer) in the Balmer series of a $\mathrm{He}^{+}$ion is_________. $\left( {{\text{in}}\,\,\,\,\,\mathop {\text{A}}\limits^ \circ } \right)$.
s:

subject: Physics
q: In a hydrogen atom, the energy of the photon emitted in a transition from $\mathrm{n}=4$ to $\mathrm{n}=2$ is E . The energy of the photon emitted in a transition from $\mathrm{n}=2$ to $\mathrm{n}=1$ is $x \times E$. The value of $x$ is_________. $\qquad$
s: Energy for $\mathrm{n}=4$ to 2 : $E=K\left(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{4^{2}}\right)=K\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}\right)=K\left(\frac{3}{16}\right)$. Energy for $\mathrm{n}=2$ to 1 : $E^{\prime}=K\left(\frac{1}{1^{2}}-\frac{1}{2^{2}}\right)=K\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)$. The ratio is $\frac{E^{\prime}}{E}=\frac{3 K / 4}{3 K / 16}=\frac{16}{4}=4$. So, $x=4$.

subject: Physics
q: A hydrogen atom, initially in the ground state, is excited by absorbing a photon of wavelength 97.2 nm . The principal quantum number of the excited state is___________. (Use $h c=1240 \mathrm{eV}$-nm).
s: Energy of the absorbed photon: $E=\frac{h c}{\lambda}=\frac{1240 \mathrm{eV}-\mathrm{nm}}{97.2 \mathrm{~nm}} \approx 12.75 \mathrm{eV}$. The initial energy of the atom in the ground state is $E_{1}=-13.6 \mathrm{eV}$. The energy of the final state is $E_{n}=E_{1}+E= -13.6+12.75=-0.85 \mathrm{eV}$. Using the energy level formula $E_{n}=-13.6 / n^{2}:-0.85=-13.6 / n^{2} \Longrightarrow n^{2}=\frac{13.6}{0.85}=16$. Thus, the principal quantum number of the excited state is $n=4$.

subject: Physics
q: In the nuclear reaction ${ }_{7}^{14} \mathrm{~N}+{ }_{0}^{1} \mathrm{n} \rightarrow{ }_{6}^{14} \mathrm{C}+X$, the particle X is a:
s: To conserve mass number (A) and atomic number (Z): Mass number: $14+1=14+A \Rightarrow A=1$. Atomic number: $7+0=6+Z \Rightarrow Z=1$. The particle with $A=1$ and $Z=1$ is a proton $\left({ }_{1}^{1} \mathrm{p}\right)$.

subject: Physics
q: An LED is constructed from a semiconductor material with a band gap of 1.9 eV . The wavelength of light emitted from this LED is approximately ________ nm. (Use $\left.h=6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}, c=3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}, e=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}\right)$ (Mention answer with 2 significant digits)
s: The energy of the emitted photon is equal to the band gap energy, $E_{g}=\frac{h c}{\lambda} . \quad \lambda=\frac{h c}{E_{g}}=\frac{\left(6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}\right)\left(3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right)}{(1.9 \mathrm{eV})\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{eV}\right)}=\frac{19.8 \times 10^{-26}}{3.04 \times 10^{-19}} \mathrm{~m} . \quad \lambda \approx 6.513 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m} =651.3 \mathrm{~nm}$ Rounding to 2 significant digits gives 650 nm .

q: A particle executes simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of 5 cm and a time period of 2 s . What is its speed when it is at a displacement of 3 cm from the mean position?
s: $\omega=\frac{2 \pi}{T}=\frac{2 \pi}{2}=\pi \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} . v=\omega \sqrt{A^{2}-x^{2}}=\pi \sqrt{5^{2}-3^{2}}=\pi \sqrt{16}=4 \pi \mathrm{cm} / \mathrm{s}$.

subject: Physics

q: In simple harmonic motion, the phase difference between acceleration and displacement is:
s:
If displacement is $x=A \sin (\omega t)$, then acceleration is $a=-\omega^{2} A \sin (\omega t)= \omega^{2} A \sin (\omega t+\pi)$. 
The phase difference is $\pi$. 
They are in opposite directions.

subject: Physics
q: The time period of a simple pendulum is T. If its length is increased by $21 \%$, the new time period will be:
s:
$T=2 \pi \sqrt{L / g}$, so $T \propto \sqrt{L}$. 
New length $L^{\prime}=L+0.21 L=1.21 L$. 
New time period $T^{\prime} \propto \sqrt{L^{\prime}}=\sqrt{1.21 L}=1.1 \sqrt{L}$. 
So, $T^{\prime}=1.1 T$.

subject: Physics
sub_topic: Simple harmonic motion/ various parameters in SHM
q: A particle in SHM has a maximum speed of $20 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$ and a maximum acceleration of $40 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}^{2}$. The time period of the motion is:
s:
$v_{\max }=A \omega=20$. $a_{\max }=A \omega^{2}=40$. 
Dividing the two equations: $\frac{A \omega^{2}}{A \omega}=\frac{40}{20} \Longrightarrow \omega=2 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. 
Time period $T=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega}=\frac{2 \pi}{2}=\pi \mathrm{s}$.

q: A particle executing SHM has an amplitude of 6 m . At a distance of 3 m from the mean position, the magnitude of its velocity is equal to the magnitude of its acceleration. The time period of the motion is $\frac{2 \pi}{\sqrt{x}} \mathrm{~s}$. Find the value of x .
s:
Given $|v|=|a|$ at $x=3 \mathrm{~m} . v=\omega \sqrt{A^{2}-x^{2}}$ and $a=\omega^{2} x . \omega \sqrt{6^{2}-3^{2}}= \omega^{2}(3)$. $\sqrt{36-9}=3 \omega \Longrightarrow \sqrt{27}=3 \omega \Longrightarrow 3 \sqrt{3}=3 \omega \Longrightarrow \omega=\sqrt{3} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. 
Time period $T=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega}=\frac{2 \pi}{\sqrt{3}}$. Comparing with $\frac{2 \pi}{\sqrt{x}}$, we get $\mathrm{x}=3$.

q:

The block slips when the static friction force reaches its maximum value

$${f_{s\,\max }} = {\mu _s}n = {\mu _s}mg.$$ The occurs when the train has moved

$$\Delta x = \frac{{{f_{s\max }}}}{k} = \frac{{{\mu _s}mg}}{k} = \frac{{\left( {0.60} \right)\left( {2.0kg} \right)\left( {10\,m/{s^2}} \right)}}{{50\,N/m}} = 24\,cm$$

The time at which the block slips is
$$t = \frac{{\Delta x}}{v} = \frac{{24cm}}{{6cm/s}} = 4s$$

subject: Physics
q: The radii of curvature of a biconvex lens are 10 cm and 15 cm . If the refractive index of the material is 1.5 , its focal length is:
s:
Using the Lens Maker's formula: $\frac{1}{f}=(n-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_{1}}-\frac{1}{R_{2}}\right)$. Here, $R_{1}=+10 \mathrm{~cm}, R_{2}=-15 \mathrm{cm}, n=1.5$.
$$
\frac{1}{f}=(1.5-1)\left(\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{-15}\right)=(0.5)\left(\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{15}\right)=0.5 \times \frac{25}{150}=\frac{1}{12}
$$
So, $f=12 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: A real, inverted image three times the size of the object is formed by a convex lens. If the distance of the image from the lens is 30 cm , the focal length of the lens is:
s: Magnification $m=-3$ (real and inverted). Image distance $v=+30 \mathrm{~cm} . m=\frac{v}{u} \Rightarrow -3=\frac{30}{u} \Rightarrow u=-10 \mathrm{~cm}$. Using the lens formula: $\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{30}-\frac{1}{-10}=\frac{1+3}{30}=\frac{4}{30}=\frac{2}{15}$. So, $f=\frac{15}{2}=7.5 \mathrm{~cm}$.

q:

The lens maker's formula is $\frac{1}{f}=(\mu-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_{1}}-\frac{1}{R_{2}}\right)$. Given: $\mu=1.5, R_{1}=+20 \mathrm{~cm}$, $R_{2}=-20 \mathrm{~cm}$.
$$
\frac{1}{f}=(1.5-1)\left(\frac{1}{+20}-\frac{1}{-20}\right)=(0.5)\left(\frac{2}{20}\right)=\frac{1}{20}
$$
Thus, $f=20 \mathrm{~cm}$. An incident ray parallel to the principal axis converges at the principal focus.

q: The focal length of a lens is related to its power P . If the power of a lens changes from 4 D to 4.2 D, the relative decrease in its focal length is:
s: $f=1 / P$. Using calculus for small changes: $\left|\frac{\Delta f}{f}\right| \approx\left|\frac{\Delta P}{P}\right|$. The question asks for the relative decrease in focal length which would be compared to the initial focal length, corresponding to the initial power. So the relative change is $\frac{4.2-4}{4}=\frac{0.2}{4}=0.05$.

q: In an experiment to determine the focal length of a concave mirror, the object distance ( $x$ ) and image distance $(y)$ are measured from the focal point. The $y-x$ plot is a hyperbola. If a point on the graph corresponds to $x=10 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $y=40 \mathrm{~cm}$, what is the focal length of the concave mirror?
s: When distances are measured from the focal point (Newton's formula), the relation is $x y=f^{2}$. Given $x=10 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $y=40 \mathrm{~cm}$, we have $f^{2}=10 \times 40=400$. So, $f=20 \mathrm{~cm}$.

q: A plano-convex lens ( $n=1.5$ ) has a focal length of 10 cm . Its curved surface has a radius of curvature of:
s:
For a plano-convex lens, $R_{1}=R$ and $R_{2}=\infty \cdot \frac{1}{f}=(n-1)\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{\infty}\right)=\frac{n-1}{R}$.
$$
\frac{1}{10}=\frac{1.5-1}{R}=\frac{0.5}{R} \Rightarrow R=0.5 \times 10=5 \mathrm{~cm}
$$

subject: Physics
q: A lens combination consists of a convex lens of power +5 D and a concave lens of power -3 D . The focal length of the combination is:
s: The power of the combination is $P_{e q}=P_{1}+P_{2}=5+(-3)=+2 \mathrm{D}$. The focal length is $f_{e q}=\frac{1}{P_{e q}}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5 \mathrm{~m}=50 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: An equiconvex lens has a power of 5 D . When it is cut into two identical plano-convex lenses, the power of each part is:
s: For an equiconvex lens, $P=(n-1)\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{-R}\right)=(n-1) \frac{2}{R}$. For each plano-convex part, $P^{\prime}=(n-1)\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{\infty}\right)=(n-1) \frac{1}{R}$. Clearly, $P^{\prime}=P / 2=5 / 2=2.5$ D.

subject: Physics
q: A parallel beam of light is incident on a convex lens. The beam emerges from the lens and converges at a point 15 cm from the lens. If a concave lens of focal length 30 cm is placed in contact with the convex lens, the beam will now converge at a distance of:
s: The focal length of the convex lens is $f_{1}=+15 \mathrm{~cm}$. The focal length of the concave lens is $f_{2}=-30 \mathrm{~cm}$. The equivalent focal length is $\frac{1}{f_{e q}}=\frac{1}{f_{1}}+\frac{1}{f_{2}}=\frac{1}{15}+\frac{1}{-30}=\frac{2-1}{30}=\frac{1}{30}$. So, $f_{e q}=30 \mathrm{~cm}$. A parallel beam will converge at the focal point.

subject: Physics
q: In an experiment to find the focal length of a convex lens, a graph is plotted between $u$ and $v$. The graph is a:
s: The lens formula is $\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f}$. With sign conventions for a real image ( $u$ is negative, v is positive), we get $\frac{1}{v}+\frac{1}{|u|}=\frac{1}{f}$. The graph of v vs u is a rectangular hyperbola.

subject: Physics
q: A liquid of refractive index 1.4 is poured over a convex lens of refractive index 1.5. If the liquid forms a plano-concave lens in contact with the convex lens, the combination will behave as a:
s:
Let the convex lens have radii $R$ and $\infty . P_{1}=(1.5-1)\left(\frac{1}{R}\right)=0.5 / R$. 
The liquid lens is plano-concave with radii $-R$ and $\infty . P_{2}=(1.4-1)\left(\frac{1}{-R}\right)=-0.4 / R$.
The equivalent power is $P_{e q}=P_{1}+P_{2}=\frac{0.5}{R}-\frac{0.4}{R}=\frac{0.1}{R}$. 
Since R is positive, $P_{e q}$ is positive, and the combination acts as a converging lens.

subject: Physics
q: To get a real image with magnification 2 using a convex lens of focal length 20 cm , the object should be placed at a distance of:
s: For a real image, $m=-2 . f=+20 \mathrm{~cm}$. Using $m=\frac{f}{f+u} \Rightarrow-2=\frac{20}{20+u}$. This gives $-40-2 u=20 \Rightarrow-2 u=60 \Rightarrow u=-30 \mathrm{~cm}$. The object distance is 30 cm .

subject: Physics
q: A biconvex lens made of glass with a refractive index of 1.6 has equal radii of curvature of 20 cm . The focal length of this lens is________(in cm). (rounded to nearest integer)
s:
Using the Lens Maker's formula: $\frac{1}{f}=(n-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_{1}}-\frac{1}{R_{2}}\right)$. For a biconvex lens, $R_{1}=+20$ cm and $R_{2}=-20 \mathrm{~cm}$.
$$
\frac{1}{f}=(1.6-1)\left(\frac{1}{20}-\frac{1}{-20}\right)=(0.6)\left(\frac{2}{20}\right)=0.06
$$
$f=\frac{1}{0.06}=\frac{100}{6} \approx 16.67 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: The distance between an object and its three times magnified real image formed by a convex lens is 80 cm . The focal length of the lens is___________(in cm).
s:
For a real image, $m=-3$ so $v=-3 u$. The distance between object and image is $D=|v-u|$. Let $u=-x$, then $v=+3 x . D=3 x-(-x)=4 x=80 \mathrm{~cm}$, which gives $x=20 \mathrm{~cm}$. So, $u=-20 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $v=+60 \mathrm{~cm}$.
$$
\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{60}-\frac{1}{-20}=\frac{1+3}{60}=\frac{4}{60}=\frac{1}{15}
$$
Focal length $f=15 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: A convex lens of focal length 40 cm and a concave lens of focal length 25 cm are kept in contact. An object is placed at a distance of 100 cm from the combination. The magnitude of the image distance from the lens combination is____________(in cm).
s:
Equivalent focal length: $\frac{1}{f_{e q}}=\frac{1}{40}+\frac{1}{-25}=\frac{5-8}{200}=-\frac{3}{200}$. So $f_{e q}=-200 / 3 \mathrm{~cm}$. Object distance $u=-100 \mathrm{~cm}$.
$$
\frac{1}{v}=\frac{1}{f_{e q}}+\frac{1}{u}=-\frac{3}{200}+\frac{1}{-100}=\frac{-3-2}{200}=-\frac{5}{200}=-\frac{1}{40}
$$
$v=-40 \mathrm{~cm}$. The magnitude of the distance is 40 cm .

subject: Physics
q: A plano-convex lens ( $n=1.5$ ) fits exactly into a plano-concave lens ( $n=1.6$ ). The radius of curvature of the curved surface is 30 cm . The magnitude of focal length of the combination is____________(in cm).
s:
For the plano-convex lens: $R_{1}=30 \mathrm{~cm}, R_{2}=\infty \cdot \frac{1}{f_{1}}=(1.5-1)\left(\frac{1}{30}\right)=\frac{0.5}{30}=\frac{1}{60}$. For the plano-concave lens: $R_{1}=-30 \mathrm{~cm}, R_{2}=\infty . \frac{1}{f_{2}}=(1.6-1)\left(\frac{1}{-30}\right)=\frac{0.6}{-30}=-\frac{1}{50}$. For the combination:
$$
\frac{1}{f_{e q}}=\frac{1}{f_{1}}+\frac{1}{f_{2}}=\frac{1}{60}-\frac{1}{50}=\frac{5-6}{300}=-\frac{1}{300}
$$
$f_{e q}=-300 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: The focal length of an equiconvex glass lens ( $n=1.5$ ) is 20 cm . If it is cut perpendicular to the principal axis into two equal halves, the focal length of each half is_________(in cm).
s:
For the original lens: $\frac{1}{20}=(1.5-1)\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{-R}\right)=(0.5)\left(\frac{2}{R}\right)=\frac{1}{R}$. So, $R=20 \mathrm{~cm}$. When cut, each half becomes a plano-convex lens with $R_{1}=20 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $R_{2}=\infty$. The focal length of each half is:
$$
\frac{1}{f^{\prime}}=(1.5-1)\left(\frac{1}{20}-\frac{1}{\infty}\right)=\frac{0.5}{20}=\frac{1}{40}
$$
So, $f^{\prime}=40 \mathrm{~cm}$.

q:
According to Descarte’s theory of the formation of the rainbow, a ray of sunlight is refracted as it enters a spherical raindrop, undergoes a single internal reflection, and is than refracted as it leaves the drop as shown in figure. The rainbow is formed from the rays whose deviation from original direction is either maximum or minimum. Taking refractive index of water as $\frac{4}{3}$, the value of $$\sin \theta = \frac{2}{n}\sqrt {\frac{5}{3}} $$. Find value of n? ($$\theta $$ = angle of incidence for rays contributing in Rainbow formation)
 [IMAGE: images/MB002975_1.webp]
s:
Given that the rainbow is formed from the rays whose deviation from original direction is either maximum or minimum and refractive index of water is, \[n = \frac{4}{3}\].Consider a ray is incident at an angle of incidence \[ = \theta \]. Light ray undergoing total internal reflection is shown in the following diagram
 [IMAGE NOT CAPTURED] 

From diagram we can say, the total deviation product is, \[\delta = \left( {\theta - \phi } \right) + \left( {\pi - 2\phi } \right) + \left( {\theta - \phi } \right)\]\[ \Rightarrow \delta = 2\theta - 4\phi + \pi \]For maximum or minimum deviation, \[\frac{{d\delta }}{{d\theta }} = 0\]\[ \Rightarrow 0 = \frac{{d\left( {2\theta - 4\phi + \pi } \right)}}{{d\theta }}\]\[ \Rightarrow 0 = 2 - \frac{{4d\phi }}{{d\theta }}\]\[ \Rightarrow \frac{{d\phi }}{{d\theta }} = \frac{1}{2}\,\,\,....\left( 1 \right)\]Also, using Snell's law \[n\sin \phi = \sin \theta \]\[\sin \phi = \frac{{3\sin \theta }}{4}\,\,....\left( 2 \right)\]Differentiating on both the sides w.r.t \[\theta \], we get: \[\cos \phi \frac{{d\phi }}{{d\theta }} = \frac{{\cos \theta }}{n}\]\[ \Rightarrow \cos \phi \frac{1}{2} = \frac{{\cos \theta }}{n}\]\[ \Rightarrow \cos \phi = \frac{{3\cos \theta }}{2}\,\,.....\left( 3 \right)\]From equations, \[1 = \frac{{9{{\sin }^2}\theta }}{{16}} + \frac{{9{{\cos }^2}\theta }}{4}\]\[ \Rightarrow 1 = \frac{{9{{\sin }^2}\theta + 36{{\cos }^2}\theta }}{{16}}\]\[ \Rightarrow 16 = 9 + 27{\cos ^2}\theta \]\[ \Rightarrow 20 = 27{\sin ^2}\theta \]\[ \Rightarrow \sin \theta = \sqrt {\frac{{20}}{{27}}} = \frac{2}{3}\sqrt {\frac{5}{3}} \]So, \[n = 0.66\,{\text{to}}\,0.67\]

q: An electron and a proton have the same de Broglie wavelength. Which of the following is true about their kinetic energies?
o: The kinetic energy of the electron is greater than the kinetic energy of the proton.
The kinetic energy of the proton is greater than the kinetic energy of the electron.
s:
Kinetic energy $K=p^{2} /(2 m)$. Since de
Broglie wavelength $\lambda=h / p$ is the same, their momenta p are the same.
Thus, $K \propto 1 / m$. As the proton mass is much greater than the electron
mass ( $m_{p}>m_{e}$ ), it follows that $K_{p}<K_{e}$.

q: The radiation pressure exerted by an electromagnetic wave of intensity I on a perfectly absorbing surface is $P_{\text {rad }}$. If the same wave is incident on a perfectly reflecting surface, the radiation pressure will be:
s: For a perfectly absorbing surface, radiation pressure is $I / c$. For a perfectly reflecting surface, the change in momentum is doubled, so the pressure is $2 I / c$. Therefore, the pressure is doubled.

q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle with mass m and kinetic energy K is $\lambda$. What will be the de Broglie wavelength of a particle with mass 2 m and kinetic energy $K / 2$ ?
s: The de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda=h / \sqrt{2 m K}$. The new wavelength is $\lambda^{\prime}=h / \sqrt{2(2 m)(K / 2)}= h / \sqrt{2 m K}=\lambda$.

q: The total energy transferred to a perfectly absorbing surface is E. For complete reflection, the magnitude of the total momentum delivered to this surface is:

q: An electron enters a uniform electric field with an initial velocity perpendicular to the field. The de Broglie wavelength of the electron will:
s: The electric field will accelerate the electron, increasing its velocity component in the direction of the field. This increases its total speed v. Since $\lambda=h / m v$, as the speed v increases, the wavelength $\lambda$ decreases.

q: The correct graphical representation of the relation between the reciprocal of kinetic energy $(1 / K)$ and de Broglie wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) for a particle is:
o: A parabola symmetric about the $1 / K$ axis
s: Kinetic energy $K=h^{2} /\left(2 m \lambda^{2}\right)$. Therefore, $1 / K=\left(2 m / h^{2}\right) \lambda^{2}$. This is the equation of a parabola of the form $y=a x^{2}$, where $y=1 / K$ and $x=\lambda$.

q: An electron moving with velocity $\vec{v}=v_{0} \hat{k}$ enters a region with a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}=B_{0} \hat{k}$. Its de Broglie wavelength will:
s: The magnetic force is $\vec{F}=q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$. Since the velocity vector is parallel to the magnetic field vector, their cross product is zero. Thus, no force acts on the electron, its velocity remains constant, and so does its de Broglie wavelength $\lambda=h / m v$.

q: A 100 W omnidirectional light bulb radiates light uniformly in all directions. The radiation pressure on a small, perfectly reflecting surface placed 3 m away from the bulb is:

q: If a proton and an alpha particle are accelerated through the same potential difference, the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths ( $\lambda_{p} / \lambda_{\alpha}$ ) is:
s:
When accelerated through potential V, kinetic energy is $K=q V$. Wavelength is $\lambda=h / \sqrt{2 m K}=h / \sqrt{2 m q V}$. So, $\lambda \propto 1 / \sqrt{m q}$.
$$
\frac{\lambda_{p}}{\lambda_{\alpha}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{\alpha} q_{\alpha}}{m_{p} q_{p}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\left(4 m_{p}\right)(2 e)}{\left(m_{p}\right)(e)}}=\sqrt{8}=2 \sqrt{2}
$$
The ratio is $2 \sqrt{2}: 1$.

q: Radiation of intensity I falls normally on a surface. The surface absorbs $70 \%$ of the radiation and reflects the remaining $30 \%$. The radiation pressure on the surface is:
s:
Note: The provided answer in the source material for this question was (B) $1.7 I / c$, which contradicts its own solution. The correct calculation leads to $1.31 / c$.
 The total pressure is the sum of pressure from the absorbed and reflected parts. $P_{\text {total }}= P_{\mathrm{abs}}+P_{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{0.7 I}{c}+2 \times \frac{0.3 I}{c}=\frac{0.7 I}{c}+\frac{0.6 I}{c}=\frac{1.3 I}{c}$.

q: A photon and an electron have the same de Broglie wavelength. The speed of the electron is $v_{e}$. The ratio of the kinetic energy of the electron to the energy of the photon is:
s:
Same wavelength implies same momentum, $p_{e}=p_{p h}=p$. The kinetic energy of the electron is $K_{e}=p^{2} /\left(2 m_{e}\right)$, and the energy of the photon is $E_{p h}=p c$. The ratio is:
$$
\frac{K_{e}}{E_{p h}}=\frac{p^{2} /\left(2 m_{e}\right)}{p c}=\frac{p}{2 m_{e} c}=\frac{m_{e} v_{e}}{2 m_{e} c}=\frac{v_{e}}{2 c}
$$

q: The de Broglie wavelength of a neutron at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is $\lambda$. What will be its wavelength at $927^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ?
s:
The kinetic energy of a neutron in thermal equilibrium is $K=\frac{3}{2} k_{B} T$. Wavelength $\lambda=h / \sqrt{2 m K}=h / \sqrt{3 m k_{B} T}$. So, $\lambda \propto 1 / \sqrt{T}$. $T_{1}=27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=300 \mathrm{~K} . T_{2}=927^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=1200 \mathrm{~K}$.
$$
\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}=\sqrt{\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{300}{1200}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{1}{2}
$$
So, $\lambda_{2}=\lambda / 2$.

q: If a proton and an alpha particle have the same kinetic energy, the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths $\left(\lambda_{p} / \lambda_{\alpha}\right)$ is:
s:
$\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m K}}$. With K constant, $\lambda \propto 1 / \sqrt{m}$.
$$
\frac{\lambda_{p}}{\lambda_{\alpha}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{p}}}=\sqrt{\frac{4 m_{p}}{m_{p}}}=\sqrt{4}=2
$$
The ratio is $2: 1$.

q: An electron and a photon possess the same de Broglie wavelength of 1 nm . The ratio of energy of photon to the kinetic energy of electron is approximately:
s:
Same wavelength implies same momentum $p=h / \lambda$. Energy of photon is $E_{\mathrm{ph}}=p c$. Kinetic energy of electron is $K_{e}=p^{2} /\left(2 m_{e}\right)$.
$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{E_{\mathrm{ph}}}{K_{e}}=\frac{p c}{p^{2} /\left(2 m_{e}\right)}=\frac{2 m_{e} c}{p}=\frac{2 m_{e} c \lambda}{h} \\
\frac{E_{\mathrm{ph}}}{K_{e}}=\frac{2\left(9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}\right)\left(3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right)\left(1 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}\right)}{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~J} \cdot \mathrm{~s}} \approx 823
\end{gathered}
$$

q: An electromagnetic wave of intensity $1200 \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$ is incident normally on a non-reflecting object in a medium of refractive index 2 . The radiation pressure on the object is:
s:
The speed of light in the medium is $v=c / n$. For a completely absorbing (non-reflecting) surface, the radiation pressure is $P_{\text {rad }}=I / v=n I / c$.
$$
P_{\mathrm{rad}}=\frac{2 \times 1200}{3 \times 10^{8}}=\frac{2400}{3 \times 10^{8}}=800 \times 10^{-8}=8 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^{2}
$$

q: An alpha particle and a proton are moving with the same speed. The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the alpha particle to that of the proton is $1: \mathrm{N}$. Find the value of N .
s:
De Broglie wavelength $\lambda=h /(m v)$. If the speed v is the same, then $\lambda \propto 1 / m$.
$$
\frac{\lambda_{\alpha}}{\lambda_{p}}=\frac{m_{p}}{m_{\alpha}}=\frac{m_{p}}{4 m_{p}}=\frac{1}{4}
$$
The ratio is $1: 4$, so $\mathrm{N}=4$.

q: A proton (mass $m_{p}$ ) and an alpha particle (mass $\approx 4 m_{p}$ ) have the same de Broglie wavelength. The ratio of the kinetic energy of the proton to the kinetic energy of the alpha particle is $\mathrm{N}: 1$. Find the value of N.
s:
Kinetic energy $K=p^{2} /(2 m)$. Since the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda=h / p$ is the same, their momentum p is the same. Therefore, $K \propto 1 / m$.
$$
\frac{K_{p}}{K_{\alpha}}=\frac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{p}}=\frac{4 m_{p}}{m_{p}}=4
$$
The ratio is $4: 1$, so $N=4$.

q: A proton (mass $m_{p}$ ) and a deuteron (mass $\approx 2 m_{p}$ ) have the same de Broglie wavelength. The ratio of the kinetic energy of the proton to the kinetic energy of the deuteron is $\mathrm{N}: 1$. Find the value of N.
s:
Kinetic Energy $K=p^{2} /(2 m)$. Since the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda=h / p$ is the same, their momentum p is the same. Therefore, $K \propto 1 / m$.
$$
\frac{K_{p}}{K_{d}}=\frac{m_{d}}{m_{p}}=\frac{2 m_{p}}{m_{p}}=2
$$
The ratio is $2: 1$, so $\mathrm{N}=2$.

q: The momentum of a photon is $1.0 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~kg} \cdot \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. Its energy in eV is approximately__________. ( $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$ )
s:
Energy of a photon $E=p c$.
$$
E=\left(1.0 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~kg} \cdot \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right) \times\left(3 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right)=3.0 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{~J}
$$
To convert to eV, divide by the charge of an electron:
$$
E(\mathrm{eV})=\frac{3.0 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{~J}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}}=1.875 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{eV}=18750 \mathrm{eV}
$$

q: When a metallic surface is illuminated with radiation of wavelength $\lambda$, the stopping potential is V . If the same surface is illuminated with radiation of wavelength $2 \lambda$, the stopping potential is $\mathrm{V} / 4$. The threshold wavelength for the metallic surface is:
s: From Einstein's equation, $e V=\frac{h c}{\lambda}-\phi_{0}$ and $e(V / 4)=\frac{h c}{2 \lambda}-\phi_{0}$. Multiplying the second equation by 4 gives $e V=\frac{2 h c}{\lambda}-4 \phi_{0}$. Equating the two expressions for $\mathrm{eV}: \frac{h c}{\lambda}-\phi_{0}=\frac{2 h c}{\lambda}-4 \phi_{0} \Longrightarrow 3 \phi_{0}=\frac{h c}{\lambda}$. Since $\phi_{0}=\frac{h c}{\lambda_{0}}$, we have $3 \frac{h c}{\lambda_{0}}=\frac{h c}{\lambda} \Longrightarrow \lambda_{0}=3 \lambda$.

q: If the intensity of incident light in a photoelectric experiment is doubled, what happens to the maximum kinetic energy ( $K_{\text {max }}$ ) of emitted electrons and the photoelectric current (i)?

q: The stopping potential for photoelectrons from a metal is $V_{1}$ when light of wavelength $\lambda_{1}$ is used and $V_{2}$ for wavelength $\lambda_{2}$. The ratio $h / e$ can be calculated from:
s: We have $e V_{1}=\frac{h c}{\lambda_{1}}-\phi_{0}$ and $e V_{2}=\frac{h c}{\lambda_{2}}-\phi_{0}$. Subtracting the second from the first: $e\left(V_{1}-V_{2}\right)=h c\left(\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{2}}\right)$. Rearranging gives $\frac{h}{e}=\frac{V_{1}-V_{2}}{c\left(1 / \lambda_{1}-1 / \lambda_{2}\right)}$.

q: Light of wavelength 200 nm is incident on a metal surface. The stopping potential required to stop the fastest photoelectrons is 4.2 V . The work function of the metal is _______(in eV). (Use hc $=1240 \mathrm{eV} \cdot \mathrm{nm}$ )
s: Energy of the incident photon is $E=\frac{h c}{\lambda}=\frac{1240 \mathrm{eV} \cdot \mathrm{nm}}{200 \mathrm{~nm}}=6.2 \mathrm{eV}$. The maximum kinetic energy is $K_{\max }=e V_{s}=e(4.2 \mathrm{~V})=4.2 \mathrm{eV}$. The work function is $\phi_{0}=E-K_{\text {max }}=6.2 \mathrm{eV}-4.2 \mathrm{eV}=2.0 \mathrm{eV}$.

q: The slope of the stopping potential ( $V_{s}$ ) versus frequency ( $\nu$ ) graph for a certain metal is found to be $4.125 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{~V} \cdot \mathrm{~s}$. The value of Planck's constant calculated from this data is $Z \times 10^{-35} \mathrm{~J} \cdot \mathrm{~s}$. The value of $Z$ is________.(Use $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C).
s: The slope of the $V_{s}$ vs $\nu$ graph is equal to $h / e$. Slope $=h / e=4.125 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{~V} \cdot \mathrm{~s} . h=$ Slope $\times e=\left(4.125 \times 10^{-15}\right) \times\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right)=6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~J} \cdot \mathrm{~s}$. We are given $h=Z \times 10^{-35} \mathrm{~J} \cdot$ s. $6.6 \times 10^{-34}=Z \times 10^{-35} \Longrightarrow Z=6.6 \times \frac{10^{-34}}{10^{-35}}=66$.

q:
Assertion (A): The Bohr model of the atom cannot be applied to the helium atom.
Reason (R): The Bohr model does not account for electron-electron interactions.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
s: The Bohr model is only applicable to single-electron species (like $\mathrm{H}, \mathrm{He}^{+}, \mathrm{Li}^{++}$) because it only considers the electrostatic attraction between one nucleus and one electron, ignoring the repulsive forces between multiple electrons. The helium atom has two electrons.

q: The ratio of the radii of the first Bohr orbit of a hydrogen atom (H), a singly ionized helium ion ( $\mathrm{He}^{+}$) and a doubly ionized lithium ion ( $\mathrm{Li}^{++}$) is:
s: The radius of the n-th orbit is $r_{n}=a_{0} \frac{n^{2}}{Z}$. For the first orbit, $n=1$, so $r_{1} \propto \frac{1}{Z}$. For H , $Z=1$; for $H e^{+}, Z=2$; for $L i^{++}, Z=3$. The ratio is $r_{H}: r_{H e^{+}}: r_{L i^{++}}=\frac{1}{1}: \frac{1}{2}: \frac{1}{3}$. To get integer ratios, we multiply by the LCM of 6, giving 6:3:2.

q: In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, if E is the total energy and K is the kinetic energy of the electron, then:
s: In any Bohr orbit, the kinetic energy (K) is equal in magnitude but opposite in sign to the total energy (E). The potential energy (U) is twice the total energy ( $U=2 E$ ). Therefore, $K=-E$.

q: Energy required for the electron excitation in $L i^{2+}$ from the first to the third Bohr orbit is:
s:
The energy of the $n^{\text {th }}$ orbit is $E_{n}=-\frac{13.6 Z^{2}}{n^{2}} \mathrm{eV}$. For $L i^{2+}, Z=3$.
$$
E_{1}=-\frac{13.6 \times(3)^{2}}{(1)^{2}}=-122.4 \mathrm{eV}
$$
$$
E_{3}=-\frac{13.6 \times(3)^{2}}{(3)^{2}}=-13.6 \mathrm{eV}
$$
The required energy is $\Delta E=E_{3}-E_{1}=(-13.6)-(-122.4)=108.8 \mathrm{eV}$.

q: The number of possible spectral lines emitted when an electron in a sample of hydrogen atoms de-excites from the energy level $n=5$ is:
s: The number of possible spectral lines emitted when an electron de-excites from the n -th state is given by $N=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. For $n=5, N=\frac{5(5-1)}{2}=\frac{5 \times 4}{2}=10$.

q: What is the ratio of the speed of an electron in the ground state of a hydrogen atom $(Z=1)$ to that in the second excited state of a $\mathrm{Li}^{++}$ion $(Z=3)$ ?
s: The speed of an electron in the n-th orbit is proportional to $Z / n$. For the ground state of hydrogen, $n=1, Z=1$, so $v_{H} \propto 1 / 1=1$. For the second excited state of $L i^{++}, n=3, Z=3$, so $v_{L i++} \propto 3 / 3=1$. The ratio is $1: 1$.

q: If the radius of the first Bohr orbit of a hydrogen atom is $a_{0}$, the de Broglie wavelength of an electron in the third orbit is:
s: According to Bohr's quantization condition, $2 \pi r_{n}=n \lambda_{n}$. The radius of the n-th orbit is $r_{n}=n^{2} a_{0}$. For the third orbit ( $n=3$ ), $r_{3}=3^{2} a_{0}=9 a_{0}$. So, $2 \pi\left(9 a_{0}\right)=3 \lambda_{3} \Rightarrow 18 \pi a_{0}=3 \lambda_{3} \Rightarrow \lambda_{3}=6 \pi a_{0}$.

q: The total energy of an electron in the first excited state of a hydrogen atom is -3.4 eV . The potential energy of the electron in this state is:
s: For any Bohr orbit, the potential energy (U) is twice the total energy (E), so $U=2 E$. Given $E=-3.4 \mathrm{eV}, U=2 \times(-3.4 \mathrm{eV})=-6.8 \mathrm{eV}$.

q: The frequency of revolution of an electron in the $n^{\text {th }}$ Bohr orbit of a hydrogen atom is proportional to:
s: Frequency $f=\frac{v}{2 \pi r}$. We know $v \propto \frac{1}{n}$ and $r \propto n^{2}$ for a hydrogen atom. So, $f \propto \frac{1 / n}{n^{2}} \propto \frac{1}{n^{3}}$.

q: If the ionization potential for a hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV , the energy required to excite the electron from the ground state to the second excited state is:
s: The ground state energy is $E_{1}=-13.6 \mathrm{eV}$. The second excited state is $n=3$. The energy of this state is $E_{3}=\frac{-13.6}{3^{2}} \approx-1.51 \mathrm{eV}$. The required energy is $\Delta E=E_{3}-E_{1}=-1.51- (-13.6)=12.09 \mathrm{eV}$.

q: The magnetic dipole moment of an electron revolving in the $n^{\text {th }}$ Bohr orbit is proportional to:
s: Magnetic moment $\mu=I \cdot A=\left(\frac{e}{T}\right)\left(\pi r^{2}\right)$. With $T=\frac{2 \pi r}{v}$, we get $\mu=\frac{e v r}{2}$. From Bohr's quantization, angular momentum is $L=m v r=\frac{n h}{2 \pi}$. So $v r=\frac{n h}{2 \pi m}$. Substituting this gives $\mu=\frac{e}{2}\left(\frac{n h}{2 \pi m}\right)=n\left(\frac{e h}{4 \pi m}\right)$. Thus, $\mu \propto n$.

q: In the Bohr model, as the principal quantum number n increases, the magnitude of the electron's energy:
s: The energy is $E_{n}=-\frac{13.6 Z^{2}}{n^{2}} \mathrm{eV}$. As n increases, $E_{n}$ becomes less negative (energy increases). However, the question asks for the magnitude, $\left|E_{n}\right|=\frac{13.6 Z^{2}}{n^{2}}$. As n increases, the magnitude $\left|E_{n}\right|$ decreases.

q: The angular momentum of an electron in a Bohr orbit is L. Its kinetic energy is proportional to:
s: $L=m v r=\frac{n h}{2 \pi}$, so $n \propto L$. The kinetic energy is $K=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$. For hydrogen-like atoms, $v \propto Z / n$. So $K \propto(Z / n)^{2}=Z^{2} / n^{2}$. Since $n \propto L$, we have $K \propto 1 / L^{2}$.

q: Two electrons are revolving around a nucleus in circular orbits of radii $r$ and $4 r$. The ratio of their orbital speeds is:
s: Radius $r \propto n^{2}$, so $r_{2} / r_{1}=4 \Rightarrow\left(n_{2} / n_{1}\right)^{2}=4 \Rightarrow n_{2}=2 n_{1}$. Speed $v \propto 1 / n$. Therefore, $v_{1} / v_{2}=n_{2} / n_{1}=2 / 1$. The ratio is $2: 1$.

q: Which of the following transitions in a hydrogen atom emits a photon of the highest frequency?
s: Highest frequency corresponds to the highest energy difference ( $E=h \nu$ ). Transitions to a lower state emit photons. The energy gap between successive levels decreases as n increases. The largest energy gap is between $n=1$ and $n=2$. Therefore, the transition from $n=2$ to $n=1$ emits the photon with the highest frequency.

q: According to Bohr's theory, the moment of momentum (angular momentum) of an electron revolving in the second orbit of a hydrogen atom is:
s: The angular momentum is quantized as $L=\frac{n h}{2 \pi}$. For the second orbit, $n=2$, so $L=\frac{2 h}{2 \pi}=\frac{h}{\pi}$.

q: If an electron in a hydrogen atom jumps from the third orbit to the second orbit, it emits a photon of wavelength $\lambda$. If it jumps from the fourth orbit to the second orbit, the wavelength of the emitted photon will be:
s: For the transition (3 to 2): $\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{3^{2}}\right)=R\left(\frac{5}{36}\right)$. For the transition (4 to 2): $\frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}=R\left(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{4^{2}}\right)=R\left(\frac{3}{16}\right)$. Dividing the two: $\frac{\lambda^{\prime}}{\lambda}=\frac{5 R / 36}{3 R / 16}=\frac{5}{36} \times \frac{16}{3}=\frac{20}{27}$. So, $\lambda^{\prime}=\frac{20}{27} \lambda$.

q: The ratio of the magnitude of the potential energy of an electron in a Bohr orbit to the magnitude of its kinetic energy is N . The value of N is________. $\qquad$
s: In any Bohr orbit, $K=-E$ and $U=2 E$. From these, we can write $U=-2 K$. The ratio of the magnitudes is $|U| /|K|=|-2 K| /|K|=2$. Therefore, $\mathrm{N}=2$.

q: A quantity $\eta=\frac{\phi_{E}}{\phi_{B}}$ is defined as the ratio of electric flux to magnetic flux. The dimensions of $\eta$ are the same as that of:
s:
Electric Flux $\phi_{E}=\vec{E} \cdot \vec{A}$. Dimensions: $\left[\phi_{E}\right]=[E]\left[L^{2}\right]=\left[M L T^{-3} A^{-1}\right]\left[L^{2}\right]= \left[M L^{3} T^{-3} A^{-1}\right]$. Magnetic Flux $\phi_{B}=\vec{B} \cdot \vec{A}$. Dimensions: $\left[\phi_{B}\right]=[B]\left[L^{2}\right]= \left[M T^{-2} A^{-1}\right]\left[L^{2}\right]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2} A^{-1}\right]$. The ratio is:
$$
[\eta]=\left[\frac{\phi_{E}}{\phi_{B}}\right]=\frac{\left[M L^{3} T^{-3} A^{-1}\right]}{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2} A^{-1}\right]}=\left[L T^{-1}\right]
$$
This is the dimension of velocity.

subject: Physics
chapter: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
q: Which of the following equations is dimensionally correct? ( $q=$ charge, $B=$ magnetic field, $m=$ mass, $v=$ velocity, $r=$ radius)
s:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force for a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field: $F_{\text {magnetic }}=F_{\text {centripetal }} \Longrightarrow q v B=\frac{m v^{2}}{r}$. Solving for $r$ gives $r=\frac{m v}{q B}$. Let's check the dimensions of this correct physical equation. $[r]=[L]$. Dimensions of the right side:
$$
\left[\frac{m v}{q B}\right]=\frac{[M]\left[L T^{-1}\right]}{[A T]\left[M T^{-2} A^{-1}\right]}=\frac{\left[M L T^{-1}\right]}{\left[M T^{-1}\right]}=[L]
$$
The dimensions match, so the equation is dimensionally correct. The other options can be shown to be incorrect dimensionally. For example, option (a):
$$
\left[\frac{m v^{2}}{q B}\right]=\left[\frac{m v}{q B}\right] \cdot[v]=[L]\left[L T^{-1}\right]=\left[L^{2} T^{-1}\right] \neq[L]
$$

q: The dimensions of the ratio of magnetic flux ( $\phi_{B}$ ) and electric flux ( $\phi_{E}$ ) is:
s:
Magnetic Flux $\left[\phi_{B}\right]=[B \cdot$ Area $]=\left[M T^{-2} A^{-1}\right] \cdot\left[L^{2}\right]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2} A^{-1}\right]$. Electric Flux $\left[\phi_{E}\right]=[E \cdot$ Area $]=\left[M L T^{-3} A^{-1}\right] \cdot\left[L^{2}\right]=\left[M L^{3} T^{-3} A^{-1}\right]$. The ratio is:
$$
\left[\frac{\phi_{B}}{\phi_{E}}\right]=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2} A^{-1}\right]}{\left[M L^{3} T^{-3} A^{-1}\right]}=\left[L^{-1} T\right]
$$
This is the reciprocal of velocity.

q: The magnetic field B inside a long, solid, cylindrical conductor of radius 'a', carrying a current I , varies with the distance 'r' from its axis according to which relation?
s:
Using Ampere's circuital law for a point inside
the conductor ( $r<a$ ), the magnetic field is given by $B=\frac{\mu_{0} I
r}{2 \pi a^{2}}$. Since $\mu_{0}, I, a$ are constants, B is directly
proportional to r.

q: Two long, parallel wires carry currents of 8 A and 5 A in the same direction. The separation between the wires is 10 cm . At what distance from the 8 A wire is the net magnetic field zero?
s: Let the point be at a distance x from the 8 A wire. The fields will be in opposite directions. For the net field to be zero, $B_{1}=B_{2} \cdot \frac{\mu_{0} I_{1}}{2 \pi x}=\frac{\mu_{0} I_{2}}{2 \pi(d-x)} \Longrightarrow \frac{8}{x}= \frac{5}{10-x} .80-8 x=5 x \Longrightarrow 13 x=80 \Longrightarrow x=80 / 13 \approx 6.15 \mathrm{~cm}$.

q: A wire is bent to form a circular coil of 'n' turns. The magnetic field at the center for a given current is B . The wire is then rewound to form a coil of 'n/2' turns. The magnetic field at the center for the same current will be:
s: Length of wire $L=n(2 \pi r)=(n / 2)\left(2 \pi r^{\prime}\right)$, so the new radius $r^{\prime}=2 r$. The magnetic field is $B=\frac{n \mu_{0} I}{2 r}$. The new field is $B^{\prime}=\frac{(n / 2) \mu_{0} I}{2 r^{\prime}}=\frac{(n / 2) \mu_{0} I}{2(2 r)}= \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{n \mu_{0} I}{2 r}\right)=B / 4$.

s: $B=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi r}=\frac{\left(4 \pi \times 10^{-7}\right) \times 10}{2 \pi \times 0.2}=\frac{2 \times 10^{-6}}{0.2}=10 \times 10^{-6}=10^{-5} \mathrm{~T}$.

q: An electron is moving in a circle of radius $r$ with speed $v$. The equivalent magnetic field at the center of the circle is:
s: The equivalent current is $I=\frac{e}{T}=\frac{e}{2 \pi r / v}=\frac{e v}{2 \pi r}$. The magnetic field at the center of a circular loop is $B=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 r}=\frac{\mu_{0}}{2 r}\left(\frac{e v}{2 \pi r}\right)=\frac{\mu_{0} e v}{4 \pi r^{2}}$.

q:
The conductor ABCDE carries a current of 4 A . The field at the centre O of the circular part of it is
 [IMAGE: images/MB001331_1.webp]
s:
The magnetic field at the center of a circular arc is given by the formula:
$$
B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r} \theta
$$
Given values are:
- Current, $I=4 \mathrm{~A}$
- Radius, $r=3 \mathrm{~cm}=3 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}$
- Angle, $\theta=\pi$ radians (for a semicircle)
- Permeability of free space, $\mu_0=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~T} \cdot \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{A}$
Substitute the values into the formula:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& B=\frac{\left(4 \pi \times 10^{-7}\right) \times 4}{4 \pi \times\left(3 \times 10^{-2}\right)} \times \pi \\
& B=\frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 4}{12 \pi \times 10^{-2}} \times \pi \\
& B=\frac{16 \pi}{12} \times \frac{10^{-7}}{10^{-2}} \\
& B=\frac{4 \pi}{3} \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~T}
\end{aligned}
$$
The magnetic field at the center $O$ is $\frac{4 \pi}{3} \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~T}$.
This corresponds to option (b).

q: A current of I flows in a square loop of side 'a'. The magnetic field at the center of the loop is:
s: The field at the center due to one side is $B_{1}=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{4 \pi(a / 2)}\left(\sin 45^{\circ}+\sin 45^{\circ}\right)= \frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi a}\left(2 \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{2} \mu_{0} I}{2 \pi a}$. The total field from all four sides is $B_{\text {total }}=4 \times B_{1}=\frac{2 \sqrt{2} \mu_{0} I}{\pi a}$.

q: Two concentric coils of 10 turns each are placed in the same plane. Their radii are 20 cm and 40 cm , and they carry 0.2 A and 0.3 A respectively in opposite directions. The magnetic field at the center is:
s: $B_{1}=N_{1} \frac{\mu_{0} I_{1}}{2 R_{1}}=10 \frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 0.2}{2 \times 0.2}=20 \pi \times 10^{-7}$ T. $B_{2}=N_{2} \frac{\mu_{0} I_{2}}{2 R_{2}}=10 \frac{4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 0.3}{2 \times 0.4}= 15 \pi \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~T}$. Since the currents are in opposite directions, the fields subtract. $B_{n e t}=\left|B_{1}-B_{2}\right|=|20 \pi-15 \pi| \times 10^{-7}=5 \pi \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~T}$.

q: According to Biot-Savart's law, the magnetic field due to a small current element $d \vec{l}$ at a distance $\vec{r}$ is:
s: The law is stated as $d \vec{B}=\frac{\mu_{0}}{4 \pi} \frac{I(d \vec{l} \times \vec{r})}{r^{3}}$. In magnitude form, this becomes $d B=\frac{\mu_{0}}{4 \pi} \frac{I d l \sin \theta}{r^{2}}$. The magnetic field is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.

q: The magnetic field at the center of a circular current-carrying loop is B. If the current is doubled and the radius is halved, the new magnetic field will be:
s: $B=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 R}$. The new field $B^{\prime}=\frac{\mu_{0}(2 I)}{2(R / 2)}=4\left(\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 R}\right)=4 B$.

q: Which of the graphs shows the variation of magnetic induction $B$ with distance $r$ from a long wire carrying a current.
s:
The magnetic induction $B$ due to a long straight wire carrying a current is inversely proportional to the distance $r$ from the wire. This relationship is given by the formula $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}$, where $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space and $I$ is the current.
This means that as the distance $r$ increases, the magnetic induction $B$ decreases. The graph of an inverse relationship is a curve that approaches the axes but never touches them, which is shown in graph (c).

q: A long wire have a bend, forming a circular loop of radius R at some point. If the current in the wire is I, the magnetic field at the center C is:
s: The total magnetic field is the sum of the field due to the long straight part and the circular loop. The straight part can be treated as an infinite wire, producing a field $B_{\text {wire }}=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi R}$. The loop produces a field $B_{\text {loop }}=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 R}$. Both fields are in the same direction (into the page). $B_{\text {total }}=B_{\text {wire }}+B_{\text {loop }}=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi R}+\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 R}=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi R}(1+\pi)$.

s: The magnetic field lines from the first wire are circles around it, and the field lines from the second wire are circles around it. The magnetic field vectors from the two wires are perpendicular to each other at every point in space (except on the wires themselves). Two perpendicular non-zero vectors can never add up to zero.

Using $\pi=3$, B net $=\left(3 \times 10^{-6}\right) \frac{5}{3}=5 \times 10^{-6}$ T. Thus, $Y=5$.

q: Three long, straight, parallel wires, carrying currents of $30 \mathrm{~A}, 10 \mathrm{~A}$, and 20 A , are arranged in a line parallel to each other. The net force per unit length on the middle wire is $Z \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$. The value of Z is___________.
s: The force on the middle wire due to the left wire is repulsive (opposite currents): $F_{L}=\frac{\mu_{0} I_{1} I_{2}}{2 \pi d_{1}}=\frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 30 \times 10}{0.05}=12 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$ (directed to the right). The net force is the vector difference: $F_{\text {net }}=\left|F_{L}-F_{R}\right|=|12-4| \times 10^{-4}=8 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$. So, Z=8.

q:
Assertion (A): A proton projected along the axis of a current-carrying solenoid moves undeviated.
Reason (R): The magnetic force on a charged particle is zero if its velocity is parallel to the magnetic field.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
s: The magnetic field inside a long solenoid is directed along its axis. A proton projected along the axis has its velocity vector $\vec{v}$ parallel to the magnetic field vector $\vec{B}$. The magnetic force is given by $\vec{F}=q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$. Since $\vec{v}$ is parallel to $\vec{B}, \vec{v} \times \vec{B}=0$, and the force is zero. Thus, the proton moves undeviated. Both statements are true and R is the correct explanation of A .
