q: When a charged particle moves in a uniform magnetic field, its kinetic energy:
s: The magnetic force $\vec{F}=q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ is always perpendicular to the velocity $\vec{v}$ of the particle. The work done by the magnetic force is $W=\int \vec{F} \cdot d \vec{l}=\int \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} d t$. Since $\vec{F}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{v}, \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}=0$. Thus, the work done is zero, and by the work-energy theorem, the kinetic energy remains constant.

q: A particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ moves in a circular orbit of radius $r$ with kinetic energy E in a uniform magnetic field B . If the kinetic energy is doubled and the magnetic field is made four times stronger, the new radius will be:
s: The radius is given by $r=\frac{\sqrt{2 m E}}{q B}$. The new parameters are $E^{\prime}=2 E$ and $B^{\prime}=4 B$. The new radius is $r^{\prime}=\frac{\sqrt{2 m E^{\prime}}}{q B^{\prime}}=\frac{\sqrt{2 m(2 E)}}{q(4 B)}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} \frac{\sqrt{2 m E}}{q B}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} r=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{2}} r$.

q: The magnetic field inside a long solenoid carrying current I is B. If its length is doubled and the number of turns is also doubled, while the current remains the same, the new magnetic field will be:
s: $B=\mu_{0} n I=\mu_{0} \frac{N}{L} I$. The new parameters are $L^{\prime}=2 L$ and $N^{\prime}=2 N$. The new number of turns per unit length is $n^{\prime}=\frac{N^{\prime}}{L^{\prime}}=\frac{2 N}{2 L}=\frac{N}{L}=n$. The new field is $B^{\prime}=\mu_{0} n^{\prime} I=\mu_{0} n I=B$. The field remains the same.

q: A current-carrying square loop is placed in a non-uniform magnetic field that increases in magnitude along the positive x -axis. The loop is in the xy -plane. The net magnetic force on the loop is:[ Given : (i) the direction of $\vec{B}$ is along $\hat{k}$ (ii) the current in loop is in CW sense as seen from + Z side.]
s: Let the field be $\vec{B}=B(x) \hat{k}$. The forces on the sides parallel to the x-axis cancel out. The force on the side at larger $x$ will be stronger than the force on the side at smaller $x$. Using the right-hand rule, the force on the side with current in the +y direction (at larger x ) will be in the $-x$ direction. The force on the side with current in the $-y$ direction (at smaller $x$ ) will be in the +x direction. Since the field is stronger at larger x , the force in the -x direction will be greater, resulting in a net force along the negative x -axis.

q: The velocity $v$ of a particle depends on time $t$ as $v=\alpha t^{2}+\frac{\beta}{t+\gamma}$. The dimension of $\alpha \beta / \gamma$ is:
s:
Using the principle of homogeneity:
- In the term $(\gamma+t)$, dimensions of $\gamma$ must be equal to dimensions of $t$. So, $[\gamma]=[T]$.
- The term $\alpha t^{2}$ must have dimensions of velocity. $[\alpha]\left[T^{2}\right]=\left[L T^{-1}\right] \Longrightarrow [\alpha]=\left[L T^{-3}\right]$.
- The term $\frac{\beta}{t+\gamma}$ must have dimensions of velocity. $\frac{[\beta]}{[T]}=\left[L T^{-1}\right] \Longrightarrow[\beta]= [L]$.
The dimensions of the expression $\alpha \beta / \gamma$ are:
$$
\left[\frac{\alpha \beta}{\gamma}\right]=\frac{\left[L T^{-3}\right][L]}{[T]}=\left[L^{2} T^{-4}\right]
$$

subject: Physics
q: The equation of state for a real gas is given by $\left(P+\frac{a}{V^{2}}\right)(V-b)=R T$. The dimensions of the quantity $a b / R$ are:
s:
From the principle of homogeneity:
- The term $\frac{a}{V^{2}}$ has dimensions of pressure $P$. $[a]=[P]\left[V^{2}\right]=\left[M L^{-1} T^{-2}\right]\left[L^{6}\right]= \left[M L^{5} T^{-2}\right]$.
- The term $b$ has dimensions of volume $V .[b]=\left[L^{3}\right]$.
- The term $R T$ has dimensions of energy ( $P V$ ). So, $[R][K]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]$, which gives $[R]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2} K^{-1}\right]$.

The dimensions of the required quantity are:
$$
\left[\frac{a b}{R}\right]=\frac{\left[M L^{5} T^{-2}\right]\left[L^{3}\right]}{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2} K^{-1}\right]}=\frac{\left[M L^{8} T^{-2}\right]}{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2} K^{-1}\right]}=\left[L^{6} K\right]
$$

subject: Physics
q: The physical quantity having dimensions $\left[M^{-1} L^{-3} T^{3} A^{2}\right]$ is:
s:
We determine the dimensions for each of the given options.
- Resistance $(R):[R]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-3} A^{-2}\right]$.
- Permittivity $\left(\epsilon_{0}\right)$ : From Coulomb's Law, $F=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0}} \frac{q_{1} q_{2}}{r^{2}} .\left[\epsilon_{0}\right]=\frac{[q]^{2}}{[F][r]^{2}}= \frac{[A T]^{2}}{\left[M L T^{-2}\right][L]^{2}}=\left[M^{-1} L^{-3} T^{4} A^{2}\right]$.
- Resistivity ( $\rho$ ): From $R=\rho \frac{l}{A},[\rho]=\frac{[R][A]}{[l]}=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-3} A^{-2}\right]\left[L^{2}\right]}{[L]}=\left[M L^{3} T^{-3} A^{-2}\right]$. Electrical Conductivity ( $\sigma$ ) is the reciprocal of resistivity, so $[\sigma]=\frac{1}{[\rho]}= \left[M^{-1} L^{-3} T^{3} A^{2}\right]$.
- Permeability $\left(\mu_{0}\right)$ : From $F=\frac{\mu_{0}}{4 \pi} \frac{I_{1} I_{2} l}{r},\left[\mu_{0}\right]=\frac{[F][r]}{[I]^{2}[l]}=\frac{\left[M L T^{-2}\right][L]}{[A]^{2}[L]}= \left[M L T^{-2} A^{-2}\right]$.
The given dimension $\left[M^{-1} L^{-3} T^{3} A^{2}\right]$ matches that of Electrical Conductivity.

subject: Physics
q: The ratio of the dimensions of Planck's constant ( $h$ ) to that of the moment of inertia $(I)$ is the same as the dimension of:
s:
Planck's constant (h) has dimensions of angular momentum. From $E=h \nu$, $[h]=[E] /[\nu]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right] /\left[T^{-1}\right]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-1}\right]$. Moment of Inertia (I) has dimensions $\left[M L^{2}\right]$. The ratio is:
$$
\left[\frac{h}{I}\right]=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-1}\right]}{\left[M L^{2}\right]}=\left[T^{-1}\right]
$$
This is the dimension of frequency.

subject: Physics
q:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer.
List – I (Physical Quantity)List – II(Dimensional Formula)(A) Poynting Vector(I) $\left[M^{-1} L T^{2}\right]$(B) Compressibility(II) $\left[M L^{2} T^{-3} A^{-1}\right]$(C) Voltage(III) $[J]$ (candela)(D) Luminous Intensity(IV) $\left[M T^{-3}\right]$
s:
- (A) Poynting Vector ( $\vec{S}$ ) represents energy flux density (Power/Area). $[\vec{S}]=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-3}\right]}{\left[L^{2}\right]}=\left[M T^{-3}\right]$. So, A matches with IV.
- (B) Compressibility ( $K$ ) is the reciprocal of the Bulk Modulus ( $B$ ). $[B]= [$ Pressure $]=\left[M L^{-1} T^{-2}\right]$. So, $[K]=\frac{1}{[B]}=\left[M^{-1} L T^{2}\right]$. So, B matches with I.
- (C) Voltage ( $V$ ): From $W=q V,[V]=\frac{[W]}{[q]}=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]}{[A T]}=\left[M L^{2} T^{-3} A^{-1}\right]$. So, C matches with II.
- (D) Luminous Intensity is a base quantity with the dimension of $[J]$ and unit Candela. So, D matches with III.
The correct matching is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

subject: Physics
q: If Planck's constant (h), the speed of light in vacuum (c) and Newton's gravitational constant ( $G$ ) are taken as fundamental constants, then the dimensions of length (Planck Length) are proportional to:
s:
Let Length $L \propto h^{a} G^{b} c^{d}$. Writing the dimensions: $\left[L^{1}\right]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-1}\right]^{a}\left[M^{-1} L^{3} T^{-2}\right]^{b}\left[L T^{-1}\right]^{d} \left[M^{0} L^{1} T^{0}\right]=\left[M^{a-b} L^{2 a+3 b+d} T^{-a-2 b-d}\right]$ Equating the powers:
- M: $a-b=0 \Longrightarrow a=b$.
- T: $-a-2 b-d=0 \Longrightarrow-a-2 a-d=0 \Longrightarrow d=-3 a$.
- L: $2 a+3 b+d=1 \Longrightarrow 2 a+3 a-3 a=1 \Longrightarrow 2 a=1 \Longrightarrow a=1 / 2$.
So, $a=1 / 2, b=1 / 2$, and $d=-3 / 2$. The relation is $L \propto h^{1 / 2} G^{1 / 2} c^{-3 / 2} \propto \sqrt{\frac{h G}{c^{3}}}$.

subject: Physics
q: The pair of physical quantities having the same dimensional formula is:
s:
Let's find the dimensions of each quantity in the options.
- Impulse: $[J]=[F \cdot t]=\left[M L T^{-2}\right][T]=\left[M L T^{-1}\right]$. Surface Tension: $[S]=[F / L]=\left[M L T^{-2}\right] /[L]=\left[M T^{-2}\right]$. Not same.
- Angular Momentum: $[L]=[I \omega]=\left[M L^{2}\right]\left[T^{-1}\right]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-1}\right]$. Work: $[W]=[F \cdot d]=\left[M L T^{-2}\right][L]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]$. Not same.
- Work: $[W]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]$. Torque: $[\tau]=[r \times F]=[L]\left[M L T^{-2}\right]= \left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]$. Same dimensions.
- Young's Modulus: $[Y]=[$ Stress $/$ Strain $]=[F / A]=\left[M L^{-1} T^{-2}\right]$. Energy: $[E]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]$. Not same.

subject: Physics
q: In Bernoulli's equation $P+\frac{1}{2} \rho v^{2}+h \rho g=\mathrm{constant}$, the dimensional formula of the constant is the same as that of:
s:
According to the principle of homogeneity, all terms in the equation must have the same dimensions. Let's find the dimension of the first term, Pressure $(P)$. $[P]=\frac{[F]}{[A]}=\frac{\left[M L T^{-2}\right]}{\left[L^{2}\right]}=\left[M L^{-1} T^{-2}\right]$. Therefore, the constant on the right side must also have the dimension $\left[M L^{-1} T^{-2}\right]$. Now let's check the options
- Surface Tension: $[F / L]=\left[M T^{-2}\right]$.
- Energy Density: $\frac{[\text { Energy }]}{[\text { Volume }]}=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]}{\left[L^{3}\right]}=\left[M L^{-1} T^{-2}\right]$. This matches.
- Angular Momentum: $\left[M L^{2} T^{-1}\right]$.
- Latent Heat: $[$ Energy $/$ Mass $]=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]}{[M]}=\left[L^{2} T^{-2}\right]$.
The dimension of the constant matches that of Energy Density.

subject: Physics
q: If pressure $P$, velocity $V$ and time $T$ are taken as fundamental physical quantities, the dimensional formula of force is:
s:
Let the dimensional formula of force be $[F]=\left[P^{a} V^{b} T^{c}\right]$. Substituting the MLT dimensions: $\left[M L T^{-2}\right]=\left[M L^{-1} T^{-2}\right]^{a}\left[L T^{-1}\right]^{b}[T]^{c}\left[M^{1} L^{1} T^{-2}\right]=\left[M^{a} L^{-a+b} T^{-2 a-b+c}\right]$ Equating the exponents for each fundamental dimension:
- M: $a=1$
- $\mathrm{L}:-a+b=1 \Longrightarrow-1+b=1 \Longrightarrow b=2$
- T: $-2 a-b+c=-2 \Longrightarrow-2(1)-2+c=-2 \Longrightarrow-4+c=-2 \Longrightarrow c=2$
Thus, the dimensional formula of force is $\left[P V^{2} T^{2}\right]$.

subject: Physics
q: The dimensions of gravitational constant $G$ are $\left[M^{a} L^{b} T^{c}\right]$. The values of $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}$, and c are:
s: From Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, $F=G \frac{m_{1} m_{2}}{r^{2}}$. So, $G=\frac{F r^{2}}{m_{1} m_{2}}$. Writing the dimensions: $[G]=\frac{\left[M L T^{-2}\right]\left[L^{2}\right]}{[M][M]}=\left[M^{-1} L^{3} T^{-2}\right]$. Comparing with $\left[M^{a} L^{b} T^{c}\right]$, we get $a=-1, b=3, c=-2$.

subject: Physics
q: The dimensions of the ratio of angular momentum to linear momentum is the same as that of:
s:
The dimensional formula for angular momentum is $[L]=[I \omega]=\left[M L^{2}\right]\left[T^{-1}\right]= \left[M L^{2} T^{-1}\right]$. The dimensional formula for linear momentum is $[p]=[m v]= [M]\left[L T^{-1}\right]=\left[M L T^{-1}\right]$. The dimensions of their ratio are:
$$
\left[\frac{\text { Angular Momentum }}{\text { Linear Momentum }}\right]=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-1}\right]}{\left[M L T^{-1}\right]}=[L]
$$
This is the dimension of length.

subject: Physics
q: If force ( F ), length ( L ) and time ( T ) are chosen as the fundamental quantities, then the dimensions of mass are:
s:
We know the dimensional formula for force is $[F]=\left[M L T^{-2}\right]$. We need to express mass (M) in terms of F, L, and T. From the formula, we can write:
$$
[M]=\frac{[F]}{\left[L T^{-2}\right]}=\left[F L^{-1} T^{2}\right]
$$

subject: Physics
q: The dimensions of $\frac{1}{2} \epsilon_{0} E^{2}$ ( $\epsilon_{0}$ : permittivity of free space; E: electric field) is:
s: The quantity $\frac{1}{2} \epsilon_{0} E^{2}$ represents the energy density of the electric field. Energy density is energy per unit volume. Dimension of Energy is $\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]$. Dimension of Volume is $\left[L^{3}\right]$. Dimension of Energy Density $=\frac{[\text { Energy }]}{[\text { Volume }]}=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]}{\left[L^{3}\right]}= \left[M L^{-1} T^{-2}\right]$. This is also the dimension of pressure.

subject: Physics
q: The potential energy of a particle varies with position $x$ according to the relation $U(x)=\frac{A \sqrt{x}}{x+B}$. The dimensions of $A B$ are:
s:
From the principle of homogeneity:
- In the denominator $(x+B)$, the dimension of $B$ must be the same as the dimension of $x$. So, $[B]=[L]$.
- The dimension of $U(x)$ is potential energy, which is $\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]$.
- The dimension of the entire expression $\frac{A \sqrt{x}}{x+B}$ must be that of energy.
$$
\begin{aligned}
& {\left[\frac{A \sqrt{x}}{x+B}\right] }=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right] \\
& \frac{[A]\left[L^{1 / 2}\right]}{[L]}=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right] \\
& {[A]\left[L^{-1 / 2}\right] }=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right] \\
& {[A]=\left[M L^{2.5} T^{-2}\right]=\left[M L^{5 / 2} T^{-2}\right] }
\end{aligned}
$$
Now, the dimensions of the product $A B$ :
$$
[A B]=\left[M L^{5 / 2} T^{-2}\right] \cdot[L]=\left[M L^{7 / 2} T^{-2}\right]
$$

subject: Physics
q: In the equation $\left(P+\frac{a}{V^{2}}\right)(V-b)=$ constant, the units of $a$ are:
s: From the principle of homogeneity, the term $\frac{a}{V^{2}}$ must have the same units as pressure $P$. So, unit of $a=$ (unit of $P$ ) $\times$ (unit of $V^{2}$ ). In the CGS system, the unit of pressure is dyne $/ \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ and the unit of volume is $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$. Unit of $a=\left(\right.$ dyne $\left./ \mathrm{cm}^{2}\right) \times\left(\mathrm{cm}^{3}\right)^{2}=\left(\right.$ dyne $\left./ \mathrm{cm}^{2}\right) \times\left(\mathrm{cm}^{6}\right)=$ dyne $\cdot \mathrm{cm}^{4}$.

subject: Physics
q: The escape velocity $v_{e}$ from a planet depends on the universal gravitational constant $G$, the mass of the planet $M$, and its radius $R$ as $v_{e}=k G^{a} M^{b} R^{c}$, where $k$ is a dimensionless constant. The value of $2(a+b+c)$ is_________.
s:
The dimensional equation is $\left[v_{e}\right]=[G]^{a}[M]^{b}[R]^{c}$. Substituting the dimensions of each quantity: $\left[L T^{-1}\right]=\left[M^{-1} L^{3} T^{-2}\right]^{a}[M]^{b}[L]^{c}\left[M^{0} L^{1} T^{-1}\right]=\left[M^{-a+b} L^{3 a+c} T^{-2 a}\right]$ Equating the exponents for M, L, and T:
- For T: $-2 a=-1 \Longrightarrow a=1 / 2$.
- For M: $-a+b=0 \Longrightarrow b=a=1 / 2$.
- For L: $3 a+c=1 \Longrightarrow 3(1 / 2)+c=1 \Longrightarrow c=1-3 / 2=-1 / 2$.
The required value is $2(a+b+c)=2(1 / 2+1 / 2-1 / 2)=2(1 / 2)=1$.

subject: Physics
q: In a thermodynamic process, the pressure $P$ of a gas is related to its volume $V$ as $P=\frac{\alpha-t^{2}}{\beta V}$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants and $t$ is time. The dimensions of $\alpha / \beta$ are given by [ $M^{x} L^{y} T^{z}$ ]. The value of $x+y+z$ is________ .
s:
From the principle of homogeneity, in the numerator ( $\alpha-t^{2}$ ), the dimensions of $\alpha$ must be the same as the dimensions of $t^{2}$. So, $[\alpha]=\left[t^{2}\right]=\left[T^{2}\right]$. Now, considering the entire equation: $[P]=\frac{[\alpha]}{[\beta][V]}$ We can find the dimensions of $\beta:[\beta]=\frac{[\alpha]}{[P][V]}=\frac{\left[T^{2}\right]}{\left[M L^{-1} T^{-2}\right]\left[L^{3}\right]}=\frac{\left[T^{2}\right]}{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]}=\left[M^{-1} L^{-2} T^{4}\right]$. Now, we find the dimensions of the ratio $\alpha / \beta$ :
$$
\left[\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right]=\frac{\left[T^{2}\right]}{\left[M^{-1} L^{-2} T^{4}\right]}=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]
$$
Comparing this with $\left[M^{x} L^{y} T^{z}\right]$, we have $x=1, y=2, z=-2$. The required value is $x+y+z=1+2+(-2)=1$.

subject: Physics
q: The velocity $v$ of water waves may depend on their wavelength $\lambda$, the density of water $\rho$, and the acceleration due to gravity $g$. It is found that $v=k \lambda^{a} \rho^{b} g^{c}$. The value of $2(a+c)$ is_________.
s:
The relation is $v=k \lambda^{a} \rho^{b} g^{c}$. Writing the dimensions: $[v]=\left[L T^{-1}\right][\lambda]= [L][\rho]=\left[M L^{-3}\right][g]=\left[L T^{-2}\right]$ Substituting into the equation: $\left[L T^{-1}\right]= [L]^{a}\left[M L^{-3}\right]^{b}\left[L T^{-2}\right]^{c}\left[M^{0} L^{1} T^{-1}\right]=\left[M^{b} L^{a-3 b+c} T^{-2 c}\right]$ Equating powers:
- For M: $b=0$.
- For T: $-2 c=-1 \Longrightarrow c=1 / 2$.
- For L: $a-3 b+c=1 \Longrightarrow a-3(0)+1 / 2=1 \Longrightarrow a=1 / 2$.
So, $a=1 / 2, b=0, c=1 / 2$. The value of $2(a+c)=2(1 / 2+1 / 2)=2(1)=2$.

subject: Physics
q: The position of a particle is given by $x=A \sin (\omega t)+B t^{2}+C t \cos (\omega t)$ ($\omega$ is angular frequency and t is time). If the dimensions of $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ and C are $\left[L^{p} T^{q}\right],\left[L^{r} T^{s}\right]$ and $\left[L^{u} T^{v}\right]$ respectively, then the value of $p+q+r+s+u+v$ is________ .
s:
From the principle of homogeneity, each term on the right side must have the dimension of position, $[L]$.
- For the term $A \sin (\omega t)$ : The argument of sine must be dimensionless, so $[\omega t]=1 \Longrightarrow[\omega]=\left[T^{-1}\right]$. The term $A$ must have the dimension of position. So, $[A]=[L]=\left[L^{1} T^{0}\right]$. This gives $p=1, q=0$.
- For the term $B t^{2}:[B]\left[t^{2}\right]=[L] \Longrightarrow[B]\left[T^{2}\right]=[L] \Longrightarrow[B]=\left[L T^{-2}\right]= \left[L^{1} T^{-2}\right]$. This gives $r=1, s=-2$.
- For the term $C t \cos (\omega t)$ : The argument of cosine is dimensionless. The term Ct must have the dimension of position. So, $[C][t]=[L] \Longrightarrow [C][T]=[L] \Longrightarrow[C]=\left[L T^{-1}\right]=\left[L^{1} T^{-1}\right]$. This gives $u=1, v=-1$.
The required sum is $p+q+r+s+u+v=1+0+1+(-2)+1+(-1)= 1+1-2+1-1=0$.

subject: Physics
q: A quantity $\alpha$ is given by $\alpha=\frac{e^{2}}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} h c}$, where $e$ is the electric charge, $\epsilon_{0}$ is the permittivity of free space, $h$ is Planck's constant and $c$ is the speed of light. If the dimensional formula of $\alpha$ is expressed as $\left[M^{p} L^{q} T^{r}\right]$, the value of $p^{2}+q^{2}+r^{2}$ is_________ .
s: The problem states that the quantity $\alpha$ (the fine-structure constant) is dimensionless. A dimensionless quantity has no dependence on the fundamental dimensions of mass (M), length (L), and time (T). This means that the dimensional formula is $\left[M^{0} L^{0} T^{0}\right]$. By comparing this with the given formula $\left[M^{p} L^{q} T^{r}\right]$, we can equate the exponents: $p=0 q=0 r=0$ The required value is $p^{2}+q^{2}+r^{2}=0^{2}+0^{2}+0^{2}=0$.

subject: Physics
q:
Given two statements:
Statement I: The dimensions of Impulse and Linear Momentum are the same.
Statement II: The dimensions of Work and Torque are the same.
Choose the correct answer from the options below.
o: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
s:
Impulse $=$ Force $\times$ Time $=\left[M L T^{-2}\right][T]=\left[M L T^{-1}\right]$. 
Linear Momentum $=$ Mass $\times$ Velocity $=[M]\left[L T^{-1}\right]=\left[M L T^{-1}\right]$. 
So, Statement I is true. 
Work $=$ Force $\times$ Distance $=\left[M L T^{-2}\right][L]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]$. 
Torque $=$ Force $\times$ Perpendicular Distance $=\left[M L T^{-2}\right][L]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]$. So, Statement II is true.

subject: Physics
q: The dimensional formula for the universal gravitational constant ( G ) is:
s: From $F=G \frac{m_{1} m_{2}}{r^{2}}$, we get $G=\frac{F r^{2}}{m_{1} m_{2}} .[G]=\frac{\left[M L T^{-2}\right]\left[L^{2}\right]}{[M][M]}=\left[M^{-1} L^{3} T^{-2}\right]$.

subject: Physics
q: A physical quantity $P$ is given by the relation $P=\frac{a^{3} b^{2}}{\sqrt{c} d}$. If the percentage errors in the measurement of a, b, c, and d are $1 \%, 2 \%, 4 \%$, and $3 \%$ respectively, what is the percentage error in P ?
s:
$\frac{\Delta P}{P} \%=\left(3 \frac{\Delta a}{a}+2 \frac{\Delta b}{b}+\frac{1}{2} \frac{\Delta c}{c}+\frac{\Delta d}{d}\right) \%$. 
%Error $=(3 \times 1 \%)+(2 \times 2 \%)+ \left(\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \%\right)+(1 \times 3 \%)=3 \%+4 \%+2 \%+3 \%=12 \%$.

subject: Physics
q:
Match List I with List II.
List IList IIA. Pressure Gradient(I) $\left[M L T^{-3}\right]$B. Power(II) $\left[M L^{-2} T^{-2}\right]$C. Impulse(III) $\left[M L^{2} T^{-3}\right]$D. Force Constant (k)(IV) $\left[M L T^{-1}\right]$(V) $\left[M T^{-2}\right]$
Choose the correct option.
s:
(A) Pressure Gradient $=\frac{\text { Pressure }}{\text { distance }}=\frac{M L^{-1} T^{-2}}{L}=\left[M L^{-2} T^{-2}\right]$. 
(B) Power $=\left[M L^{2} T^{-3}\right]$. 
(C) Impulse $=\left[M L T^{-1}\right]$. 
(D) Force Constant from $\mathrm{F}=\mathrm{kx}$ is $k=\frac{F}{x}= \frac{M L T^{-2}}{L}=\left[M T^{-2}\right]$.

subject: Physics
q: The dimensions of $\frac{1}{2} \epsilon_{0} E^{2}$ ( $\epsilon_{0}$ : permittivity of free space, E: electric field) are:
s: The quantity $\frac{1}{2} \epsilon_{0} E^{2}$ represents energy density (Energy/Volume). Dimensions $= \frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]}{\left[L^{3}\right]}=\left[M L^{-1} T^{-2}\right]$.

subject: Physics
q: The density of a cube is measured by measuring its mass and the length of its side. If the maximum errors in the measurement of mass and length are $3 \%$ and $2 \%$ respectively, the maximum error in the measurement of density will be:
s: Density $\rho=\frac{M}{V}=\frac{M}{L^{3}} \cdot \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \%=\left(\frac{\Delta M}{M}+3 \frac{\Delta L}{L}\right) \%=(3 \%+3 \times 2 \%)=9 \%$.

subject: Physics
q: Which of the following pairs does NOT have the same dimensions?
s:
Dimensions of Work are $\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]$. Dimensions of Power are $\left[M L^{2} T^{-3}\right]$. They are different. 
All other pairs have identical dimensions.

subject: Physics
q: The dimensional formula for thermal conductivity is: (Thermal conductivity is given by $k = \frac{Q \cdot d}{A \cdot \Delta T \cdot t}$, where $Q$ is heat transferred, $d$ is thickness, $A$ is area, $\Delta T$ is temperature difference, and $t$ is time.)
s:
From the heat flow equation $\frac{d Q}{d t}=-K A \frac{d T}{d x}$, we get $K=\frac{(d Q / d t) \cdot d x}{A \cdot d T}$. 
$[K]=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-3}\right][L]}{\left[L^{2}\right][K]}=\left[M L T^{-3} K^{-1}\right]$.

subject: Physics
q: The resistance of a wire is given as $R=(100 \pm 2) \Omega$ and the current through it is $I=(10 \pm 0.5) A$. The percentage error in the measurement of Voltage ( $V=I R$ ) is:
s:
$\frac{\Delta V}{V} \%=\left(\frac{\Delta I}{I}+\frac{\Delta R}{R}\right) \% . \frac{\Delta R}{R} \%=\frac{2}{100} \times 100 \%=2 \% . \frac{\Delta I}{I} \%=\frac{0.5}{10} \times 100 \%=5 \%$. 
Total percentage error $=2 \%+5 \%=7 \%$.

subject: Physics
q: The dimensions of the ratio of magnetic flux ( $\Phi$ ) to permeability ( $\mu_{0}$ ) are:
s:
$[\Phi]=\left[M L^{2} T^{-2} I^{-1}\right]$. Permeability from $B=\frac{\mu_{0} I}{2 \pi r}$ gives $\left[\mu_{0}\right]=\frac{[B][L]}{[I]}= \frac{\left[M T^{-2} I^{-1}\right][L]}{[I]}=\left[M L T^{-2} I^{-2}\right]$. 
Ratio $=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2} I^{-1}\right]}{\left[M L T^{-2} I^{-2}\right]}=[L I]$.

subject: Physics
q: In an experiment, the time period of a simple pendulum was observed to be T . The length of the pendulum is measured with an error of $1 \%$ and the acceleration due to gravity is known with an error of $2 \%$. The percentage error in T is:
s: $T=2 \pi \sqrt{L / g}$. So $T \propto L^{1 / 2} g^{-1 / 2} . \frac{\Delta T}{T} \%=\left(\frac{1}{2} \frac{\Delta L}{L}+\frac{1}{2} \frac{\Delta g}{g}\right) \%=\left(\frac{1}{2} \times 1 \%+\right. \left.\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \%\right)=0.5 \%+1 \%=1.5 \%$.

subject: Physics
q: The dimensional formula of specific heat capacity is:
s: From $Q=m c \Delta T$, we get $c=\frac{Q}{m \Delta T} .[c]=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]}{[M][K]}=\left[M^{0} L^{2} T^{-2} K^{-1}\right]$.

subject: Physics
q: The error in the measurement of the radius of a sphere is $0.5 \%$. The percentage error in the calculation of its surface area is:
s: Surface area $A=4 \pi r^{2} . \frac{\Delta A}{A} \%=2 \frac{\Delta r}{r} \%=2 \times 0.5 \%=1.0 \%$.

subject: Physics
q: The dimensions of $(L / R)$, where L is inductance and R is resistance, are the same as that of:
s: In an L-R circuit, the time constant is given by $\tau=L / R$. Thus, $\mathrm{L} / \mathrm{R}$ has the dimensions of time, $[T]$.

subject: Physics
q: A student measures the length of a rod and writes it as 3.50 cm . Which instrument did he use to measure it?
o: A vernier caliper where 10 divisions in vernier scale match with 9 divisions in main scale and main scale has 10 divisions in 1 cm
A screw gauge having 100 divisions in the circular scale and a pitch of 1 mm
A vernier caliper where 20 divisions in vernier scale match with 19 divisions in main scale and main scale has 10 divisions in 1 cm
s: The measurement 3.50 cm has two decimal places, which means the least count is 0.01 cm . For option (b), $1 \mathrm{MSD}=1 / 10 \mathrm{~cm}=0.1 \mathrm{~cm}$. Least Count $=1 \mathrm{MSD}-1 \mathrm{VSD}=1 \mathrm{MSD}-(9 / 10) \mathrm{MSD}=(1 / 10) \mathrm{MSD}=(1 / 10)^{*} 0.1 \mathrm{~cm}=0.01$ cm . This matches the precision of the measurement.

subject: Physics
q: Dimensions of capacitance C in terms of $\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{L}, \mathrm{T}$, and I (Current) are:
s: $C=Q / V . \quad Q=I t . \quad V=W / Q$. So $C=Q^{2} / W=(I t)^{2} / W . \quad[C]= \frac{\left[I^{2} T^{2}\right]}{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]}=\left[M^{-1} L^{-2} T^{4} I^{2}\right]$.

subject: Physics
q: The length, breadth and thickness of a rectangular sheet of metal are $4.234 \mathrm{~m}, 1.005 \mathrm{~m}$, and 2.01 cm respectively. The volume of the sheet to correct significant figures is:
s: $l=4.234 \mathrm{~m}$ ( 4 s.f.), $\mathrm{b}=1.005 \mathrm{~m}$ ( 4 s.f.), $\mathrm{t}=2.01 \mathrm{~cm}=0.0201 \mathrm{~m}$ ( 3 s.f.). Volume $=l \times b \times t=4.234 \times 1.005 \times 0.0201=0.085536 \ldots \mathrm{~m}^{3}$. The result must be rounded to the minimum number of significant figures, which is 3 . So, Volume $= 0.0855 \mathrm{~m}^{3}$.

subject: Physics
q: If the error in the measurement of the momentum of a particle is $(+100 \%)$, then the error in the measurement of kinetic energy is:
s: Kinetic Energy $K=p^{2} / 2 m$. Let initial momentum be $p$. Final momentum $p^{\prime}=p+100 \%$ of $p=2 p$. Initial K.E. $K=p^{2} / 2 m$. Final K.E. $K^{\prime}=(2 p)^{2} / 2 m= 4\left(p^{2} / 2 m\right)=4 K$. Percentage error $=\frac{K^{\prime}-K}{K} \times 100 \%=\frac{4 K-K}{K} \times 100 \%=300 \%$.

subject: Physics
q: The dimensional formula of electric potential is:
s: Electric Potential V $=$ Work $/$ Charge $=\mathrm{W} / \mathrm{Q} .[V]=\frac{\left[M L^{2} T^{-2}\right]}{[I T]}=\left[M L^{2} T^{-3} I^{-1}\right]$.

subject: Physics
q: The focal length of a convex lens is measured using the formula $\frac{1}{f}= \frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}$. The percentage errors in u and v are $2 \%$ each. The percentage error in f is:
o: Can't be determined without values of $u$ and $v$.
s: Differentiating the lens formula, we get $-\frac{\Delta f}{f^{2}}=-\frac{\Delta v}{v^{2}}-\left(-\frac{\Delta u}{u^{2}}\right)$. For maximum error, $\frac{\Delta f}{f^{2}}=\frac{\Delta u}{u^{2}}+\frac{\Delta v}{v^{2}} . \Delta f=f^{2}\left(\frac{\Delta u}{u^{2}}+\frac{\Delta v}{v^{2}}\right) . \frac{\Delta f}{f}=f\left(\frac{\Delta u}{u^{2}}+\frac{\Delta v}{v^{2}}\right)=\left(\frac{u v}{u-v}\right)\left(\frac{\Delta u}{u^{2}}+\right. \frac{\Delta v}{v^{2}}$ ). The error depends on the values of u and v .

subject: Physics
q: A physical quantity Z is related to three variables $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$, and C by the equation $Z=\frac{A^{2} \sqrt{B}}{C^{3}}$. The percentage errors in the measurement of $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$, and C are $2 \%, 4 \%$, and $1 \%$ respectively. The percentage error in Z is________ (in %).
s:
The percentage error in Z is given by: $\frac{\Delta Z}{Z} \%=\left(2 \frac{\Delta A}{A}+\frac{1}{2} \frac{\Delta B}{B}+3 \frac{\Delta C}{C}\right) \%$. $\%$ 
Error $=(2 \times 2 \%)+\left(\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \%\right)+(3 \times 1 \%)=4 \%+2 \%+3 \%=9 \%$.

subject: Physics
q: The time period of a mass suspended from a spring is $T=2 \pi \sqrt{m / k}$, where k is the spring constant. In an experiment, the error in the measurement of mass ' $m$ ' is $2 \%$ and the error in the measurement of the time period ' $T$ ' is $1 \%$. The percentage error in the calculated value of the spring constant ' $k$ ' is_________ (in %).
s: From the formula, $T^{2}=4 \pi^{2} \frac{m}{k}$, so $k=\frac{4 \pi^{2} m}{T^{2}}$. The percentage error in k is given by: $\frac{\Delta k}{k} \%=\left(\frac{\Delta m}{m}+2 \frac{\Delta T}{T}\right) \%=(2 \%+2 \times 1 \%)=2 \%+2 \%=4 \%$.

subject: Physics
q: The resistance of a wire is given by $R=\rho \frac{l}{\pi r^{2}}$. The percentage error in the measurement of length ' $l$ ' is $1 \%$, and in the radius ' $r$ ' is $2 \%$. Assuming the resistivity $\rho$ is constant, the percentage error in the resistance R is______ (in %).
s: The percentage error in R is given by: $\frac{\Delta R}{R} \%=\left(\frac{\Delta l}{l}+2 \frac{\Delta r}{r}\right) \%=(1 \%+ 2 \times 2 \%)=1 \%+4 \%=5 \%$.

subject: Physics
q: For a simple pendulum, the length is measured as ( $20.0 \pm 0.2$ ) cm and the time for 50 oscillations is measured as $(40 \pm 1) \mathrm{s}$. The maximum percentage error in ' $g$ ' is______ (in %).
s: $g=4 \pi^{2} \frac{L}{T^{2}}$. $\frac{\Delta L}{L} \%=\frac{0.2}{20.0} \times 100 \%=1 \%$. Time period $T=\frac{40}{50}=0.8 \mathrm{~s}$. Error in time period $\Delta T=\frac{\text { resolution }}{\text { oscillations }}=\frac{1}{50}=0.02$ s. $\frac{\Delta T}{T} \%=\frac{0.02}{0.8} \times 100 \%=2.5 \%$. $\frac{\Delta g}{g} \%=\frac{\Delta L}{L} \%+2 \frac{\Delta T}{T} \%=1 \%+2(2.5 \%)=1 \%+5 \%=6 \%$.

subject: Physics
q: The number of significant figures in the numbers $4.8000 \times 10^{4}, 0.04080$, and 3.010 are $\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y}$, and z respectively. Find the value of $\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y}-\mathrm{z}$.
s:
For $4.8000 \times 10^{4}$ : All trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant. So, $\mathrm{x}=5$. For 0.04080: Leading zeros are not significant. 
Trailing zero after the decimal is significant. So, $\mathrm{y}=4(4,0,8,0)$. For 3.010: Zeros between non-zero digits and trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant. 
So, $\mathrm{z}=4 . \mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y}-\mathrm{z} =5+4-4=5$.

subject: Physics
q: In a Vernier caliper, N divisions of the Vernier scale coincide with (N-1) divisions of the main scale. If one main scale division is 1 mm , the least count of the instrument is:
s: Least Count $(\mathrm{LC})=1 \mathrm{MSD}-1 \mathrm{VSD}$. Given, N VSD $=(\mathrm{N}-1) \mathrm{MSD} \Longrightarrow 1 \mathrm{VSD}=\frac{N-1}{N} \mathrm{MSD} . \mathrm{LC}=1 \mathrm{MSD}-\frac{N-1}{N} \mathrm{MSD}=\left(1-\frac{N-1}{N}\right) \mathrm{MSD}=\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{MSD}$. Since $1 \mathrm{MSD}=1 \mathrm{~mm}, \mathrm{LC}=\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{~mm}$.

subject: Physics
q: The least count of a Screw gauge is 0.02 mm . If each division on the main scale is 0.5 mm , how many divisions are there on the Screw gauge?
s: Let N be the number of divisions on the Vernier scale. $\mathrm{LC}=\frac{\text { Value of } 1 \mathrm{MSD}}{\text { Number of divisions on Vernier scale }} 0.02 \mathrm{~mm}=\frac{0.5 \mathrm{~mm}}{N} \Longrightarrow N=\frac{0.5}{0.02}=25$.

subject: Physics
q: When the jaws of a Vernier caliper are closed, the zero of the Vernier scale is to the left of the main scale zero, and the 7th division of the Vernier scale coincides with a main scale division. If the least count is 0.1 mm , the zero error is:
s: The error is negative because the Vernier zero is to the left. For negative error, if there are 10 divisions on the Vernier scale, Error $=-($ Total VSD - Coinciding VSD) $\times$ LC . Error $=-(10-7) \times 0.1 \mathrm{~mm}=-0.3 \mathrm{~mm}$.

subject: Physics
q: A spherometer has 100 divisions on its circular scale. The pitch of the spherometer is 0.5 mm . What is the least count of the spherometer in cm ?
s:
The formula for the least count of a spherometer is:
Least Count = Number of divisions on circular scalePitch
Given values:
- Pitch $=0.5 \mathrm{~mm}$
- Number of divisions on circular scale $=100$
First, convert the pitch from mm to cm : Pitch $=0.5 \mathrm{~mm}=0.05 \mathrm{~cm}$
Now, substitute the values into the formula: Least Count $=1000.05 \mathrm{~cm}$ Least Count $=0.0005 \mathrm{~cm}$

subject: Physics
q: A Vernier caliper has 1 mm marks on the main scale. It has 20 equal divisions on the Vernier scale which match with 19 main scale divisions. The least count of the Vernier caliper is:
s:
$$LC = 1MSD - 1VSD.20VSD = 19MSD$$$$1VSD = \frac{{19}}{{20}}MSD$$
$$LC = \left( {1 - \frac{{19}}{{20}}} \right)MSD = \frac{1}{{20}}MSD = \frac{1}{{20}} \times 1\;mm = 0.05\;mm$$

subject: Physics
q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The least count of a Vernier caliper is the difference between one main scale division and one Vernier scale division.
Statement II: A zero error in a Vernier caliper is always subtracted from the observed reading to get the corrected reading.
o: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
s: Statement I is the definition of least count. Statement II is false because the zero correction is subtracted, and zero correction has the opposite sign to the zero error. (Corrected Reading = Observed Reading - Zero Error). So a negative error is added.

subject: Physics
q: The smallest division on the main scale of a Vernier caliper is 0.5 mm . 10 Vernier scale divisions coincide with 9 main scale divisions. While measuring the length of a key, the zero of the Vernier lies between 3.2 cm and 3.25 cm . The 7th division of the Vernier coincides with a main scale division. The length of the key is:
s: $1 \mathrm{MSD}=0.5 \mathrm{~mm}=0.05 \mathrm{~cm} . \mathrm{LC}=(1 / 10) \mathrm{MSD}=0.005 \mathrm{~cm} . \mathrm{MSR}$ is the reading just before the Vernier zero, which is 3.2 cm . VSC $=7$. Total Reading $=3.2 \mathrm{~cm}+(7 \times 0.005 \mathrm{~cm})=3.2 \mathrm{~cm}+0.035 \mathrm{~cm}=3.235 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: In a Vernier caliper, n divisions of its main scale coincide with ( $\mathrm{n}+1$ ) divisions of its Vernier scale. If one division of the main scale is 'a' units, then the least count of the instrument is:
s: $(\mathrm{n}+1) \mathrm{VSD}=\mathrm{n} \mathrm{MSD} \Longrightarrow 1 \mathrm{VSD}=\frac{n}{n+1} \mathrm{MSD} . \mathrm{LC}=1 \mathrm{MSD}-1 \mathrm{VSD} =\left(1-\frac{n}{n+1}\right) \mathrm{MSD}=\frac{1}{n+1} \mathrm{MSD}=\frac{a}{n+1}$.

subject: Physics
q: A traveling microscope has 20 divisions per cm on its main scale. The Vernier scale has 50 divisions which coincide with 49 divisions of the main scale. The least count of the microscope is:
s: $1 \mathrm{MSD}=\frac{1}{20} \mathrm{~cm}=0.05 \mathrm{~cm} . \mathrm{LC}=\frac{1}{N} \mathrm{MSD}=\frac{1}{50} \times 0.05 \mathrm{~cm}=0.001 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: The diameter of a steel ball is measured using a Vernier caliper which has divisions of 0.1 cm on its main scale and 10 divisions on its Vernier scale that match 9 divisions on the main scale. Three such measurements for the diameter are $0.54 \mathrm{~cm}, 0.55 \mathrm{~cm}$, and 0.53 cm . The average corrected diameter if the zero error is -0.03 cm is:
s: Average observed diameter $=\frac{0.54+0.55+0.53}{3}=0.54 \mathrm{~cm}$. Corrected Reading $=$ Observed Reading - Zero Error $=0.54 \mathrm{~cm}-(-0.03 \mathrm{~cm})=0.57 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: A Vernier caliper has a least count of 0.01 cm . When measuring the internal diameter of a beaker, the MSR is 4.5 cm and the VSC is 3 . What is the internal diameter?
s: Reading $=\mathrm{MSR}+\mathrm{VSC} \times \mathrm{LC}=4.5 \mathrm{~cm}+3 \times 0.01 \mathrm{~cm}=4.53 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: Assertion (A): A Vernier caliper with 20 VSD matching 19 MSD is more precise than one with 10 VSD matching 9 MSD , assuming 1 MSD is the same for both. Reason (R): Precision is determined by the least count, and a smaller least count means higher precision.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
s: Case 1: $\mathrm{LC}=(1 / 20) \mathrm{MSD}$. Case 2: $\mathrm{LC}=(1 / 10) \mathrm{MSD}$. LC in case 1 is smaller, so it's more precise. Reason (R) correctly explains this.

subject: Physics
q: A spherometer has a pitch of 0.1 cm and 50 divisions on its circular scale. What is the least count of the spherometer?
s:
The least count of a spherometer is calculated using the formula:
Least Count = Number of circular scale divisionsPitch
Given:
- Pitch $=0.1 \mathrm{~cm}$
- Number of circular scale divisions $=50$

subject: Physics
q: The value of one main scale division is ' x ' $\mathrm{cm} . \mathrm{N}$ divisions of the main scale coincide with ( $\mathrm{N}+1$ ) divisions of the vernier scale. The least count of the vernier calipers is:
s: $(\mathrm{N}+1) \mathrm{VSD}=\mathrm{N}$ MSD. So, $1 \mathrm{VSD}=\frac{N}{N+1} \mathrm{MSD} . \mathrm{LC}=1 \mathrm{MSD}-1 \mathrm{VSD} =\left(1-\frac{N}{N+1}\right) \mathrm{MSD}=\frac{1}{N+1} \mathrm{MSD}=\frac{x}{N+1}$.

subject: Physics
q: A Vernier caliper's main scale is marked in millimeters. 20 of its Vernier scale divisions are equal in length to 19 mm . When measuring the length of a cube's side, the reading is 2.48 cm . What is the Vernier Scale Coincidence (VSC)?
s:
$$1MSD = 1\;mm.20VSD = 19MSD = 19\;mm.$$$$LC = 1MSD - 1VSD = 1\;mm - (19/20)mm$$$$ = 1/20\;mm = 0.05\;mm = 0.005\;cm$$
Reading = MSR + VSC $\times \mathrm{LC} . \mathrm{MSR}=2.4 \mathrm{~cm}$ (the reading just before the Vernier zero). 
$2.48 \mathrm{~cm}=2.4 \mathrm{~cm}$ + VSC $\times 0.005 \mathrm{~cm} .0 .08 \mathrm{~cm}=$ VSC $\times 0.005 \mathrm{~cm} \Longrightarrow$ VSC $=0.08 / 0.005=16$.

subject: Physics
q: The internal diameter of a hollow tube is measured. The reading on the main scale is 1.1 cm , and the fourth division on the Vernier scale coincides with a mark on the main scale. Given that the LC is 0.1 mm , and the instrument has a positive zero error of 0.04 cm , the correct internal diameter is:
s: $\mathrm{LC}=0.1 \mathrm{~mm}=0.01 \mathrm{~cm}$. Observed reading $=\mathrm{MSR}+\mathrm{VSC} \times \mathrm{LC}= 1.1 \mathrm{~cm}+4 \times 0.01 \mathrm{~cm}=1.14 \mathrm{~cm}$. Zero error $=+0.04 \mathrm{~cm}$. Corrected reading $=$ Observed reading - Zero error $=1.14 \mathrm{~cm}-0.04 \mathrm{~cm}=1.10 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: The length of a simple pendulum is measured to be 90.54 cm using a Vernier caliper. The least count of the caliper is:
s: The measurement is given to two decimal places in centimeters (90.54 $\mathrm{cm})$. This implies that the smallest value the instrument can measure is 0.01 cm , which is its least count.

subject: Physics
q: In a traveling microscope, 1 cm of the main scale is divided into 20 parts. If 20 VSD coincide with 19 MSD , the least count of the instrument is:
s: 1 MSD $=1 / 20 \mathrm{~cm}=0.05 \mathrm{~cm}$. Number of Vernier divisions $\mathrm{N}=20$. LC $=(1 / \mathrm{N}) \mathrm{MSD}=(1 / 20) * 0.05 \mathrm{~cm}=0.0025 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: If 10 main scale divisions of a Vernier caliper are equal to 8 Vernier scale divisions, and $1 \mathrm{MSD}=1 \mathrm{~mm}$, what is the least count?
s: $8 \mathrm{VSD}=10 \mathrm{MSD} \Longrightarrow 1 \mathrm{VSD}=10 / 8 \mathrm{MSD}=1.25 \mathrm{MSD}$. Since VSD ¿ MSD, this is a retrograde Vernier. LC = - 1 VSD - $1 \mathrm{MSD}-=-1.25 \mathrm{MSD}-1 \mathrm{MSD}-=0.25 \mathrm{MSD}=0.25^{*} 1 \mathrm{~mm}=0.25 \mathrm{~mm}$.

subject: Physics
q: To measure the depth of a beaker, a Vernier caliper is used. The main scale reading is 8.6 cm , and the 8th Vernier division coincides. The least count is 0.01 cm . The depth is:
s: Depth $=\mathrm{MSR}+\mathrm{VSC} \times \mathrm{LC}=8.6 \mathrm{~cm}+8 \times 0.01 \mathrm{~cm}=8.68 \mathrm{~cm}$.

subject: Physics
q: In a Vernier caliper, 1 cm on the main scale is divided into 10 parts. 10 divisions of the Vernier scale coincide with 9 divisions of the main scale. When measuring the diameter of a sphere, the main scale reads 1.2 cm and the 5th Vernier division coincides. The diameter of the sphere is found to be $\mathrm{X} / 100 \mathrm{~cm}$. Find the value of $X$.
s: $1 \mathrm{MSD}=1 / 10 \mathrm{~cm}=0.1 \mathrm{~cm}=1 \mathrm{~mm} . \mathrm{LC}=(1 / 10) \mathrm{MSD}=(1 / 10) * 0.1 \mathrm{~cm}=0.01 \mathrm{~cm}$. Diameter $=\mathrm{MSR}+\mathrm{VSC} \times \mathrm{LC}=1.2 \mathrm{~cm}+5 \times 0.01 \mathrm{~cm}=1.25$ cm . Given diameter $=\mathrm{X} / 100 \mathrm{~cm}$. So, $1.25=\mathrm{X} / 100 \Longrightarrow \mathrm{X}=125$.

subject: Physics
q: The main scale of a Vernier caliper has 10 divisions in 1 cm .50 divisions of the Vernier scale coincide with 49 divisions of the main scale. When the jaws are closed, the zero of the Vernier scale is to the right of the main scale zero, and the 2nd division of the Vernier scale coincides. The zero error is $\mathrm{Y} \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~cm}$. Find Y .
s: $1 \mathrm{MSD}=0.1 \mathrm{~cm} . \mathrm{LC}=(1 / 50) \mathrm{MSD}=0.002 \mathrm{~cm}$. Error is positive. Zero Error $=+\mathrm{VSC} \times \mathrm{LC}=+2 \times 0.002 \mathrm{~cm}=+0.004 \mathrm{~cm}$. We are given the error is $\mathrm{Y} \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~cm} .0 .004=Y \times 10^{-4} \Longrightarrow Y=0.004 / 10^{-4}=40$.

subject: Physics
q: A Vernier caliper has a least count of 0.05 mm . The value of one main scale division is 1 mm . If N divisions of the Vernier scale coincide with ( $\mathrm{N}-1$ ) divisions of the main scale, what is the value of N ?
s: $\mathrm{LC}=\frac{1 \mathrm{MSD}}{N} .0 .05 \mathrm{~mm}=\frac{1 \mathrm{~mm}}{N} . N=\frac{1}{0.05}=20$.

subject: Physics
q: Measurement using a Vernier caliper gives a reading of 3.56 cm . The instrument has a positive zero error of 0.06 cm . The corrected length, in millimeters, is______. $\qquad$
s:
Corrected length $=3.56 \mathrm{~cm}-0.06 \mathrm{~cm}=3.50 \mathrm{~cm}$. 
In millimeters, length $=3.50 \mathrm{~cm} \times 10 \mathrm{~mm} / \mathrm{cm}=35 \mathrm{~mm}$.

subject: Physics
q: The side of a cube is measured with a Vernier caliper. $1 \mathrm{MSD}=1 \mathrm{~mm}$. $10 \mathrm{VSD}=9 \mathrm{MSD}$. The MSR is 2.0 cm and the 4th VSD coincides. The volume of the cube is found to be $\mathrm{X} \mathrm{cm}^{3}$. Find the value of X , rounding your final answer to the nearest integer.
s:
$\mathrm{LC}=(1 / 10) \mathrm{MSD}=0.1 \mathrm{~mm}=0.01 \mathrm{~cm}$. 
Side length (a) = MSR + VSC $\times \mathrm{LC}=2.0 \mathrm{~cm}+4 \times 0.01 \mathrm{~cm}=2.04 \mathrm{~cm}$. Volume $=a^{3}=(2.04)^{3} \mathrm{~cm}^{3}=8.489 \ldots \mathrm{cm}^{3}$. 
Rounding to the nearest integer, $\mathrm{X}=8$.
